name: Matt Pocock
domain: TypeScript and engineering practice: type safety, inference, avoiding any, generics, error handling, library and API design, teaching developers, and working with AI coding agents

sources.title: How Matt Pocock fixes the PR bottleneck: automated checks, automated review, then lighter human review
sources.originalTitle: Fixing the PR Bottleneck — Matt Pocock, AIHero
sources.summary: Matt argues AI-driven PR volume needs "brakes" so a software factory doesn't become a slop cannon. He layers cheap automated checks, a separate coding-standards reviewer agent that commits fixes, and a human-friendly PR (merge danger, diagrams, retro) so human review gets faster.

principles.text: Layer automated checks, automated review, and human review so human review gets faster, not skipped.
principles.quote: the goal here is to make human review faster by leaning on those first two phases.

principles.text: Checks are cheap, so add many, but a green CI can lie; review layers exist to detect those lies.
principles.quote: Does a green CI mean that the code is ready for merge? No, it does not.

principles.text: Tautological and structure-sensitive tests restate the implementation and break on any rename or refactor.
principles.quote: They're very sensitive to the actual internal workings of the system.

principles.text: Design deep modules (simple interface, big hidden implementation) so agents test at the interface, not internals.
principles.quote: you're going to have fewer structure sensitive tests because you're hiding more of the implementation behind that interface.

principles.text: Keep coding standards out of the overloaded implementer; enforce them in a separate review subagent that commits fixes.
principles.quote: don't put coding standards in your implementer agent.

principles.text: Treat the process producing code as reviewable too: never write the same review comment twice, use a retro to compound.
principles.quote: you never want to write the same comment twice.

sources.title: Software fundamentals matter more than ever: why specs-to-code fails and how old books fix AI coding
sources.originalTitle: "Software Fundamentals Matter More Than Ever" — Matt Pocock
sources.summary: Matt Pocock argues that "specs-to-code" produces ever-worse code because it divests from design, and that classic books (Ousterhout, Pragmatic Programmer, Brooks, DDD, Beck) give the fixes. He walks through AI coding failure modes with a skill for each: grilling for shared understanding, a ubiquitous language, TDD, deep modules, and delegating implementation behind designed interfaces.

principles.text: Bad code is more expensive than ever; code is not cheap, because a hard-to-change codebase blocks what AI can offer.
principles.quote: I think code is not cheap. In fact, bad code is the most expensive it's ever been.

principles.text: Specs-to-code fails: repeatedly recompiling specs without looking at the code just yields software entropy and garbage.
principles.quote: The idea that we can just ignore the code and just have the code let it manage itself is just sort of vibe coding by another name.

principles.text: Reach a shared design concept with the AI before building by having it grill you relentlessly, rather than rushing to a plan.
principles.quote: Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this plan until we reach a shared understanding.

principles.text: Create a ubiquitous language with the AI; shared terms make its thinking less verbose and implementation more aligned.
principles.quote: It's essentially a markdown file full of a list of terms that you and the AI have in common.

principles.text: Feedback rate is your speed limit; use static types, browser access and tests, and use TDD to force small steps.
principles.quote: The rate of feedback is your speed limit, which means that you should be testing as you go, taking small deliberate steps.

principles.text: Structure code as deep modules with simple interfaces; they are easier for AI to navigate and for you to test.
principles.quote: They should be relatively few large deep modules with simple interfaces.

sources.title: How Matt Pocock runs an AI coding workflow: grill, PRD, Kanban issues, AFK agents, deep modules
sources.originalTitle: Full Walkthrough: Workflow for AI Coding — Matt Pocock
sources.summary: A 2-hour workshop where Matt applies old-school software engineering fundamentals to coding agents. He covers the smart/dumb zone, aligning with a "grill me" session, a PRD as destination, vertical-slice Kanban issues, AFK Ralph loops with TDD, and deepening modules so code bases are testable.

principles.text: LLMs get dumber as context grows, so size tasks to stay in the smart zone (~100K tokens).
principles.quote: it doesn't matter whether you're using 1 million uh context window or 200K, it's always going to be about this. It starts to just get dumber.

principles.text: Prefer clearing context to compacting so every session starts from the same known state.
principles.quote: I much prefer my AI to behave like uh the guy from Memento because this state is always the same.

principles.text: Reach a shared design concept with the agent through a relentless grilling session, not an eager plan.
principles.quote: I didn't need a plan, I needed to be on the same wavelength as the AI, as my agent.

principles.text: Reject specs-to-code: keep a handle on the code, because the code is the battleground.
principles.quote: You need to keep a handle on the code. You need to understand what's in it. You need to shape it because the code is your battleground.

principles.text: Split work into vertical slices (tracer bullets), not horizontal layers, so the agent gets feedback early.
principles.quote: You don't get feedback on your work until you've really started or completed phase three.

principles.text: Build code bases from deep modules with small interfaces; design the interface, delegate the implementation.
principles.quote: Modules that have a little interface on there that expose a small, simple interface that have a lot of functionality inside them.

sources.title: How Matt Pocock builds AI agent skills from classic software fundamentals
sources.originalTitle: AI Skills with Matt Pocock
sources.outlet: The Pragmatic Engineer and Matt Pocock
sources.summary: Matt Pocock explains how he moved from TypeScript education to AI agent skills (grill me, wayfinder, spec and tickets). He argues that old books like The Pragmatic Programmer, Philosophy of Software Design and DDD are the best way to steer agents, and that strategic thinking now matters most.

principles.text: Knowledge is now cheap, but wisdom is not; the strategic layer is where humans add value as AI eats tactical programming.
principles.quote: knowledge is now very cheap to acquire right very very cheap you can just look it up

principles.text: Agents can't read your mind; use an interview skill like grill me to communicate your values, scope and decisions before implementation.
principles.quote: there is a communication gap between you and the agent right there is a barrier there.

principles.text: Respect the smart zone: split big work into a spec plus one ticket per session so each context stays small.
principles.quote: I started thinking, how do I take work that's bigger than 150k tokens, which is not very large, and portion it out over multiple context windows, multiple sessions.

principles.text: Seed prompts with classic-book phrases (tracer bullets, vertical slices, deep modules); models repeat them and change behavior because they sit in the priors.
principles.quote: This is what I call a leading word, a lightvert, let's say, which is a sort of fancy literary term where you lead the agent just with a simple phrase that you repeat a couple of times in the skill or the prompt to change its behavior.

principles.text: Optimize your codebase for an agent that wakes up with no memory every session; software fundamentals have always aimed at this.
principles.quote: we are trying to optimize our code bases for new starters

principles.text: Align up front only when work is large and hard to roll back; for small changes, shift right and align afterwards.
principles.quote: where you can you should shift right as much as possible.

sources.title: Matt Pocock's agentic workflow: strategic programming, AFK agents, harness over model
sources.originalTitle: Matt Pocock’s Agentic Engineering Workflow (just copy him)
sources.summary: Matt argues AI has eaten tactical programming, so strategic skill (design, interfaces, scoping, codebase quality) is the ceiling on what agents can do. He covers procedure vs ability skills, grill-me, AFK agents in sandboxes, queues over loops, and optimizing the harness and codebase over chasing new models.

principles.text: AI has eaten tactical programming; win by being great at strategic programming and delegating the tactical work.
principles.quote: AI has basically eaten tactical programming. It's gone, right? It's all gone.

principles.text: Your own skills are the ceiling on what AI can do, so upskill rather than delegate your thinking.
principles.quote: So your skills are the ceiling on what AI can do. And if your skills are low, then AI is not going to be able to go past that, you know.

principles.text: A codebase that's easy to change lets cheaper models do the work; optimize the codebase, not the model.
principles.quote: Have a code base that's easier to make changes in? Because then you can employ a stupider model.

principles.text: Prefer skills as procedures you invoke yourself over abilities the model invokes; stay in control of the thinking.
principles.quote: I don't want to delegate my thinking to the model.

principles.text: Use an adversarial interviewer skill (grill me) before implementing, instead of plan mode, to reach shared understanding.
principles.quote: it just turns the agent into an adversarial interviewer asking you questions interviewing you and popping up with ideas that you might not have considered until you reach a shared understanding.

principles.text: Strip all skills, plugins, MCPs and CLAUDE.md, observe the bare agent, then layer back only what you choose.
principles.quote: First thing I would do is I would delete every single skill, every single plugin, every single MCP server.

sources.title: Matt Pocock on why communication and codebase quality matter most when working with AI agents
sources.originalTitle: Matt Pocock: The Most Valuable Skill to Learn in the Age of AI
sources.outlet: Nate Herk | AI Automation and Matt Pocock
sources.summary: Matt Pocock explains how he works with coding agents after the late-2025 threshold: raise the floor of the codebase, tell agents what you care about, and surface unknown unknowns with his grill-me skill. He covers why spec-driven development failed him, domain-driven design's ubiquitous language, and why teaching sessions should point to primary sources.

principles.text: The agent's environment is the codebase; a garbage codebase yields garbage output, so care about it.
principles.quote: If they're in like a garbage vibe-coded crappy code base that has never had any care put into it, no one cares about the code base, they only care about the outputs, then you're going to get garbage in, garbage out, right?

principles.text: Raise the floor with old engineering fundamentals: good tests and checks that stop classes of bugs.
principles.quote: How you make good tests. How you add checks to make sure that your code base gets better and better over time to raise the floor, to stop classes of bugs, to prevent mistakes.

principles.text: Agents can't read your mind, so interview-style prompting surfaces unknown unknowns before building.
principles.quote: What that does is the agent essentially tells the agent to interview me relentlessly about the thing that we're trying to build.

principles.text: Use a ubiquitous language (DDD) shared across code, database, UI and client conversations to align with agents.
principles.quote: The language in the code, the terms you use in the code, should be the same as the ones the developers use to talk about the product, which is the same as the client asking you to build the thing

principles.text: Spec-driven development failed: ignoring the code made it and agent output worse; focus on code that is easy to change.
principles.quote: A good code base is a code base that's easy to make changes in. A change is not going to screw up something that the agent didn't think about.

principles.text: Don't trust AI teaching blindly; use it to get oriented, then read the primary source.
principles.quote: I will just get it to introduce me to a topic, and then I'll just go and read the primary source, because that primary source has the actual information I need.

sources.title: How Matt Pocock works with AI agents: grilling, ubiquitous language, disposable specs and the smart zone
sources.originalTitle: Agent Skills - with Matt Pocock
sources.summary: Matt Pocock explains why his "grill me" skill works, how he keeps shared language and decisions in the repo, and why specs should be disposable. He also covers keeping agent sessions in the "smart zone" and designing interfaces while delegating implementation.

principles.text: Hide the build step from the agent so it interviews you thoroughly instead of rushing to a plan.
principles.quote: You're essentially hiding information from the agent and saying don't implement it yet. Just interview me, interview me, interview me.

principles.text: Establish a ubiquitous language with the agent during planning so you share precise terms.
principles.quote: once you understand and establish the language of something you understand it right

principles.text: Treat specs as temporary scheduling artifacts, delete them once the code lands, and don't persist them.
principles.quote: they are temporary artifacts that are supposed to be discarded that are essentially just useful for scheduling work over multiple agent sessions.

principles.text: Break big work into sessions that fit the early part of the context window, where agents perform best.
principles.quote: I like to do the bulk of my work in the smart zone because it's cheaper.

principles.text: Design the interface yourself and delegate the implementation to the agent.
principles.quote: I think in a lot of cases you should design the interface and delegate the implementation.

principles.text: One developer should own a whole spec and the agent running it, to avoid a crisis of responsibility.
principles.quote: A single developer should own an entire spec.

sources.title: Matt Pocock on aligning with AI agents: Grill Me, glossaries, and pruning skills
sources.originalTitle: Matt Pocock Built the Skills Repo Every AI Coder Is Using
sources.outlet: The Next New Thing and Matt Pocock
sources.summary: Matt Pocock demos his open-source skills repo, showing how a short "grill me" interview before work beats a generic agent run. He covers glossaries for consistent language, splitting specs into tickets, looping agents deterministically, and cutting no-op lines from skills.

principles.text: Spend time aligning with the agent before it implements or reviews anything.
principles.quote: most people don't spend enough time on the pre-alignment phase, right? On the aligning before you do the thing.

principles.text: Start at low fidelity (plain text) and only move up to higher fidelity later.
principles.quote: when you're first starting out, it's often really good to operate at a really low fidelity. In other words, just text.

principles.text: Your priorities are invisible to the agent, so you must surface them through conversation.
principles.quote: there's a communication gap between you and the agent. And that's always going to be there, right?

principles.text: Agree on names for concepts and use them everywhere, since consistent language helps agents navigate code.
principles.quote: the thing about agents is that they thrive off consistent language.

principles.text: Prune no-ops from skills: lines that change nothing about agent behavior.
principles.quote: they will write things inside the skill that do nothing to change the actual outputs of the skill or the behavior of the agent reading that skill. And I call these no-ops.

principles.text: Looping over tickets can be a deterministic script rather than an agent.
principles.quote: You just have to just loop over that, and that can be deterministic. It doesn't have to be an agent.

sources.title: Matt Pocock on building trust with AI agents: brakes first, automated review, and one-way doors
sources.originalTitle: It's just all about building trust - Matt Pocock
sources.summary: Matt Pocock explains how to move toward a software factory without producing slop. Build verification and review brakes before accelerating, use a fresh reviewer agent to stop cheating, and let a well-shaped codebase steer agents. He also covers Effect's dependency injection and why skills are really process plus leading words.

principles.text: Install brakes (verification, testing, evidence) before accelerating agent work, or the app turns into a slop cannon.
principles.quote: You need to get your brakes in first because if you don't push the quality high enough, you're going to turn your app into a slop cannon.

principles.text: Use a separate automated reviewer agent to catch cheating; a prohibition given to the implementer becomes a positive search task for the reviewer.
principles.quote: if you pass that to a reviewer agent, that then becomes a positive instruction, right? Then, the reviewer agent is goes, "Okay, I'm looking for X in the diff, and I will attempt to um find it and excise it."

principles.text: Your codebase steers agent output as much as agents.md does, so improving it benefits every later session.
principles.quote: People underestimate the amount of steering that your code base can do on your output. You think of agents.md is the place where you put all of your instructions, but actually your code base is kind of like a massive agents.md but only code.

principles.text: Prioritize human review by door type: any one-way (hard to reverse) change must be reviewed by a human.
principles.quote: every one-way door must be reviewed by human, is my opinion. There's no way that an agent should be doing that stuff

principles.text: Constrain agents with strong types and small swappable modules; Effect's real payoff is dependency injection, not just error handling.
principles.quote: I think the reason you go for effect is dependency injection, actually. It allows you to create these beautiful small modules that you can just swap out as needed

principles.text: When borrowing skills, steal the process and the 'leading words': compressed phrases that make agents do a whole complex behavior.
principles.quote: the things that I think are most valuable in skills are what I call the leading words, right? Are the phrases, the compressions that people have made where they're able to take a large complicated process and compress it into a few words

sources.title: Your codebase is NOT ready for AI: deep modules as gray boxes for coding agents
sources.originalTitle: Your codebase is NOT ready for AI (here's how to fix it)
sources.summary: Matt argues the codebase shapes AI output more than prompts or agents.md. A web of small shallow modules is hard for an amnesiac agent to navigate, test and hold in your head. Restructure into deep modules with simple, taste-designed interfaces, tested as gray boxes, so the AI manages the insides.

principles.text: Your codebase influences AI output more than prompts or agents.md; software quality matters more than ever.
principles.quote: Your code base, way more than the prompts that you use, way more than your agents.md file, is the biggest influence on AI's output.

principles.text: Treat the AI as a forgetful new starter in your codebase and make the code friendly to new starters.
principles.quote: it's that it's a new starter in your code base. So, you need to make your code base friendly and ready for new starters because you're going to be spawning like 20 new starters every day

principles.text: Make the file system match your mental map of the codebase so the AI can find things from a prompt.
principles.quote: you need to make sure that the file system and the design of your code base matches this internal map that you have of it.

principles.text: Prefer deep modules: lots of implementation behind a simple interface, instead of many shallow modules.
principles.quote: you have a deep module, so lots of implementation controlled by a simple interface.

principles.text: Treat deep modules as gray boxes: design and taste the interface yourself, delegate the implementation to AI, and lock behavior down with tests.
principles.quote: I can write tests that completely lock down the module in terms of its behavior. So these are not just deep modules with simple interfaces, they're also gray box modules.

principles.text: Use progressive disclosure: expose typed interfaces first so the AI reads them before deciding to look inside.
principles.quote: we've designed our code base for progressive disclosure of complexity. The interface sits at the top and it just explains what the module does.

sources.title: How Matt Pocock de-slops an AI-ruined codebase using deep modules and one skill
sources.originalTitle: How To De-Slop A Codebase Ruined By AI (with one skill)
sources.summary: Matt argues AI has accelerated software entropy and walks through the cure: a shared vocabulary from Ousterhout's deep-module ideas (module, interface, seam, adapter, locality, leverage), then applies his improve-codebase-architecture skill to a real repo. The skill finds deepening candidates, but the human acts as the strategic "general" making the judgment calls.

principles.text: AI accelerates software entropy: changes made without regard to the whole codebase snowball into a ball of mud.
principles.quote: AI has simply accelerated software entropy. In other words, codebases are falling apart faster than they ever have before because every time that you make a change that doesn't take into account the entire codebase, you are likely to introduce little things, weird things that make the codebase harder to change.

principles.text: Share precise vocabulary with the AI so you can ask for exactly what you want.
principles.quote: Having a shared vocabulary with the AI is super important because it means that you can talk using the same language. You can understand what each other's language is and you can be a lot more precise with what you're asking for.

principles.text: Prefer deep modules: lots of implementation behind a small interface, so callers learn less and get more.
principles.quote: A deep module hides lots of implementation behind a relatively simple interface. A shallow module has a complex interface and kind of not much implementation actually behind it.

principles.text: Deep modules give maintainers locality and users leverage; aim improvements at those two attributes.
principles.quote: For the maintainers, the people maintaining this module, they get locality. Changes to that module and bugs and all the fixes to do with them, they concentrate in one place, in that deep module.

principles.text: Treat agents as tactical programmers; the human must be the strategic one who decides what is good for long-term codebase health.
principles.quote: I think of agents as really, really good tactical programmers. They're able to get on the ground and make changes quickly. But they need someone on the level above them who is the strategic programmer.

principles.text: Before using AI on a legacy codebase, build a test harness around deep modules with good seams.
principles.quote: What you really need before you start making changes in a legacy code base is a harness around the code base to make sure that your changes don't mess anything up.

sources.title: Never Trust An LLM: why hallucinations happen and how to work around them
sources.originalTitle: Never Trust An LLM
sources.summary: Matt explains the types of LLM hallucination (factual errors, fabricated entities, contextual inconsistency), why they happen (compression of training data and benchmarks that reward guessing), and practical workarounds. The core advice is to feed the model information in context, tell it to use its search tool, and manually verify anything critical.

principles.text: Never implicitly trust an LLM; hallucinations are common enough to warrant constant paranoia, even while staying pro-LLM.
principles.quote: These hallucinations are so unbelievably common that I am now paranoid about everything an LLM says to me and I will never ever trust an LLM.

principles.text: Distinguish intrinsic hallucinations (contradicting context you sent) from extrinsic ones (guessing beyond context).
principles.quote: There are two types of hallucinations. There are hallucinations based on intrinsic information and extrinsic information.

principles.text: LLMs are far more reliable when you send them the information first than when they rely on training data.
principles.quote: My experience with LLMs is that they're much, much more reliable when you send them the information first.

principles.text: Expect LLMs to invent packages, laws and entities; hallucinated packages open developers to supply chain attacks.
principles.quote: Attackers can exploit a common AI experience, false recommendations, to spread malicious code via developers that use ChatGPT to create software.

principles.text: Hallucinations occur because training and evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty.
principles.quote: We argue that the language models hallucinate because the training and evaluation procedures reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty.

principles.text: Prompt the model with 'Use your search tool' so it pulls sources into context; for critical matters, still read the documents yourself.
principles.quote: whenever you're prompting the LLM to ask it for information, say, "Use your search tool." Because then it will pull the articles into its context

sources.title: Matt Pocock reviews Cursor's thermonuclear code review skill: ambition, file size, types and false positives
sources.originalTitle: Can Cursor's HARDCORE Review Skill Stop The Slop?
sources.summary: Matt tries Cursor's "thermonuclear code quality review" skill on his Sandcastle repo and critiques the prompt. He likes its ambition, small-file and type-boundary rules, finds it duplicative and blind to tests, and concludes noisy ambitious reviews beat missed opportunities.

principles.text: Automated code review is one of the most impactful ways to raise the quality of code coming out of your agent.
principles.quote: Automated code review is one of the most impactful ways that you can improve the code quality coming out of your agent.

principles.text: Agents treat a diff as their bounds, so tell the reviewer to be ambitious and look across the whole codebase.
principles.quote: If you pass an agent a diff, then it will usually treat that diff as its bounds within which it can work.

principles.text: Keep files small: agents must ingest a whole file to find one thing, so split files and let the file name be a context pointer.
principles.quote: Large files are just quite hard for agents to navigate because they need to ingest the entire file into their context window in order to find the thing that's actually useful within it.

principles.text: Question unnecessary optionality: agents add props as optional even when they are always required.
principles.quote: Whenever an agent adds a prop onto a React component, let's say, it always adds it as optional.

principles.text: Vague review criteria like "improve or worsen" mean nothing to an agent unless you spell out what good and bad look like.
principles.quote: You've got to say exactly what good and bad looks like to an agent in order for improve or worsen to mean anything.

principles.text: An ambitious review gives more false positives, but those are easy to reject; the missed opportunities are the dangerous ones.
principles.quote: It's the ones that you miss, that you never know about, the opportunity for improvement that you never see, those are the dangerous ones.

sources.title: How Matt Pocock uses Claude Code for real engineering: plan mode, multi-phase plans, GitHub issues
sources.originalTitle: How I use Claude Code for real engineering
sources.summary: Matt walks through building a CLI feature with Claude Code. He starts in plan mode, answers clarifying questions, splits the work into phases, stores the plan as a GitHub issue, and clears context between phases. His memory file keeps replies concise and ends each plan with unresolved questions.

principles.text: Start big work in plan mode so the agent explores the codebase and asks clarifying questions before writing code.
principles.quote: Whenever I embark out on a big piece of work, I'm always thinking about creating a plan first.

principles.text: Tell the agent to be extremely concise in every interaction; it makes plans easy to read.
principles.quote: in all interactions and commit messages, be extremely concise and sacrifice grammar for the sake of concision.

principles.text: Have each plan end with a list of unresolved questions so you can answer them before execution.
principles.quote: at the end of each plan, give me a list of unresolved questions to answer, if any, and again, make the questions extremely concise.

principles.text: Break large plans into phases so work can span multiple context windows without overrunning the LLM.
principles.quote: if this piece of work is too large, it's going to overrun the context window of the LLM. It's going to be much better going forward if I break this into a multi-phase plan

principles.text: Do heavy upfront planning, then run execution with auto-accept edits; review the diff at the end of each phase.
principles.quote: Now that we've done the planning, we can be pretty aggressive with accept edits on because we understand the implementation a bit and we kind of get what's going on.

principles.text: Store the multi-phase plan as a GitHub issue so it survives context resets and teammates can comment async.
principles.quote: I really like keeping these assets in the cloud because then actually people can comment on them, add stuff overnight, add stuff async.

sources.title: How Matt Pocock builds a real feature with Claude Code: grill, PRD, issues, AFK loop, QA
sources.originalTitle: Building a REAL feature with Claude Code: every step explained
sources.summary: Matt walks through a full feature build in his course video manager: a "grill me" session to harden vague requirements, a PRD, issues, an AFK Ralph loop in Docker, then human QA that feeds new issues back to the agent. He treats the LLM like a delegate: invest in the idea and architecture, lean on shared language, tests and feedback loops, and review inputs and outputs rather than every line.

principles.text: Treat Claude Code like a teammate you delegate to: focus on architecture and feedback loops, the practices that have worked for 20 years.
principles.quote: You get the most out of it when you treat it like someone you would delegate to in your team. In other words, you focus on the architecture, you focus on making sure that you've got good feedback loops

principles.text: Always explain the why, not just the what, so the LLM can suggest alternatives.
principles.quote: if the LLM has the what, then it understands what you want to build, but if it doesn't know the why, then it can't suggest alternatives.

principles.text: Keep a ubiquitous-language glossary shared with the LLM so you can talk about the system precisely and tersely.
principles.quote: I'm the domain expert and the LLM is the dev. And we need some kind of shared language so that we can talk together precisely.

principles.text: Have the agent answer from the code when it can, and ask you only what the code cannot answer; spend the human time on the grilling session.
principles.quote: if it's a question that can only be answered by or can be answered by looking at the code, it should look at the code first.

principles.text: Design and name module interfaces carefully and care less about implementation; make modules testable and legible to future agents.
principles.quote: Notice how I'm thinking about the interface more than I'm actually thinking about the implementation here.

principles.text: Run AFK agents on issues while you QA, and feed bugs back as issues; specs-to-code alone misses edge cases found in QA.
principles.quote: the specs to code approach is just never going to work because when you're in there, when you're in the QA loop, when you're iterating towards something, you are going to find little weird edge cases

sources.title: Enums considered harmful: why Matt Pocock replaces TypeScript enums with as const objects
sources.originalTitle: Enums considered harmful
sources.summary: Matt explains why TypeScript's enum keyword is a poor fit: it is not native JavaScript, produces surprising runtime objects, and makes TypeScript nominal. He recommends plain objects with `as const` plus a derived union type, which is more flexible and structurally typed, and says to flag enums in PRs without rejecting them.

principles.text: Prefer `as const` objects over enums; they fit TypeScript's structural typing and let callers pass plain values.
principles.quote: the thing that I do instead of using enums and I've seen this all over the place in open source application code is using a pojo a plain old JavaScript object that's just got this as const annotation on it

principles.text: Numeric enums compile to a reverse-mapped object, so Object.values returns surprising results at runtime.
principles.quote: it actually doesn't if we look at the transpiled JavaScript here then this log level actually ends up as a slightly different object

principles.text: Enums make TypeScript nominal, which clashes with the structural type system everywhere else.
principles.quote: for enums typescript becomes a nominal type system it cares about either whether it's a log level enum or a log level 2 2 enum here

principles.text: Avoid const enums, especially in library code, because they are dangerous when you don't control the compiler emitting them.
principles.quote: you should also never ever ever use them if you're inside Library code too because cons enums are really dangerous if you don't control the compiler that's emitting them

principles.text: `as const` objects can map semantic keys to richer values, and the type can be derived from keys or values, with less code than enums.
principles.quote: the other really cool thing about as const is it lets you be super flexible with the object that you create these keys in

principles.text: Be pragmatic in review: flag enums in PRs and suggest as const, but don't reject PRs just for using them.
principles.quote: I don't think you should reject PRS that have enums in but I do think you should try to monitor when they go into your code base and see if they're really necessary

sources.title: Generics: 10 tips to make TypeScript generics click
sources.originalTitle: Generics: The most intimidating TypeScript feature
sources.summary: Matt walks through ten tips that take generics from intimidating to usable: generic types as type functions, generic functions, inference from runtime arguments, constraints, multiple type parameters, defaults, and linking Zod schemas to inferred return types. The recurring theme is to concentrate the advanced typing in one place so function users never pass type arguments.

principles.text: A generic type is a type function that takes type arguments and produces new types.
principles.quote: this pattern lets you create type helpers type functions that you can create other types out of that's what's called a generic type

principles.text: A generic function is a normal function with a type helper mapped on top of it.
principles.quote: a generic function is just a normal function with a type helper mapped on top of it

principles.text: Let TypeScript infer type arguments from runtime arguments instead of passing them manually.
principles.quote: understanding that they can actually infer the type arguments you pass them without actually needing to pass any type arguments this is the source of a lot of the magic that you can do with generics

principles.text: Constrain type parameters with extends to control what callers can pass and reduce logic inside the function.
principles.quote: when you have a generic function you're usually going to want to put a constraint on this gives you control over what the users of your function can pass in

principles.text: Use multiple type parameters, with one constrained by another, to link arguments to a precise return type.
principles.quote: you can get this inference happening between the arguments of your functions which then maps on to the return type and lets you sort of propagate these types beautifully through your app

principles.text: Using 'as' inside a highly generic function body is acceptable when you know better than the compiler.
principles.quote: sometimes inside generic functions you know better than typescript typescript is going to lose its way in really complicated generic signatures

sources.title: Effect: why Matt Pocock thinks you should learn the unreadable TypeScript library
sources.originalTitle: Effect: the unreadable library that captured my heart
sources.summary: Matt explains why, after 18 months of skepticism, he now recommends Effect. He covers its ugly generator syntax, type-safe error tracking, compile-time dependency injection, the built-in batteries, and how it can be adopted incrementally as a backend TypeScript framework.

principles.text: Treat Effect's ugly syntax like Tailwind's: it looks horrible at first, but it enables TypeScript magic that other libraries can't.
principles.quote: Remember when you first looked at Tailwind code? These huge long disgusting class names and then you tried writing some Tailwind code and you realized, oh, it's actually really nice to use.

principles.text: Track errors in the type system: a function's return type should list which errors it can fail with, across an arbitrarily deep call stack.
principles.quote: This effect tracks what the function returns when it's successful, which is this string here. But it also tracks which errors may occur in this function.

principles.text: Effect's error handling is far more flexible than homebrew Result types, and handling an error removes it from the type, like a type-safe try/catch.
principles.quote: all of the homebrewed library sort of result type things that I've come up with haven't felt as flexible as effect.

principles.text: Make dependencies part of the type signature, so a program can't run until its required services are provided.
principles.quote: Not only is effect tracking the success values of our program, not only is it tracking the errors, it's also tracking the dependencies of each function.

principles.text: Dependency injection makes code modular and testable: write business logic first, leaving typed holes you implement later.
principles.quote: my flow tends to be write the business logic first, then sort of create these kind of typed holes in my application that I then go back and implement later.

principles.text: Effect is a big batteries-included standard library, which pays off for hard backend projects built by a team of TypeScript developers.
principles.quote: Effect is a big fat batteries included standard library. So what that means is when you invest into it, you get back all of these pre-made solutions to difficult problems

sources.title: Types vs Interfaces: why Matt Pocock reversed his 2022 take and now defaults to interface extends
sources.originalTitle: Types vs Interfaces: What I Got Wrong In 2022
sources.summary: Matt revisits his 2022 types-vs-interfaces video and corrects it. The real performance issue is interface extends versus intersections, not type versus interface for a plain object. He now defaults to interface for extending, and says single-object choice barely matters.

principles.text: The TypeScript perf advice contrasts interface extends with intersections, not types with interfaces; declaring a basic object either way has no performance difference.
principles.quote: Declaring an interface and a type just as a basic object are not going to give you any performance differences. It's about when you smoosh object types together.

principles.text: Interface extends is faster than intersections because TypeScript checks each hierarchical level and errors on incompatible properties rather than silently producing never.
principles.quote: This hierarchical relationship means that TypeScript is able to check at each level. Whereas when you smoosh these guys together with the intersection, it's not quite so easy for TypeScript.

principles.text: Intersections used repeatedly across a large codebase, such as extending a button's props, can wreck type-checking performance; interface extends gave Sentry a big speedup.
principles.quote: They halved their compile times and made the developer experience instantly reflect type changes.

principles.text: Default to interface extends over intersections when composing object types.
principles.quote: I think that just the thing you need to remember is default to interface extends over intersections.

principles.text: Interface declaration merging is a risk, but a lint rule (no-unsafe-declaration-merging) handles it, so it is not a big deal.
principles.quote: You can handle the edge cases with declaration merging with an ESLint rule.

principles.text: Interfaces are not assignable to index-signature record types because they could later be extended, whereas type aliases are; this edge case comes up rarely.
principles.quote: The reason for this is that an interface could later be extended. In other words, it could be declaration merged by something else.

sources.title: Matt Pocock livestream: building a TypeScript test-fixture library (fromPartial, proxies, naming, publishing)
sources.originalTitle: Testing in TypeScript SUCKS - let's make it better
sources.summary: Matt live-builds a small testing utility that lets you pass partial, deeply partial test data into strictly typed functions without using `as`. He debates naming, tries a Proxy for runtime safety, sets up CI with changesets, and publishes to npm. Useful for testing ergonomics, library naming and shipping small helper libraries.

principles.text: Replace `as` casts in tests with a helper that infers the needed type and accepts a deep partial.
principles.quote: it looks at the type that you want to get back and then just lets you pass in a partial of that type and it's a deep partial too

principles.text: `as` feels bad because you must manually specify the type; an inferring helper detects it from the slot.
principles.quote: I think part of the reason that as feels bad is that you need to actually manually specify the type here so you actually need to dig out what type it needs to be whereas the thing about this partial function is you can actually just like pass it in and it just acts as it understands what type you need

principles.text: If you are tricking the compiler, be explicit about it; use clearly named primitives rather than silent casts.
principles.quote: if you want to trick the compiler I think it's good to be explicit about that

principles.text: Wrapping partial data in a Proxy that throws on undeclared property access gives runtime safety on top of type safety.
principles.quote: it should throw an error when the test itself accesses a property not defined on the input

principles.text: Prefer small, focused helper libraries that are cheap to maintain.
principles.quote: I want to maintain small little libraries Little Helper libraries

principles.text: Library naming is hard and can dominate the work; choose names that are plain and boring rather than clever.
principles.quote: 90 of it was picking the names of stuff

sources.title: Matt Pocock on TypeScript mental models, open objects, TS expect error vs as any, and becoming an educator
sources.originalTitle: Matt Pocock: How to Maximize Success with TypeScript and Career
sources.summary: Matt explains TypeScript as a shorter feedback loop in your IDE, why its open object types surprise people, and why a targeted as any beats TS ignore or TS expect error. He also argues complex types usually come from complex JavaScript and favors JSDoc plus handwritten docs.

principles.text: TypeScript is mainly a shorter feedback loop in your IDE, so you can code longer before checking in the browser.
principles.quote: in TypeScript you have a shorter feedback loop, which is you have the feedback loop inside your IDE.

principles.text: TypeScript object types are open: excess properties are allowed unless the object is a fresh literal, so don't assume keys are exact.
principles.quote: TypeScript has open objects, whereas Flow Flow would actually error there.

principles.text: Complex types usually mean complex JavaScript; simplify the code and its abstractions before reaching for harder types.
principles.quote: complex TypeScript comes from complex JavaScript, cuz TypeScript is just an effort to describe JavaScript.

principles.text: Avoid chaining derived types across boundaries; decoupled types let each part change independently.
principles.quote: They end up creating these chains of linked types linked through generic functions they're not even really aware of that end up making the system really coupled.

principles.text: TS ignore and TS expect error are sledgehammers hitting the whole next line; prefer a targeted as any on the specific node.
principles.quote: as any targets a specific node, a specific thing. It's not destroying the entire next line.

principles.text: Write rich JSDoc comments on APIs and pair them with handwritten docs rather than relying on auto-generated doc sites.
principles.quote: tons and tons of jsdoc comments of real high quality explaining all of the stuff uh of what your API should do and then a really nicely written documentation site to kind of match that up

sources.title: Matt Pocock on inferred types, any, reading errors, and adopting TypeScript
sources.originalTitle: TypeScript, React, and API Issues with Matt Pocock
sources.summary: A casual podcast interview where Matt explains why he prefers inferred types, how any is a tool not a sin, why people misread TypeScript errors, and how he got into TypeScript. Also covers the new using keyword and how to approach TypeScript adoption on a team.

principles.text: Prefer inferred return types; annotating them overrides what the compiler already knows.
principles.quote: inferred types make most sense because they're most likely to be correct

principles.text: Explicit return types only make sense when you need to lock down a function used in many places.
principles.quote: the only way return types really make sense is if you want to make sure that the function you're creating is secure and like used in a bunch of different places

principles.text: any is just a tool; fine inside a well-typed, tested function boundary.
principles.quote: as long as the outside of your function is properly typed it's kind of fine if you're just using any inside it sort of doesn't matter too much

principles.text: Read TypeScript errors from the bottom up; the most relevant info is at the end.
principles.quote: you've actually got the least relevant information at the very top and then the most relevant information right at the very bottom which is the actual comparison that failed

principles.text: Generic components let you drop type annotations because inference flows from what callers pass in.
principles.quote: one that actually changed its sort of like type information based on the stuff that you passed in and so again that just meant okay we can actually drop a load of type annotations

principles.text: Typed interfaces make refactors trivial: change the shape once and the compiler lists every place to update.
principles.quote: a four hour job turned into a five minute job because it just told me everywhere that needed to be updated

sources.title: Maintaining React's TypeScript types: how @types/react works, versioning, and breaking changes
sources.originalTitle: React's TypeScript types with Sebastian Silbermann and Matt Pocock | Maintain Podcast #1
sources.summary: Matt Pocock joins Sebastian Silbermann, maintainer of @types/react, to walk through how React's types live in DefinitelyTyped, how they're versioned, and why changes are hard. Matt's own contributions are mostly questions and framing on semver for types, breaking changes, and why more accurate types are good errors. Sebastian supplies most of the technical detail.

principles.text: Semver is well defined for runtime code but fuzzy for types: removing a type export is arguably a breaking change.
principles.quote: SemVer is really well defined for runtime stuff, you know, like when you have major breaking changes and you have minors and you have patches. And but it's less well defined for types, right?

principles.text: Library types should track the runtime's major version, or the numbering feels strange.
principles.quote: it's sort of funny that like the types for React sort of need to stay in step with the major of React itself. Because it would feel very strange if you had like 18 on React and then like 26 on React types

principles.text: A library that ships its own types can release a types-only change as a minor version with a changelog entry.
principles.quote: I could ship a feature in my library that is TypeScript only, you know, that has a minor version bump that basically indicate that has a change log that says, "Okay, something in the types changed and this necessitated a new version of the library."

principles.text: Type changes that make types more truthful and surface new errors are positive changes, not harmful breakage.
principles.quote: So the types after the change are more truthful. Exactly. Um and more accurate. So actually doesn't that make the errors that are then uncovered uh good errors?

principles.text: Coordinating a breaking type change with a runtime-led release means waiting for the next major.
principles.quote: With React, you can't really do that, right? Because every change has to be led from the runtime. It has to be led from the actual code base itself.

principles.text: Open source maintainers mostly hear about problems they cause, not the services they provide; decisions can echo far beyond one PR.
principles.quote: Sometimes when you're maintaining open source software, you have to make decisions that may not make sense at a PR level but there's like a macro scale you have to think about. And the decisions you make can echo to eternity.

sources.title: Matt Pocock on JSJ 538: why TypeScript beats JSDoc, inference, branded types and the safety-first mindset
sources.originalTitle: To TypeScript or Not to TypeScript - JSJ 538
sources.summary: Matt Pocock defends TypeScript against panelists who prefer plain JavaScript with JSDoc. He covers refactor safety against changing back-end data contracts, TypeScript's inference strength, branded types, types-first design, and why generics mostly matter for library authors.

principles.text: TypeScript turns changing data contracts into compile errors, cutting bugs and runtime checking.
principles.quote: we would just get all these squiggly red lines wherever the data contract had changed and it meant that we didn't even have to test in the runtime anymore we knew that the types would be okay

principles.text: Adopting TypeScript can dramatically speed up a team by eliminating a whole class of bugs.
principles.quote: we put typescripts in and we immediately kind of almost doubled our velocity pretty much just by reducing a whole class of bugs

principles.text: You can adopt TypeScript gradually without embracing classes or inheritance; it doesn't force patterns on you.
principles.quote: you don't necessarily need to embrace classes or inheritance or anything like that

principles.text: TypeScript's real strength is deep inference and narrowing that understands JavaScript's own type system.
principles.quote: the thing that typescript is really really good at is inference

principles.text: Use branded types to stop mixing up values like different entity IDs at compile time.
principles.quote: I had different entity IDs mapped to different types and so you couldn't pass a user ID into something that was expecting a post ID

principles.text: Most app developers rarely need generics; complex type-level work is mainly for library authors.
principles.quote: most typescript users are not going to be dealing with generics really like maybe a couple of sort of basic stuff

sources.title: Matt Pocock on when `any` is the right choice: generic constraints and conditional returns
sources.originalTitle: `any` Considered Harmful, Except For These Cases
sources.summary: Matt argues you should ban `any` by default but shows two advanced cases where it is correct: wide type argument constraints like `(...args: any[]) => any`, and returning conditional types from generic functions where TypeScript's narrowing falls short. He advises backing the latter with unit tests and using eslint-disable.

principles.text: Use `any` in type argument constraints when you deliberately want to accept any function shape.
principles.quote: The solution is to use `any[]` as the type argument constraint:

principles.text: `unknown` in a function constraint silently rejects functions with real parameters, so a wide constraint needs `any`.
principles.quote: So accidentally, we've created a `ReturnType` function that only works on functions which accept `unknown` as an argument. This is not what we wanted.

principles.text: A deliberately wide `any` constraint is safe because it states you don't care about the shape.
principles.quote: The reason this is safe is because we're deliberately declaring a wide type.

principles.text: When returning conditional types from generic functions, use `as any` plus a unit test, since TypeScript can't verify it.
principles.quote: in these situations, it's often better to use `as any` and add a unit test for this function's behavior.

principles.text: Inside generic functions, `any` is an acceptable workaround for TypeScript's limitations.
principles.quote: There are several other use cases like this, where inside generic functions you need to use `any` to get around TypeScript's limitations. To me, this is fine.

principles.text: Ban `any` by default with ESLint, and use eslint-disable for the legitimate exceptions.
principles.quote: You should turn on the ESLint rule which prevents its use, and you should avoid it wherever possible.

sources.title: Why generics, not unknown, are how Matt Pocock removes any from utility functions
sources.originalTitle: An `unknown` can't always fix an `any`
sources.summary: Matt shows that swapping `any` for `unknown` only moves the problem: `any` causes bugs, `unknown` forces runtime validation boilerplate. Using a groupBy utility as the example, he argues generics are the only way to type such functions so consumers get exact types with no casts or checks.

principles.text: Any `any` disables type checking on what it touches and leaks across your app to everything that consumes it.
principles.quote: Any `any` in a codebase is a cause for concern. That's because it disables type checking on the thing it's assigned to.

principles.text: Reaching for `any` is often a way to silence a TypeScript error you don't understand; fix the type instead.
principles.quote: One reason could be that you're trying to solve a bug you don't understand.

principles.text: For indexing objects built in loops, use Record or an `as` cast, depending on how specific the type should be.
principles.quote: the best way to solve and error like the above is either with a Record, or with an `as` type - depending on how specific a type you want `obj` to be

principles.text: Too few generics is another way `any`s creep in; utility functions need them to relate inputs to outputs.
principles.quote: Another way `any`s creep into your code is when you don't use enough generics.

principles.text: `unknown` is safer than `any` but just moves the problem: consumers must add runtime validation boilerplate.
principles.quote: Unnecessary `unknown`s in your codebase are bad because they bloat your runtime code with boilerplate.

principles.text: Generics break the any/unknown Catch-22: consumers get exact types with no casts or validation, even if the signature is complex.
principles.quote: The way out of this Catch-22 is generics.

sources.title: Should You Declare Return Types? Matt Pocock's .cursor rule for top-level functions
sources.originalTitle: Should You Declare Return Types?
sources.summary: A short essay sharing a .cursor/rules snippet: declare explicit return types on top-level module functions so future AI assistants understand each function's purpose. The one exception is JSX components, whose return type is always JSX.

principles.text: Declare return types on functions declared at the top level of a module.
principles.quote:
When declaring functions on the top-level of a module,
declare their return types.

principles.text: Explicit return types help AI assistants understand a function's purpose.
principles.quote:
This will help future AI
assistants understand the function's purpose.

principles.text: Skip return types on JSX-returning components; the type is always JSX.
principles.quote:
One exception to this is components which return JSX.
No need to declare the return type of a component,
as it is always JSX.

principles.text: Encode TypeScript habits as .cursor/rules so AI agents follow your conventions.
principles.quote: Here's a quick `.cursor/rules` addition you can make for handling return types in TypeScript.

sources.title: Discriminated unions over 'bag of optionals': modeling frontend state in TypeScript
sources.originalTitle: TypeScript Discriminated Unions for Frontend Developers
sources.summary: Matt Pocock argues that most frontend complexity comes from handling states, and that handling starts with how states are typed. He contrasts a 'bag of optionals' type, which permits impossible shapes, with a discriminated union that makes each state carry exactly its own data. He also extends the idea to component props.

principles.text: Most frontend complexity is state handling, and handling states starts with how they are represented in types.
principles.quote: Most of the complexity in frontend comes from handling all the various states your app can be in.

principles.text: A 'bag of optionals' type permits impossible states; use optionals only when a value truly may or may not be present.
principles.quote: Optional properties are best used when a value might or might not be present. In this case, that isn't right.

principles.text: Model state as a discriminated union so each status carries exactly the data that exists in that state.
principles.quote: The more accurate way to represent this is using a discriminated union.

principles.text: Build the union by scaffolding the discriminant branches first, then adding each branch's own properties.
principles.quote: Now that we've got our scaffolding, we can start adding elements to each branch of the union.

principles.text: TypeScript's strictness on unions is a feature; it pushes you to think in states and access data only where it exists.
principles.quote: By ensuring you can only access data when the status equals `success`, you're encouraged to think of your app in terms of its states, and only access data in the states it's available.

principles.text: Use discriminated unions for component props when a component renders in different variants, so variant-specific props are required only when relevant.
principles.quote: What if you need to display a component in two slightly different ways? Use a discriminated union:

sources.title: When should you use Zod? Validate untrusted and uncontrolled inputs, skip trusted ones
sources.originalTitle: When should you use Zod?
sources.summary: Matt Pocock gives a decision rule for runtime validation with Zod based on how much you trust and control an input. Validate anything untrusted, validate trusted-but-uncontrolled third-party data to fail early, and usually skip validation for inputs you both trust and control, with version drift as the debatable edge case.

principles.text: Always validate inputs you don't trust (public APIs, forms, websockets, localStorage, CLI args) with Zod.
principles.quote: In each of these cases, you don't _trust_ the data entering your app. For those cases, you should use Zod.

principles.text: Zod schemas give you inferred types for free, so parsing unknown input also yields type safety.
principles.quote: The nice thing about using Zod here is that `name` is inferred as a `string` without any other work needed.

principles.text: Use safeParse at API boundaries so you return a 400 with a readable error instead of throwing.
principles.quote: We use `.safeParse` here so that we don't throw an error - instead, we return `400` and pass back the error.

principles.text: Validate third-party API data too: errors surface early at the boundary, making bugs far easier to debug.
principles.quote: Validating that data with Zod will still cause an error in your app - but that error will be thrown _early_, right when the data enters your app.

principles.text: Prioritise robustness over bundle size and speed; unexpected data is the most frequent source of bugs.
principles.quote: 'Impossible data' - or data you don't expect - has been probably the most frequent cause of bugs throughout my dev life.

principles.text: For inputs you trust and control, such as your own full-stack API, usually skip Zod; version drift is the debatable exception.
principles.quote: When your app has inputs you **trust** and **control**, I usually don't validate them with Zod.

sources.title: Matt Pocock's advice for security-critical TS apps: learn the type wizardry, use branded types
sources.originalTitle: My advice for security-critical TS apps
sources.summary: A short essay arguing that TypeScript expertise, especially turning `any` into safe types and designing type-safe abstractions, saves teams bugs and speeds them up. For security-critical apps specifically, Matt says he'd lean heavily on branded types.

principles.text: Most TS app code is written under time pressure, which is how `any` creeps in.
principles.quote: The vast majority of TypeScript application code out there is written under severe time constraints.

principles.text: Knowing how to turn `any` into safe types saves your team bugs.
principles.quote: Having the knowledge to transform any’s into safe types will save your team bugs.

principles.text: Advanced type skills enable DX wins: custom forms, type-safe API endpoint creators, flexible components.
principles.quote: Want a custom form abstraction? A type-safe REST API endpoint creator? A flexible Table component?

principles.text: Enabling teammates to develop faster is what advances your career.
principles.quote: The more you can enable your teammates to develop faster, the faster you’ll rise up the ladder.

principles.text: For security-critical apps, use branded types extensively.
principles.quote: If I were building an app where security was critical, I’d use the crap out of branded types.

principles.text: Designing APIs that help others code faster is satisfying work.
principles.quote: You’ll be designing and implementing API’s that help folks code faster.

sources.title: Deriving vs Decoupling: when Matt Pocock says to skip clever TypeScript types
sources.originalTitle: Deriving vs Decoupling: When NOT To Be A TypeScript Wizard
sources.summary: Matt Pocock explains when to derive one type from another (Pick, Omit, indexed access) and when to write a plain, decoupled type. The test is future workload: derive when types share a concern and must change together, decouple when coupling would create busywork or tie unrelated concerns.

principles.text: Decide derive vs decouple by asking which choice reduces your future workload.
principles.quote: The decision to derive or decouple is all about reducing your future workload.

principles.text: Derive when updates to one type must ripple to the other.
principles.quote: Are the two types so related that updates to one will need to ripple to the other? Derive.

principles.text: Decouple when coupling unrelated types would cause extra work later.
principles.quote: Are they so unrelated that coupling them could result in more work down the line? Decouple.

principles.text: Make components and functions require only the data they need, not whole domain types.
principles.quote: It's a good idea to make your functions and components only require the data they need to run.

principles.text: Deriving with Pick couples a type to the source's shape and its existence and location; a decoupled type survives moves, splits and deletion.
principles.quote: We can move `User` around, split it into separate interfaces, or even delete it, and `AvatarImageProps` will be unaffected.

principles.text: Don't reach for advanced features like Pick just to feel clever; the simple decoupled type is often smarter.
principles.quote: But often, it's smarter to do the simple thing, and keep your types decoupled.

sources.title: Where To Put Your Types in Application Code: three placement rules
sources.originalTitle: Where To Put Your Types in Application Code
sources.summary: Matt Pocock gives three opinionated rules for organizing types in an application: colocate or inline single-use types, move shared types to the smallest shared location, and put cross-package types in a shared monorepo package. He treats types like functions, so they follow the same sharing logic.

principles.text: Colocate single-use types in the file where they're used, instead of a separate .types file.
principles.quote: When a type is **used in only one place**, put it in **the same file where it's used**.

principles.text: Editing implementation and types together is easier when they sit in one file.
principles.quote: When I'm working on `MyComponent`, I'll often need to be editing both its implementation and its types. Having them in separate files just makes that harder.

principles.text: Inlining truly single-use types is fine and cheap to refactor later; don't feel you must always extract a named type.
principles.quote: don't feel that you _always_ need to extract out a type into a separate `type` or `interface` - inlining is absolutely fine, and it's very low-cost to refactor it into a separate type later if you need to.

principles.text: Treat types like functions: once used in multiple places, move them to a shared location.
principles.quote: You should think of types in your application as functions. If you've got a function that's used in multiple modules, you'll probably want to move it to a shared location. Same goes for types.

principles.text: Scope shared types as narrowly as possible: share across the smallest number of modules that need them.
principles.quote: In other words, I share the type across the smallest number of modules that need it.

principles.text: In a monorepo, types used by more than one package belong in a dedicated shared package.
principles.quote: Types that are **used in more than one package** in a monorepo should be **moved to a shared package**.

sources.title: Type vs Interface: default to type, use interface for object inheritance
sources.originalTitle: Type vs Interface: Which Should You Use?
sources.summary: Matt Pocock argues you should default to `type` aliases and reach for `interface` only when you need object inheritance via `extends`. He covers the performance benefit of `extends`, the surprise of declaration merging, and the implicit index signature difference, and why these push him to the opposite default from the TypeScript team.

principles.text: Default to `type` aliases; switch to `interface` only when you need a feature like `extends`.
principles.quote: You should use types by default until you need a specific feature of interfaces, like 'extends'.

principles.text: Use interfaces for objects that inherit from each other, since `extends` is cached by name and checks faster than `&`.
principles.quote: When you create an interface using `extends`, TypeScript can cache that interface by its name in an internal registry.

principles.text: Declaration merging on same-named interfaces is a surprising footgun; guard against it with the ESLint no-redeclare rule.
principles.quote: But if you're not prepared for this, it can lead to really confusing bugs.

principles.text: Type aliases have an implicit index signature that interfaces lack, so interfaces may not be assignable to Record-like types.
principles.quote: Type aliases have an implicit index signature, but interfaces don't.

principles.text: Declaration merging and implicit index signatures are surprising enough to scare you off defaulting to interfaces.
principles.quote: The features of declaration merging and implicit index signatures are surprising enough that they should scare you off using interfaces by default.

principles.text: The type vs interface difference is small, so either choice is workable; prefer the more flexible, less surprising `type`.
principles.quote: Interfaces are still my recommendation for object inheritance, but I'd recommend you use `type` by default. It's a little more flexible and a little less surprising.

sources.title: Why Matt Pocock avoids TypeScript enums and what he recommends instead
sources.originalTitle: Why I Don't Like Enums
sources.summary: Matt explains why he likes the idea of enums but won't recommend TypeScript's implementation: numeric enums generate reverse mappings and accept raw numbers, mixed enums are allowed, and enums are nominally typed, breaking the "JavaScript with types" ideal. If you must use them, use string enums only.

principles.text: TypeScript should be plain JavaScript with types; enums break that rule.
principles.quote: I like my TypeScript to be just JavaScript with types. Enums feel like they break that rule.

principles.text: Numeric enums emit both key-to-value and value-to-key maps, doubling the runtime keys.
principles.quote: Because TypeScript generates both a value-to-key and a key-to-value mapping for numeric enums.

principles.text: Numeric enums are unsafe: a raw number passes where the enum is expected.
principles.quote: But with numeric enums, you can pass a raw number in places where the enum is expected. What?

principles.text: Enums are nominally typed, so identical-valued enums aren't interchangeable.
principles.quote: you can't use an enum in place of another enum, even if the values are the same

principles.text: Don't mix numeric and string values inside one enum.
principles.quote: Hilariously, you can even mix and match numeric and string values in the same enum.

principles.text: Leave existing enums alone, but don't add them to a fresh codebase; use string enums if you must.
principles.quote: But I wouldn't add an enum to a fresh codebase.

sources.title: There Is No Such Thing As A Generic: type arguments, type parameters, and 'generic' as an adjective
sources.originalTitle: There Is No Such Thing As A Generic
sources.summary: Matt Pocock argues that 'generic' is not a noun in TypeScript. There are generic types, functions and classes, which declare type parameters and receive type arguments. Using precise vocabulary makes generics easier to learn and teach.

principles.text: 'Generic' is an adjective, not a noun: you can't pass, declare or infer 'a generic'.
principles.quote: In other words, 'generic' is not a noun, it's an adjective.

principles.text: Generics feel hard partly because the word is overloaded across functions, calls, types and declarations.
principles.quote: That's why it's such a hard concept for folks to grasp - the word is too overloaded.

principles.text: What you pass in angle brackets is a type argument, which works like a function argument.
principles.quote: We're not passing a 'generic' to `useState`. We are passing it a **type argument**.

principles.text: A type parameter is declared by the type, function or class, like a function parameter, and signals that it accepts type arguments.
principles.quote: So, a **type parameter** is like a function parameter. It declares that you can pass a type argument to the type, function, or class.

principles.text: Define generic precisely: a type, function or class that declares one or more type parameters.
principles.quote: **generic** - _adj_: a type, function, or class that declares one or more type parameters.

principles.text: Generic functions and classes infer type arguments from runtime arguments; generic types must have them passed explicitly.
principles.quote: if you don't pass a type argument to a generic function or generic class, it'll attempt to **infer it from the runtime arguments**.

sources.title: TypeScript Generics in 3 Easy Patterns: types to types, types to functions, inference
sources.originalTitle: TypeScript Generics in 3 Easy Patterns
sources.summary: Matt Pocock argues that "generics" is really three separate concepts: passing types to types, passing types to functions, and inferring types from function arguments. Splitting them apart makes generics easier to learn. Type functions like DataShape<T> remove repetition, and inference removes the need to pass types by hand.

principles.text: Generics are three distinct concepts, not one: types to types, types to functions, and inference from arguments.
principles.quote: What you might think of as generics in TypeScript is actually three separate concepts:

principles.text: Use a generic 'type function' to stay DRY when several types share a structure.
principles.quote: But it's more concise to create a 'type function', which takes in the type of data and returns the new data shape:

principles.text: A type argument works like a function argument: name it anything and treat it as a parameter.
principles.quote: We can name `TData` anything, it's just like an argument to a function.

principles.text: Generic types can take multiple type arguments, defaults and constraints.
principles.quote: Generic types can accept multiple type arguments. You can provide defaults to type arguments, as well as set constraints so only certain types can be passed.

principles.text: Functions accept type arguments just like types do, which lets you control what a function produces.
principles.quote: That's right- just like types can accept types as arguments, so can functions.

principles.text: Let TypeScript infer the type argument from the runtime argument instead of passing it manually.
principles.quote: In other words, the type argument will be inferred from the runtime argument.

sources.title: How to test your types: Vitest, Expect/Equal helpers, ts-expect-error and tsd for library authors
sources.originalTitle: How to test your types
sources.summary: Matt Pocock explains why library authors should test their types and lays out three approaches: vitest's type-testing APIs, a hand-rolled Expect/Equal helper plus ts-expect-error run through tsc, and the tsd library. He notes that type testing is rarely worth it in application code but critical for widely consumed libraries.

principles.text: If you ship library code, test your types, because they are part of the API you expose to users.
principles.quote: Types are a crucial part of your API that you're exposing to users, and you want to make sure that your logic on the type level works.

principles.text: Use vitest's type-testing APIs to colocate type tests with your runtime tests.
principles.quote: having it built into a test runner is really valuable, because it lets you colocate your type tests with your runtime tests.

principles.text: Without a type-testing runner, roll your own with Expect and Equal helpers to assert the exact type, then run tsc over the test suite.
principles.quote: You can use type helpers like `Expect` and `Equal` to be really specific with the type that you're trying to narrow to.

principles.text: Use ts-expect-error to assert that invalid usage is rejected, but know it only proves that some error occurs, not which one.
principles.quote: It's not exactly perfect since it doesn't let you be that granular - you can't check that a specific error is thrown, only that _an_ error has been thrown.

principles.text: Application code rarely justifies type tests; libraries consumed by many people do, so getting good at type testing is critical there.
principles.quote: for application development, you're rarely going to be in a position where testing your types will be worth it.

sources.title: Testing with TypeScript is painful: why test code needs looser types and how shoehorn fixes it
sources.originalTitle: Testing with TypeScript is Painful: Here's a Solution
sources.summary: Matt Pocock argues that test code shouldn't be held to the same type strictness as application code. Tests must often pass wrong or partial values, forcing noisy `as any` or `as unknown as X` casts. He introduces shoehorn, a library that makes passing partial or wrong types first-class in tests.

principles.text: Test code doesn't need the same type strictness as application code.
principles.quote: Tests don't need to live up to the same level of strictness as the rest of your application code.

principles.text: A broken type in app code means user-facing bugs; in passing tests it is often just busywork.
principles.quote: If you've got a broken type in your app, that'll likely end up in your users finding a bug.

principles.text: Tests must be able to pass the wrong type to verify a function handles bad input.
principles.quote: Sometimes, your tests will need to test that when a function receives the _wrong_ thing, it behaves in the right way.

principles.text: Double assertions like `as unknown as string` are un-ergonomic for a very common testing need.
principles.quote: This is extremely un-ergonomic - a DOUBLE assertion, just to be able to do something extremely common.

principles.text: Mocking large external types (e.g. express Request) forces repeated casts and imports everywhere.
principles.quote: In this case, you might only care about the `req.body` property. But you still need to pass the entire `Request` type to the function.

principles.text: Provide a first-class API for passing partial/wrong values in tests instead of ad hoc casts.
principles.quote: It gives you a first-class way to pass the wrong type to a function.

sources.title: Method Shorthand Syntax Considered Harmful: why to avoid bivariant method signatures in TypeScript
sources.originalTitle: Method Shorthand Syntax Considered Harmful
sources.summary: Matt Pocock explains that TypeScript's method shorthand syntax is bivariant, letting a narrower parameter type slip through and cause runtime errors the compiler never flags. Declaring members as function properties makes the check strict, and the typescript-eslint method-signature-style rule enforces it.

principles.text: Avoid method shorthand syntax in interfaces and types in almost all cases; it can cause runtime errors TypeScript won't catch.
