principles.quote: method shorthand syntax should be avoided in almost all cases.

principles.text: Method shorthand is bivariant, so it accepts parameter types narrower or wider than declared, which is the source of the unsound runtime errors.
principles.quote: This happens because the method shorthand syntax is _bivariant_. This means that the method can accept a type that is both narrower and wider than the original type.

principles.text: Declare function members with object property syntax so TypeScript rejects narrower parameter types that would break at runtime.
principles.quote: If we use object property syntax to define the method, TypeScript will throw an error if we try to assign a narrower type to the method

principles.text: The shorthand-vs-property difference has nothing to do with arrow functions versus function declarations; both work with either syntax.
principles.quote: A common misconception is that the syntax above refers to arrow functions vs function declarations. This is not the case.

principles.text: The problem occurs with both interface and type aliases, so switching between them doesn't avoid it.
principles.quote: I've used `interface` in the example above, but the same problem occurs with `type`

principles.text: Enforce the property style with the @typescript-eslint/method-signature-style rule set to "property".
principles.quote: This rule will enforce the use of the object property syntax for method signatures.

sources.title: Four essential TypeScript patterns: branded types, globals, assertion functions, classes
sources.originalTitle: Four Essential TypeScript Patterns You Can't Work Without
sources.summary: Matt Pocock argues that knowing TypeScript means combining its pieces into patterns. He walks through branded types for validation boundaries, declare global for typing globals, type predicates and assertion functions for narrowing, and classes for builder-style library design.

principles.text: Knowing TypeScript means combining its pieces into patterns, not just knowing generics and conditional types individually.
principles.quote: There’s a difference between using TypeScript and **_knowing_** TypeScript.

principles.text: Use branded types to create validation boundaries: validate once, then pass the value around safely.
principles.quote: This creates validation boundaries in your app’s code - you can validate that something is a valid password, then safely pass it around your application.

principles.text: If you use globals in JavaScript, you must be able to describe them in TypeScript, using declare global.
principles.quote: Love them or hate them, globals are a part of the way we use JavaScript. And if we use them in JavaScript, we need to be able to describe them in TypeScript.

principles.text: Type predicates let a boolean-returning function describe its argument, improving narrowing such as filtering out undefined.
principles.quote: Type predicates let you specify that a function returns a boolean which _describes_ one of the arguments passed to it

principles.text: Assertion functions throw inside a function to assert a value's type, improving TypeScript's narrowing.
principles.quote: Both of these patterns let you improve TypeScript’s ability to narrow your code.

principles.text: Classes are a pragmatic tool in library code, notably for the builder pattern that underpins tRPC.
principles.quote: when you’re writing TS in library-land, classes are a force of pragmatic utility that you can’t sleep on.

sources.title: TypeScript types don't exist at runtime: what gets erased and the exceptions
sources.originalTitle: No, TypeScript Types Don't Exist At Runtime
sources.summary: Matt Pocock corrects a common misconception: TypeScript types are erased at compile time and have no runtime effect. He walks through types, type assertions and function parameters as examples, then covers the exceptions (enums, namespaces, parameter properties) and why TypeScript's modern philosophy is to only add types to JavaScript.

principles.text: TypeScript types exist only at compile time; they are erased and never influence runtime behavior.
principles.quote: TypeScript's types don't exist at runtime. They're only used to help you catch errors at compile time.

principles.text: Type assertions are not runtime checks, so they can cause runtime errors and are discouraged.
principles.quote: Just because `num` has been asserted to be a number doesn't mean it is one at runtime.

principles.text: Parameter types don't validate arguments at runtime; the emitted JavaScript contains no checking code.
principles.quote: Notice that there is no extra code in the transpiled JavaScript to check that `add` is being called with the right arguments.

principles.text: Enums, namespaces and parameter properties are the exceptions that have a runtime representation.
principles.quote: Most features in TypeScript disappear at runtime, but these three are the exception.

principles.text: TypeScript's job is adding types to JavaScript, not new language features; those old features wouldn't be added today.
principles.quote: If enums, namespaces or parameter properties were proposed now, they wouldn't be added to TypeScript.

principles.text: A useful rule of thumb: TypeScript is just JavaScript plus types, apart from the three runtime exceptions.
principles.quote: thinking of TypeScript as just adding types to JavaScript is a useful rule of thumb - with the exception of enums, namespaces and parameter properties.

sources.title: Handle Errors with a Generic Result Type: Matt Pocock on explicit error handling in TypeScript
sources.originalTitle: Handle Errors with a Generic Result Type
sources.summary: Matt shows a generic Result<TResult, TError> discriminated union, modeled on Rust, as an alternative to try/catch. Checking result.success narrows to typed data or typed error, which makes error flow explicit in complicated imperative code.

principles.text: Model results as a generic discriminated union with success and error branches.
principles.quote: We have a type result is tResult and tError, so there's two type parameters on result. And we're returning a discriminated union here

principles.text: Checking the success flag narrows the type, so data is safely typed in the success branch.
principles.quote: when we get this result back, we can actually check if result.success, we end up with result.data and it's typed as number.

principles.text: The compiler enforces returning the right shape in each branch of the Result.
principles.quote: it's going to yell at me if I don't return the right thing in the right branch because type number is not assignable to type string.

principles.text: A Result type avoids try/catch as the default error check, as Rust does.
principles.quote: if you've ever used Rust before, you might notice that this is how Rust handles errors. And this is just lovely because it means that you don't have to do any try-catching.

principles.text: try/catch errors are untyped and can obscure where failures originate across boundaries.
principles.quote: the error that you get back is not safe as we've seen in previous exercises. And it means that you can just end up with really complicated logic where you're catching errors at certain boundaries and you're not quite sure where they're coming from.

principles.text: Result makes error flow explicit: check success, proceed, else handle the error.
principles.quote: it's pretty explicit and it means that you can just say, is my result a success? If so, proceed. If not, handle that error.

sources.title: The /code-review Skill: reviewing a diff against repo standards and the spec in separate axes
sources.originalTitle: The /code-review Skill
sources.summary: Describes Matt Pocock's code-review agent skill, which reviews a diff along two independent axes (Standards and Spec), each in its own sub-agent. Covers prerequisites, the Fowler smell baseline, and known pitfalls: name clash, runaway sub-agents, self-review bias, and non-convergence.

principles.text: Review along two independent axes, Standards and Spec, never blended into one verdict.
principles.quote: The skill never merges or re-ranks the two axes. The report ends with a worst issue _per axis_ and declines to name a single winner across them.

principles.text: A blended verdict lets a passing axis hide a failing one; code can follow conventions yet build the wrong thing.
principles.quote: A blended verdict lets the passing axis hide the failing one.

principles.text: Run each review axis in its own sub-agent so neither sees the other's reasoning.
principles.quote: Each axis runs in its own sub-agent so neither sees the other's reasoning.

principles.text: Make the repo's own documented standards the primary source and let them override any generic baseline.
principles.quote: So the repo's own documentation is the primary source on the Standards axis, and **the repo always overrides**.

principles.text: Review in a fresh session, not the one that wrote the code, to avoid confirmation bias.
principles.quote: An agent that reviews in the authoring session has every assumption that shaped the code in its context.

principles.text: Treat sub-agent findings as hypotheses and require every finding to carry a checkable citation.
principles.quote: Sub-agent output is a hypothesis, not evidence.

sources.title: The /codebase-design skill: the vocabulary Matt Pocock uses for designing deep modules
sources.originalTitle: The /codebase-design Skill
sources.summary: Describes Matt Pocock's codebase-design skill, a reference glossary (module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality) plus four principles for designing deep modules. Covers its limits as a reference rather than a process, and how it relates to neighbouring skills and agent workflows.

principles.text: Depth is leverage at the interface, not a ratio of implementation to interface lines.
principles.quote: The skill does _not_ define depth as the ratio of implementation lines to interface lines, which is Ousterhout's own definition. That metric rewards padding the implementation, so the skill uses depth-as-leverage instead.

principles.text: Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation; internals can be many small swappable parts.
principles.quote: **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be built internally from small swappable parts. Callers just don't see them.

principles.text: Use the deletion test: if complexity vanishes when you delete a module, it was a pass-through.
principles.quote: Imagine deleting the module. If complexity disappears, the module was a pass-through. If it reappears across N callers, the module was hiding real complexity.

principles.text: The interface is the test surface; wanting to test past it means the module is the wrong shape.
principles.quote: Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test _past_ the interface, the module is the wrong shape.

principles.text: Don't cut a seam until something varies across it; one adapter is just indirection.
principles.quote: **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't cut a seam until something varies across it. A single-adapter seam is just indirection.

principles.text: An interface is everything a caller must know, not just the type signature.
principles.quote: Everything a caller must know to use it correctly: the type signature, plus invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required config, performance characteristics.

sources.title: The /tdd skill: Matt Pocock's rules for a red-green loop with coding agents
sources.originalTitle: The /tdd Skill
sources.summary: Explains Matt's /tdd agent skill: build one failing test at a time at pre-agreed seams, write just enough code, and avoid three anti-patterns (implementation-coupled, tautological, horizontal slicing). Also covers why refactoring was dropped, mocking rules, and honest limits of agents following the loop.

principles.text: Work in vertical slices: one test, minimal implementation, repeat. Never write all tests first.
principles.quote: Write one test at one seam, then the minimal implementation, then repeat. The first cycle is a **tracer bullet** that proves a single path end to end.

principles.text: Agree test seams (public boundaries) with the human before any test is written; no exceptions.
principles.quote: A seam is the public boundary you observe behaviour at without reaching inside. The rule has no exceptions. No test goes at an unconfirmed seam.

principles.text: Tests that break on internal renames are implementation-coupled; test behaviour through the public interface.
principles.quote: The test breaks when you rename an internal function, though behaviour did not change. Mocked internal collaborators, asserted call counts, database queries used to verify instead of the interface.

principles.text: Expected values must come from an independent source, not be computed the way the code computes them.
principles.quote: The expected value is computed the way the code computes it, so the test passes by construction. Expected values have to come from somewhere else: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.

principles.text: Mock only system boundaries (external APIs, time, randomness), never your own modules.
principles.quote: Mocks are for system boundaries only: external APIs, time, randomness, sometimes the filesystem or the database. Never mock your own modules.

principles.text: Don't expect agents to comply 100% with a skill; the loop is worth running anyway, and you should watch runs when strictness matters.
principles.quote: No instruction makes an agent comply 100% of the time, and stricter wording restricts the agent's creativity for little gain. The loop is worth running even when the agent does not follow it strictly, because the results are still better overall.

sources.title: The /improve-codebase-architecture skill: finding shallow modules worth deepening
sources.originalTitle: The /improve-codebase-architecture Skill
sources.summary: Describes a skill that surveys a codebase for deepening opportunities (shallow modules that could become deep), writes a visual HTML report, and then grills you on the candidate you pick. It never changes code; it queues up refactors for a later spec-and-build flow.

principles.text: Deep modules put lots of behaviour behind a small, stable interface; shallow ones expose their implementation.
principles.quote: A deep module puts a lot of behaviour behind a small, stable interface. A shallow module exposes its implementation through an interface nearly as wide as the code beneath it.

principles.text: Apply the deletion test: only flag modules whose complexity would move behind a smaller interface if removed.
principles.quote: if you removed this module, would its complexity move behind a smaller interface, or spread across the callers? Only the first case gets a card.

principles.text: Focus architecture review on frequently changing code; deepening untouched code never pays back.
principles.quote: A deepening in code that nobody touches is a refactor that never pays back.

principles.text: Treat architecture review as a survey, not a refactor: it outputs a decision, and implementation goes through the normal build flow.
principles.quote: The output of that session is a decision, not a diff. From there the normal flow applies: take the decision into to-spec, then to-tickets, then implement.

principles.text: Prompt the review with the next thing you are building: ask how to make the change easy.
principles.quote: point it at the spec and ask "how can we make this change easy?"

principles.text: Work one refactor candidate per session to keep the context window from filling with report, grilling and edits.
principles.quote: Use one candidate per session.

sources.title: The /diagnosing-bugs skill: no theories until a tight, red-capable feedback loop exists
sources.originalTitle: The /diagnosing-bugs Skill
sources.summary: Matt Pocock describes his diagnosing-bugs agent skill, a six-phase process that forbids an agent from theorising until it has a fast, deterministic, sharp repro command that goes red on the bug. It covers the gates between phases, hypothesis ranking, tagged instrumentation, regression tests, and known limitations.

principles.text: Block the agent from forming theories until a command exists that goes red on this exact bug.
principles.quote: It will not let the agent form a theory until a **tight** feedback loop exists: one named command, already run once, that goes red on _this_ bug and green when it is fixed.

principles.text: By default, coding agents read code and guess at bugs; a repro loop gate stops that.
principles.quote: Given a bug report, a coding agent by default reads code and guesses. This skill blocks that.

principles.text: A useful loop is tight: fast, deterministic, sharp on your symptom, and runnable without you.
principles.quote: _A_ loop is not the goal. **Tight** is: fast (seconds), deterministic (same verdict every run), sharp (asserts your exact symptom, not "didn't crash"), and runnable by the agent without you.

principles.text: For intermittent bugs, aim to raise the reproduction rate rather than get a clean repro.
principles.quote: For a bug that only shows up sometimes, the target is not a clean repro but a **higher reproduction rate**: loop the trigger, parallelise, add stress, inject sleeps, until the flake rate is high enough to debug against.

principles.text: If no loop can be built, the agent must stop, say so, and ask for access instead of guessing.
principles.quote: When the agent cannot build one, the skill tells it to stop and say so, list what it tried, and ask you for environment access, a captured artifact, or permission to add temporary instrumentation.

principles.text: Show ranked, falsifiable hypotheses with predictions before testing any; tag debug logs so cleanup is one grep.
principles.quote: 3–5 ranked, falsifiable hypotheses exist, each stating its prediction, shown to you before any is tested

sources.title: The /pr Skill: PR bodies with a visual summary, before/after evidence, and a one-way/two-way door call
sources.originalTitle: The /pr Skill
sources.summary: Matt Pocock explains his `pr` skill, which defines the shape of a pull request body: Summary (smallest useful visual), Evidence (before and after), and Merge Danger (one-way vs two-way door plus blast radius). It also covers limits: the agent grading its own door call is suspect, and the skill only writes the body.

principles.text: A PR summary should be a visual of the change's shape, not a prose description of the diff.
principles.quote: The summary is a visual, not a paragraph.

principles.text: Pick the smallest view that makes the key point clear and keep surrounding words brief.
principles.quote: This one picks the **smallest view** that makes the key point clear (pseudocode, a call tree, a component tree, a file tree, a Mermaid diagram, or a shaped diff) and keeps the words around it brief.

principles.text: Evidence must be a before and after (screenshot, failing-then-passing test, changed output), not a claim that tests pass.
principles.quote: "Tests are green" on its own is a claim, not a before and after.

principles.text: State whether a change is a one-way or two-way door so reviewers can disagree with an explicit claim and spend attention accordingly.
principles.quote: It changes "is this safe to merge?" from a gut feeling into a stated claim the reviewer can disagree with.

principles.text: Be most suspicious of the agent's own 'two-way, small blast radius' call, since the author is grading its own change.
principles.quote: The agent that wrote the change is the one grading it, so be most suspicious when it says "two-way, small blast radius".

principles.text: Give the agent the ticket or spec, not just the diff, and document your repo's always-one-way changes where it will read them.
principles.quote: make sure the agent has the [ticket](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/ticket) or [spec](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/spec) in front of it, not just the diff

sources.title: How to make codebases AI agents love: deep modules and grey box design
sources.originalTitle: How To Make Codebases AI Agents Love
sources.summary: Matt Pocock argues the codebase, not the prompt or AGENTS.md, is the biggest influence on AI output. Restructure into deep modules with simple interfaces, tests that lock behaviour, and AI-owned implementations, so agents get fast feedback and humans keep a small mental map.

principles.text: Treat AI agents as memoryless new starters; the codebase shapes output more than prompts or AGENTS.md.
principles.quote: Your codebase, way more than your prompt or your `AGENTS.md` file, is the biggest influence on AI's output.

principles.text: A badly designed codebase costs you through poor feedback loops, hard navigation, and cognitive burnout.
principles.quote: AI is not a super-powered developer. It's a new starter with no memory.

principles.text: Make the file system and design match your internal mental map, using deep modules.
principles.quote: The file system and design of your codebase needs to match the internal map you have of it. The best way I've found to do that is with **deep modules**.

principles.text: Deep modules put lots of implementation behind a simple interface; all exports go through it.
principles.quote: Deep modules comes from "A Philosophy of Software Design." The idea is simple: lots of implementation controlled by a simple interface.

principles.text: Grey box modules: you own the interface, AI owns the implementation, tests keep it honest.
principles.quote: These are **grey box modules**. You own the interface. AI owns the implementation. Tests keep it honest.

principles.text: Design for progressive disclosure of complexity: each module in its own folder with a clear public interface.
principles.quote: **We've designed our codebase for progressive disclosure of complexity.** The interface sits at the top and explains what the module does.

sources.title: Essential AI coding feedback loops for TypeScript projects: type checking, tests, pre-commit hooks
sources.originalTitle: Essential AI Coding Feedback Loops For TypeScript Projects
sources.summary: Matt Pocock explains how to give AI coding agents, especially AFK ones, ways to verify their own work. He recommends TypeScript type checking, automated tests, Husky pre-commit hooks and lint-staged formatting. Failures block commits, so agents retry until the code passes.

principles.text: AI agents working independently need feedback loops so they can verify their own work.
principles.quote: When working with AI coding agents, especially those operating independently, you need feedback loops so the AI can verify its own work.

principles.text: TypeScript gives AI agents free feedback, so prefer it over JavaScript and expose a typecheck script.
principles.quote: TypeScript is essentially free feedback for your AI. Use it over JavaScript.

principles.text: Type checking catches errors an agent would never find without running the code in a browser.
principles.quote: TypeScript catches errors the AI would never find without testing in a browser.

principles.text: Add automated tests, even basic unit tests of core functionality, to catch logical errors and keep the AI on track.
principles.quote: Basic unit tests covering core functionality help keep the AI on track.

principles.text: Enforce feedback loops with pre-commit hooks that run lint-staged, typecheck and tests; a failure blocks the commit and returns an error to the AI.
principles.quote: If any step fails, the commit is blocked and the AI gets an error message.

principles.text: Agents don't tire of repetition, so on failure they simply retry. That makes feedback loops, pre-commit hooks especially, very powerful.
principles.quote: AI agents don't get frustrated by repetition. When code fails type checking or tests, the agent simply tries again.

sources.title: Tracer Bullets: how to stop AI agents outrunning their headlights
sources.originalTitle: Tracer Bullets: Keeping AI Slop Under Control
sources.summary: Matt argues AI agents' sycophancy makes them build whole horizontal layers in isolation, producing slop and a heavy review burden. The fix is the Pragmatic Programmer's tracer bullet: one thin end-to-end slice, tested immediately, then repeated in a fresh context window. He supplies a prompt to force this.

principles.text: AI's sycophancy makes it build complete solutions in one leap without validating assumptions, which produces slop.
principles.quote: It doesn't stop to validate assumptions or get feedback. It just keeps going, building entire layers in isolation, without ever testing whether the critical path actually works.

principles.text: Build one thin vertical slice through every layer, test it, get feedback, then move to the next slice in a fresh context window.
principles.quote: Instead of building horizontal layers in isolation, you build one tiny vertical slice:

principles.text: Agents outrun their headlights when they build without feedback loops; tracer bullets build those loops into the process.
principles.quote: The AI is building too much in the dark, without feedback loops to validate assumptions early.

principles.text: Be explicit in prompts, because the agent's default is big isolated layers rather than an end-to-end slice.
principles.quote: You have to be extremely explicit with your prompt. AI's natural inclination is to build big layers in isolation.

principles.text: When breaking down a task, make the first item a tracer bullet: the backend wired to a single UI location, not all of them.
principles.quote: Rather than building all four UI locations at once, I focused the AI on building just one end-to-end slice: the backend endpoint connected to a single UI location.

principles.text: Classic practices like tracer bullets and TDD apply even harder to AI because context window limits make the discipline non-negotiable.
principles.quote: But the principles apply harder to AI than they ever did to humans.

sources.title: Never Run Claude /init: Matt Pocock on keeping CLAUDE.md nearly empty
sources.originalTitle: Never Run Claude /init
sources.summary: Matt argues that auto-generated CLAUDE.md or agents.md files burn tokens, eat the agent's instruction budget, and go stale. He recommends trusting the agent's explore step, putting steering in skills, and keeping CLAUDE.md to only what is undiscoverable and globally relevant.

principles.text: Never run the agent init command; delete any auto-generated CLAUDE.md or agents.md you find.
principles.quote: Never run it. If you find one that was auto-generated, delete it.

principles.text: The system prompt is hardwired at start, so every CLAUDE.md line shrinks room for exploration, implementation and testing.
principles.quote: But the system prompt is hardwired the moment the agent starts. Everything in your CLAUDE.md inflates it, leaving less room for the phases that actually do the work.

principles.text: LLMs have an instruction budget of roughly 300 to 400 instructions; irrelevant CLAUDE.md lines burn it before work begins.
principles.quote: If you're stuffing dozens of irrelevant instructions into CLAUDE.md, you're burning that budget before the agent even starts working on your task.

principles.text: CLAUDE.md is global, so a rule added for one kind of session taxes every other session.
principles.quote: Every line you add has a cost that compounds across every session, whether it's relevant or not.

principles.text: Init output is either trivially discoverable from source or will go stale, and stale file references actively mislead the agent.
principles.quote: The throughline: everything init generates is either trivially discoverable from source or will go stale. Your file system is the documentation.

principles.text: Put steering in skills the agent pulls in when relevant; CLAUDE.md should hold only what is both undiscoverable and globally relevant.
principles.quote: That's the bar: only include what is both undiscoverable and globally relevant.

sources.title: How AI coding rewired Matt Pocock's brain: tests, deep modules, and friction
sources.originalTitle: 9 Ways AI Coding Has Rewired My Brain
sources.summary: Matt Pocock lists nine shifts after months of fully AI-written code. He now invests in integration tests, strong feedback loops (types, hooks, CI), deep grey-box modules, aggressive UI prototyping, and just-in-time docs, while managing the extra cognitive load of keeping up with agent changes.

principles.text: Raise test boundaries to integration/e2e level so AI agents can run code and you catch more bugs.
principles.quote: Raising test boundaries lets you catch more bugs and work more comfortably with AI agents running code automatically.

principles.text: Run pre-commit hooks, CI and type checking on every AI change; immediate feedback gives agents real-world context.
principles.quote: Every single change the AI makes should trigger your pre-commit hooks, CI, and type checking so bugs get caught immediately.

principles.text: Prototype UI aggressively: ask for several options on throwaway routes before committing to a PRD.
principles.quote: Ask the LLM for five different options for the UI change. Put them on throwaway routes so you can look at them.

principles.text: Prefer a few deep modules with simple interfaces over many shallow modules with big interfaces.
principles.quote: Bad codebases have lots of shallow modules with big interfaces. Good codebases have a few big modules with simple interfaces.

principles.text: Treat deep modules as grey boxes: test at the boundaries and leave the implementation to the AI.
principles.quote: Break your codebase into large modules and test at the boundaries. Then leave the implementation to the AI.

principles.text: Avoid stuffing repos with markdown docs; they rot and confuse LLMs. Let the AI generate docs just in time.
principles.quote: Let the AI generate its own docs during the exploration phase instead. Those docs never go out of date because they're just-in-time generated.

sources.title: Matt Pocock Q&A: Why TypeScript fits alongside JavaScript, inference, generics, and failing early
sources.originalTitle: Matt Pocock: Q&A transcript (January 2023)
sources.summary: Matt Pocock, in a January 2023 Reactiflux Q&A, covers how TypeScript shortens feedback loops, why generics and inference improve team developer experience, and why avoiding codegen and validating external data with Zod keeps apps robust. He also covers his path from voice coaching to XState, Vercel and Total TypeScript.

principles.text: TypeScript's core benefit is a shorter time to error; catch mistakes in the IDE, not the browser or production.
principles.quote: The time from when you make a mistake to when you know about the mistake in TypeScript is smaller than JavaScript.

principles.text: Prefer inference through ordinary APIs over a codegen step when you can; codegen adds a sidecar process and a worse experience.
principles.quote: if you can avoid it, then avoiding the codegen step is the way to go.

principles.text: Use discriminated and union types so TypeScript checks every possible case of your code, especially for component props.
principles.quote: Union types in TypeScript let you basically see into every possible future of your code

principles.text: Adding generics to a function means teammates never need to annotate; advanced TypeScript effort shifts burden off the team.
principles.quote: when you add a generic to a function, you're basically saying when people use this function, they won't need to annotate it in any way.

principles.text: TypeScript types are not runtime safe; validate third-party and external data with a schema library like Zod so failures happen early.
principles.quote: TypeScript is not actually type safe. It just gives you the feeling of being type safe.

principles.text: Design data structures and types before writing runtime code; it gives you velocity and avoids falling back to any.
principles.quote: doing the types before you start working on the runtime stuff that can give you a lot of extra velocity going forward.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt argues AI-driven PR volume needs "brakes" so a software factory doesn't become a slop cannon. He layers cheap automated checks, a separate coding-standards reviewer agent that commits fixes, and a human-friendly PR (merge danger, diagrams, retro) so human review gets faster.

chunks.heading: Matt's model for the PR bottleneck: speed needs brakes
chunks.text:
- Matt describes a "software factory" as a setup where agents and deterministic code initiate work, not just humans. Examples: a classifier that turns a bug report into a fix or reproduction, or PlanetScale slow-query reports triggering a pipeline.
- This acceleration pushes more PRs through, which risks a "slop cannon" of PRs nobody can review.
- He argues you need brakes that raise quality and let you go faster counterintuitively, because "code is the environment your agent operates in" and bad code begets more bad code.
- The three brakes form a layered cake: automated checks (lint, tests, type checking, code quality metrics), automated review (agents), then human review.
- The goal is faster human review by leaning on the first two layers. Higher-quality code means fewer human interventions.

chunks.heading: Automated checks are cheap, but they can lie
chunks.text:
- Checks cost CPU cycles, not tokens or human effort, so Matt says you can layer on loads of them and most people don't use enough or aren't creative enough.
- A green CI does not mean the code is ready to merge. Automated and human review are "lie detectors" for finding lies in the checks.
- Tautological tests: a test that reasserts the implementation. His agent (he says Opus 5 got "addicted" to these) wrote `expect(X_POST_CHARACTER_LIMIT).toBe(280)` against a constant set to 280. This ties the test to structure: you can't change or rename the constant without a failing test.
- A worse example: a UI-order test that reads the module's source file into memory and asserts the videos section appears after the content plan in the source text, rather than rendering anything. Changing how the source looks breaks it.
- Tests that cannot fail: a `useAudioBoost` hook test stubs the DOM `AudioContext` API with fake methods. Real `AudioContext` has complicated error modes, so the stub hides them and production hits errors the tests can't catch.
- Matt notes the agent isn't acting in bad faith; it follows instructions and writes tests tied to structure rather than executing real code.

chunks.heading: Design the codebase so checks are harder to cheat
chunks.text:
- Matt's first fix is codebase design: deep modules, from John Ousterhout's *A Philosophy of Software Design*. A deep module hides complex behavior behind a simple interface; a shallow one exposes many small functions that each do little.
- Deep modules mean fewer structure-sensitive tests, because tests sit at the small interface instead of reaching into implementation details. The job is to force agents to use that interface.
- His skill for improving architecture works even on a badly vibe-coded codebase. It outputs an HTML document of opportunities for deepening modules, with before/after views showing reduced duplication and a testable deep module, which you can then implement.
- A codebase design skill defines a shared vocabulary, since reading about structure turns up "20 different approaches" all called DDD. Terms include locality (how well changes stay together, so a small change doesn't ripple), leverage (callers get a lot of value from a simple call to a deep module), and seam. Both help agents too.

chunks.heading: Keep coding standards out of the implementer agent
chunks.text:
- Matt's advice: "don't put coding standards in your implementer agent." The implementer's single context window is already overloaded: exploring code, changing files, and debugging against the automated checks. Adding standards makes it perform worse.
- Instead, use a code review skill that takes a diff, reads a customizable `coding-standards.md` in the repo, and checks the code against it, run in a sub-agent with its own context window.
- Review is underloaded: it needs some exploration for wider context, but no implementation or debugging, so you can pile coding standards into it.
- He frames this as a two-part process: implement to make it work, then review to make it good. He compares it to red-green-refactor, with one context window for red-green and another for refactor.
- Don't put the standards in global scope like `AGENTS.md`, where they drown out the implementer. Put them in `coding-standards.md` so only the review agent reads them.

chunks.heading: Build your own automated reviewer, and make it commit
chunks.text:
- Many people told Matt they use third-party reviewers such as Cursor Bugbot or CodeRabbit. He says "don't outsource automated review. Build your own."
- His reason: generic review skills either give irrelevant false positives when too general, or exclude users when too specific (a TypeScript-focused one doesn't help Rust people).
- Build coding standards over time and share them across the team. Docs nobody reads are a good source to pour in.
- The reviewer should commit fixes, not just comment on the PR. Comments create more work for the human, who must read verbose notes and decide what to implement. If it has genuine questions it can comment, but "the default should be commits."
- His summary: stop trying to one-shot good code by making the implementer perfect.

chunks.heading: A human-friendly PR body
chunks.text:
- Matt is finishing a PR skill (due soon), built by "steal[ing] all the best ideas that everyone's got."
- Principle one: some reviews matter more than others. Classify PRs with AWS's one-way door vs two-way door idea. Most PRs are two-way doors you can revert.
- One-way doors need heavy review: a change that accidentally emails 60,000 people, expensive migrations, data loss. Also assess blast radius: what can go wrong and how bad it is.
- Each PR ends with a "merge danger" summary, for example "two-way door, blast radius localized," so he knows how much attention to give.
- Principle two: explain what the PR does using pseudocode, diagrams and images instead of prose. He credits the "show me" skill from Dex Horthy's HumanLayer skills repo (the transcript renders the name as "Dex Hadley"). Mermaid and UML sequence diagrams help, and so do simple visuals, like a CLI diagram showing a new command and two new flags.

chunks.heading: Review the system that produces the code: the retro skill
chunks.text:
- Matt's third principle: treat the process that produces your code as important as the code. Human review reviews the system, and "you never want to write the same comment twice."
- His new `retro` skill (retrospective) takes a single agent session, a PR plus its session, or a batch of the last week's PRs and reviews, and suggests automated checks and `coding-standards.md` updates to improve the next round.
- It also checks navigation pointers (can a pointer in `AGENTS.md` help the agent find information next time), tool economy (can tools be made more token efficient, which he says is hard to debug from outside), and bloat in steering files or skills.
- The compounding effect: human review makes the next review's quality higher and saves work later.
- His conclusion: layer automated checks and automated review so human review is "as painless, as simple, and as kind of optional" as needed. You don't need to review every two-way door, but you do review every one-way door.
- His skills are at aihero.dev/skills, with version 1.3 shipping that week.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock argues that "specs-to-code" produces ever-worse code because it divests from design, and that classic books (Ousterhout, Pragmatic Programmer, Brooks, DDD, Beck) give the fixes. He walks through AI coding failure modes with a skill for each: grilling for shared understanding, a ubiquitous language, TDD, deep modules, and delegating implementation behind designed interfaces.

chunks.heading: Deep modules beat shallow modules for AI-friendly, testable codebases
chunks.text:
- Matt draws on John Ousterhout's *A Philosophy of Software Design*: a bad codebase is a complex one, meaning anything in the structure that "makes it hard to understand and modify the system." Good codebases are easy to change.
- He prefers relatively few large, deep modules with simple interfaces over many shallow modules.
  - Deep module: lots of functionality hidden behind a simple interface. You can look inside if you want to, but you don't need to.
  - Shallow module: little functionality behind a complex interface.
- AI is "really good at creating codebases" full of shallow modules (many tiny blobs), and those are hard for it to explore. It may not reach the right module in time or may miss dependencies, so it doesn't understand what the code does.
- Matt's fix is a reusable skill, "Improve codebase architecture": explore the codebase, look for related code, and wrap it in a deep module.
- Deep modules are testable because the boundary is simple. You test and verify at the interface, which makes the codebase "reward" TDD.
- Matt says good codebases are easy to test, so the better the codebase, the better the feedback loops, and the better the code the LLM produces.

chunks.heading: Design the interface, delegate the implementation
chunks.text:
- Shipping more code than ever leaves Matt's brain unable to keep up. He says he's more tired than ever in his development career, and a codebase of shallow modules makes it worse because both he and the AI must hold everything in their heads.
- With deep modules he treats each one as a "gray box." He designs the interface carefully, controls it closely, and leaves the implementation to the AI, with less review of the internals.
- He caveats this: it works for less critical modules, not for things like finance.
- Conditions he sets: a testable boundary outside the module, and understanding its purpose well enough to design it from the outside.
- His summary: "Design the interface, delegate the implementation." He says this saved his brain.
- He needs to know the module map really well. It should be part of the ubiquitous language and built into planning skills. His write-a-PRD skill specifies module changes and how each module's interface is modified.
- He cites Kent Beck: "Invest in the design of the system every day."

chunks.heading: Why specs-to-code fails and why code is not cheap
chunks.text:
- Matt describes the specs-to-code movement: write a spec, have AI generate code, and when something is wrong, edit the spec and re-run the "compiler" without looking at the code.
- He tried it. Each re-run produced worse code, ending in garbage. He calls it "vibe coding by another name."
- He ties this to software entropy from *The Pragmatic Programmer*. If every change considers only that change and not the whole system's design, the codebase gets worse and worse.
- He rejects the premise that "code is cheap." His view: "bad code is the most expensive it's ever been." A codebase that is hard to change can't capture what AI offers, while AI does very well in a good codebase.
- His thesis: good codebases matter more than ever, so software fundamentals matter more than ever.
- Specs-to-code divests from system design, while he wants to invest in it.
- His model of roles: AI is a tactical programmer, "a sergeant on the ground making the code changes." Someone must think at the strategic level, and that's the human. It requires fundamentals engineers have used for 20+ years.

chunks.heading: Failure mode: the AI didn't build what I wanted (Grill Me)
chunks.text:
- Cause, per *The Pragmatic Programmer*: no one knows exactly what they want, and there is a communication barrier between you and the AI. The AI's conversation with you is its requirements gathering.
- He cites Frederick P. Brooks' *The Design of Design* and the "design concept": the ephemeral, invisible theory of the thing being built that floats between collaborators. It isn't an asset or a markdown file. When AI goes wrong, he and the AI don't share a design concept.
- His skill, "Grill Me": "Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this plan until we reach a shared understanding. Walk down each branch of the design tree, resolving dependencies between decisions one by one."
  - A few lines make the AI ask 40, 60, or even 100 questions, turning it into an adversary.
  - The skill's repo has around 13,000 stars.
  - The resulting conversation can become a PRD, or for small changes, issues directly, which an AFK agent then picks up.
- He believes it's better than the default plan mode in Claude Code, which is "extremely eager to create an asset" and start working. He prefers reaching a shared design concept first.

chunks.heading: Failure mode: the AI is too verbose (ubiquitous language)
chunks.text:
- Verbosity feels like talking at cross-purposes with the AI. It resembles a developer working with a domain expert (his example: microchips) when no shared vocabulary exists, so terms get mistranslated into code neither side understands.
- Matt turned to domain-driven design (DDD), which he's still exploring but says is "music to my ears." Its concept is the ubiquitous language: developer conversations, code, and domain expert conversations all derive from the same domain model.
- In practice it's a markdown file listing the terms you and the AI share. Use those terms consistently in code, in talking about code, with domain experts, and with AI.
- His skill: the "ubiquitous language" skill scans the codebase for terminology and generates a markdown file of tables. He passes it to the AI and keeps it open himself while grilling and planning.
- Reading the AI's thinking traces, he found it improves planning, lets the AI think less verbosely, and makes implementation align better with what was planned. He calls it a "powerhouse."

chunks.heading: Failure mode: it built the right thing but it doesn't work (feedback loops and TDD)
chunks.text:
- Obvious fixes: static types ("if you're not using TypeScript, that's crazy"), giving the LLM browser access for front-end apps, and automated tests.
- Even with these loops, LLMs use them badly compared to a veteran developer. They produce a huge amount of code, then think to type check or run a test afterward.
- *The Pragmatic Programmer* calls this "outrunning your headlights." The rate of feedback is your speed limit, so take small deliberate steps and test as you go.
- His third skill: TDD. It forces the LLM into small steps: write a test, make it pass, then refactor with design in mind.
- Testing has always been hard because of interdependent decisions: unit size, what to mock, which behaviors to test. A very large unit may be flaky, and testing one unit means mocking another.
- His conclusion from years of thinking about it: good codebases are easy to test, which leads to deep modules.

chunks.heading: Where to find his skills and training
chunks.text:
- The skills are in his GitHub repo, mattpocock/skills (spoken as "macpocockskills" in the transcript).
- He teaches a course on Claude Code for real engineers, and also publishes on YouTube, on Twitter, and at aihero.dev, where he has a newsletter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2-hour workshop where Matt applies old-school software engineering fundamentals to coding agents. He covers the smart/dumb zone, aligning with a "grill me" session, a PRD as destination, vertical-slice Kanban issues, AFK Ralph loops with TDD, and deepening modules so code bases are testable.

chunks.heading: Why the smart zone and the Memento constraint drive Matt's whole AI coding workflow
chunks.text:
- LLMs have a "smart zone" and a "dumb zone" (a idea Matt credits to Dex Hardy of Human Layer). A fresh context does its best work, and each added token strains attention relationships, which scale quadratically, like adding a team to a football league.
- Matt puts the dumb-zone boundary at roughly 100K tokens, regardless of whether the window is 200K or 1 million. He says the 1M window "shipped a lot more dumb zone" to people. It helps retrieval (e.g. large documents), not coding.
- Size tasks to fit the smart zone. This is old advice (Refactoring, The Pragmatic Programmer): don't bite off more than you can chew.
- LLMs are "like the guy from Memento": a session goes system prompt, exploration, implementation, testing, and clearing returns to the system prompt. Keep the always-on system prompt tiny (he's seen people put 250K tokens there).
- Matt prefers clearing to compacting. A cleared context returns to the same known state every time, so he optimizes for that. Compacting leaves sediment.
- He keeps a status line showing the exact token count in every session, "absolutely essential" to know how close you are to the dumb zone. He has an article on this on AI Hero.
- Multi-phase plans (phase 1, 2, 3, 4) are really a loop. Matt used them until December last year, then moved toward Ralph Wiggum-style loops (a PRD for the destination, then "make a small change that gets us closer"), but prefers more structure than plain Ralph.

chunks.heading: Grill-me: reaching a shared design concept before any plan
chunks.text:
- Matt starts virtually every piece of work with a `grill me` skill, invoked as `/grill-me` plus the input (in the demo, a Slack message from a client about adding gamification to a course platform).
- The skill is tiny: "Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this plan until we reach a shared understanding. Walk down each branch of the decision tree resolving dependencies one by one. For each question provide your recommended answer." One question at a time.
- Motivation: in plan mode the AI eagerly produces a plan too early. He wanted what Frederick P. Brooks calls the "design concept" in The Design of Design, a shared idea between all participants. "I didn't need a plan, I needed to be on the same wavelength as the AI."
- The AI first explores the repo via an explore sub-agent (about 93.7k tokens in the demo) which has an isolated context and reports a summary back, so the main context barely grows.
- Its recommended answers are often good; Matt frequently accepts them. In the demo it surfaced non-obvious questions such as whether points should be retroactive for existing lesson-progress records.
- Sessions can run 22, 40, 80 or even 100 questions, up to an hour. Matt usually dictates answers rather than typing. The demo session used about 25k tokens, "all of that is gold".
- It works as a team activity: feed a domain-expert meeting transcript into a grilling session to test assumptions. Matt likes pair/mob programming with an AI as the relentless third person. Real decisions need humans in the loop; implementation can be AFK.
- If grilling is too intense, tune the skill (e.g. add stop points).
- He avoids the AskUserQuestion UI in Claude Code, calling it "broken in a ton of different ways".
- He argues against "specs to code": editing specs and ignoring the code is "vibe coding by another name". "I tried this. I really tried it. And it sucks." The code is "your battleground".
- He urges owning your planning stack rather than adopting frameworks (Spec Kit, OpenSpec, Taskmaster): with no clear winner, you need control and observability to fix it when it breaks.

chunks.heading: PRD as destination, Kanban board as journey
chunks.text:
- After grilling, Matt runs a `write a PRD` skill to summarize the design concept into a destination document: problem statement, solution, user stories (18 in the demo), implementation decisions, testing decisions, and an out-of-scope section (which also records negative decisions and gives a definition of done).
- The PRD includes proposed modules to modify, so the code stays in mind during planning. The skill can interview again and explore the repo if run fresh.
- He does not review the PRD: LLMs are good at summarization and the shared design concept already exists, so reading it would only test summarization. He also sees little value in endlessly optimizing the PRD; the effort belongs in QA.
- He then converts the PRD into a Kanban board of issues with blocking relationships, each tagged HITL or AFK. In the demo: 5 issues, e.g. schema plus gamification service, streak tracking, wiring into lesson/quiz completion, retroactive backfill, and a final issue blocked by all.
- Unlike a sequential multi-phase plan (one agent only), a Kanban DAG can be picked up by multiple agents in parallel. Blocking order defines phases: e.g. one task first, then two in parallel, then a third.
- The PRD and issues are his own workflow: he uses GitHub issues in his course-video-manager repo (744 closed issues; roughly a thousand videos recorded with the app), and local markdown files for the workshop.
- He deletes or closes PRDs after implementation to avoid doc rot, where stale docs mislead later agents. On GitHub he just marks the issue closed.

chunks.heading: Tracer bullets and vertical slices, not horizontal layers
chunks.text:
- Matt uses the "tracer bullet" idea from The Pragmatic Programmer for issue breakdown. His PRD-to-issues skill says: break a PRD into independently grabbable issues using vertical slices.
- Analogy: tracer rounds glow so an anti-aircraft gunner sees where they're aiming. In code, that means feedback on the entire flow early.
- AI loves coding horizontally (all the database work, then all the API, then the front end), so it gets no integrated feedback until phase three and codes blind until then.
- A good first slice cuts through all layers: schema changes, a new service, and a minimal front-end representation. In the demo the AI proposed a service-only first slice; Matt told it "the first slice is too horizontal". It corrected to "award points for lesson completion, visible on dashboard".
- He values 20-year-old books because they already verbalize best software practices in English, a gold mine to feed into prompts.

chunks.heading: AFK implementation: the Ralph loop, TDD and feedback loops
chunks.text:
- Matt frames it as the human "day shift" (grill, PRD, Kanban, QA) and the AI "night shift" (implementation).
- His `once.sh` script (human-in-the-loop version) cats all local issue markdown files into a variable, grabs the last five commits, and runs Claude with permission mode accept edits and the prompt. An AFK version loops it inside a Docker sandbox. Run the once version first to watch and tune the prompt.
- The prompt: work on AFK issues only; output a "no more tasks" marker when done; pick the next task by priority (critical bug fixes, dev infrastructure, tracer bullets, then polish, quick wins and refactors); explore the repo; use TDD; run feedback loops.
- TDD is "absolutely essential". A red-green-refactor skill makes the agent write one failing test first, confirm red, then implement. This adds good tests and makes it harder for the AI to cheat, which it does when it writes the whole implementation and then tests below it.
- Feedback loops (tests, type checking) set the ceiling on AI output quality. In the demo it ran `npm run test` and `npm run type check`, fixed a type error, and ended with 284 tests. If AI output is bad, improve the feedback loops.
- Sandcastle, a TypeScript library Matt built over about a week, runs this in parallel: a planner reads the backlog and picks issues, each gets a git worktree/branch in a Docker sandbox with an implementer, then a reviewer, then a merger agent merges branches and fixes type and test failures. He uses Sonnet for implementation and Opus for review.

chunks.heading: QA, review and taste
chunks.text:
- Manual QA is the human's job. In the demo, the app threw a SQLite error because the migration hadn't been applied (a table he found oddly named "point events"), which he fixed with a DB migrate/push. He skipped showing QA since "there's nothing less exciting than watching someone else QA".
- QA is where he imposes taste. Teams that automate every stage (idea, research, prototype, QA) end up with "apps that lack taste" and "slop". QA findings become new issues on the Kanban board, even while implementation runs.
- Always add an automated review step with a cleared context. A reviewer in the same context as the implementer works in the dumb zone; a fresh context reviews in the smart zone. Tokens are cheap and AI reviews well.
- To enforce coding standards: "push" (always sent, e.g. CLAUDE.md) versus "pull" (skills the agent may fetch). Make standards available by pull to the implementer, and push them to the reviewer along with the code.
- Matt admits he does more code review now and doesn't know how to square this with small PRs. "I think we just need to be ready to be doing more code review."
- For front end, AI can't judge visuals well yet; he asks for three throwaway prototype routes to click between, then feeds the chosen one back into grilling.

chunks.heading: Deep modules: making a codebase agent-friendly
chunks.text:
- "Bad code bases make bad agents." Matt uses John Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design: many shallow modules (small files, tangled dependencies) are hard for AI to navigate and hard to test, and the AI tends to produce them unaided. Tests end up wrapped around each tiny function, missing the interactions.
- Deep modules expose a small, simple interface over a lot of functionality. Put one test boundary around the module and test through its interface.
- Design the interfaces yourself and delegate the implementation. Treat modules as grey boxes: know their shape and behavior, not every line. This keeps your mental map of the codebase while moving fast, which counters the common feeling of knowing your code less well.
- His `improve codebase architecture` skill scans the repo and proposes clusters of related modules to deepen. In the demo it flagged a quiz scoring service with zero tests as the biggest gap. On his video editor it helped build one large module spanning front end to back end (using a discriminated union between the two types), testable from outside, which was "night and day" for the AI's ability to change it. "If you take one thing away from today, just try running this skill on your repo."
- On TypeScript depth: he says deep understanding of code and tools makes you much better with AI.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock explains how he moved from TypeScript education to AI agent skills (grill me, wayfinder, spec and tickets). He argues that old books like The Pragmatic Programmer, Philosophy of Software Design and DDD are the best way to steer agents, and that strategic thinking now matters most.

chunks.heading: Why Matt moved from TypeScript courses to AI skills
chunks.text:
- Matt was a voice coach for six years (singing, accents, Shakespeare, public speaking for consulting firms) before becoming a developer around 2017. He left coaching because doing it well meant living in London, which he hated.
- He taught himself JavaScript by building tools for his own lessons, including a web audio spectrogram analyzer for voice resonance. He says it ran terribly but made his lessons better.
- His coaching background gave him an unusual edge: little technical knowledge at first, but the ability to explain it. He rose quickly through agencies.
- At an agency building a learning management system for a car maker, TypeScript fixed a slow front-end team whose backend (in Portugal) kept changing contracts without telling them. He says velocity "just went" up and the team outpaced the backend.
- He joined the XState core team, then the Stately company, then Vercel (under Jared Palmer), where he stayed about 3 months on a 3-days-a-week contract while testing his own idea.
- Two-minute advanced TypeScript tips on Twitter took him from about 4,000 to 10,000 followers. Total TypeScript, built with Joel Hooks, reached seven figures within a couple of years of its early-2023 launch.
- His business model: sell products, offer a generous refund policy, avoid sponsored content, and aim for a lifestyle where he spends most of his time with family. He tries never to work weekends and dislikes "996" culture.
- Total TypeScript revenue has fallen with AI. His framing: AI made knowledge cheap, but wisdom is no easier to learn. He moved from courses on putting AI into apps to teaching how to work with agents.

chunks.heading: Tactical vs strategic programming in the AI age
chunks.text:
- Matt, borrowing John Ousterhout's distinction, says AI has largely eaten tactical programming (syntax, knowledge) and it is up to developers to handle strategic programming (long-term design).
- He thinks of strategic programming as a huge mixing desk with sliders (more microservices vs a monolith), where you can't hear the mistakes until about 9 months later.
- His view is that AI speeds up that feedback loop, so strategic mistakes now come back faster. He says "your code is the environment the agent operates in" and should keep improving it.
- He argues the strategic layer is more valuable than ever because of the leverage it gives. He is skeptical of hiring juniors and treating them as agents until their mistakes surface (the advice Uncle Bob gave him), calling it a waste of money.
- Spec-driven development ("English is the hot new programming language") disappointed him: each edit-the-spec, regenerate loop made the code worse. The agent gets bad signal from a bad test suite, just as a human would.
- Software entropy, from The Pragmatic Programmer, is his lens: agents produce entropy faster than ever. Tech debt is anything that makes the codebase harder to change, and agents make it easy to produce even in tiny codebases.

chunks.heading: Smart zone, dumb zone, and why work is split across sessions
chunks.text:
- Matt credits Dex Horthy's idea of a smart zone and a dumb zone. Every token competes for attention, so more context degrades the model's grasp of the important parts.
- He puts the smart zone at roughly the first 150,000 tokens, regardless of the model's total context window size.
- Ralph loops fit this: give a goal, do the smallest change toward it, clear context, repeat. Only a little state persists in the filesystem and environment, not in the model.
- His take on his agent-app experience: building apps with agents taught him to think about data flow (where state lives, its shape, how to compact or clear it), which made harnesses feel familiar. He compares loops to finite state machines, like his XState work.
- His workflow separates a destination document (a spec declaring when you've arrived) from tickets, one per session. A grilling session becomes a spec, which becomes 30 to 40 tickets run by an implement loop.
- He likes a "day shift / night shift" model: plan during the day, let agents work AFK overnight, review clean code in the morning. He wants chunks of planning plus chunks of review rather than constant terminal-switching.

chunks.heading: The grill-me skill and aligning with the agent
chunks.text:
- Grill-me is a very small skill that tells the agent to interview you relentlessly about a topic. Matt says it has "this weird emergent behavior where the models start thinking a little bit outside the box" and throws ideas at you. He got the idea from Tariq of the Claude Code team.
- Why it works: there is a communication gap between you and the agent. It "can't read your mind," so left to itself it produces something misaligned with your values. Grilling establishes what is in scope, what is out, and what you consider important.
- Grilling makes you decide while also reminding you of things you hadn't considered. Matt says it felt like discussions with a very senior engineer, such as Andarist at XState.
- Choosing when to grill:
  - Small change (a five-line fix, moving a button): don't grill, align afterwards ("shift right").
  - Fits a single session: grill-me.
  - Spans multiple sessions: wayfinder.
- Example of a no-grill flow: a feedback button in his video editor files a GitHub issue, an implement agent picks it up, a review agent checks it, and he aligns at the end.
- On the "this is waterfall" criticism, he says he does heavy, aggressive prototyping before writing a spec. Agents make prototypes cheapest ever (build 3 or 4 versions and pick one). He sees the agentic setup as closer to agile, though he doesn't mind waterfall as a cautionary tale.

chunks.heading: Wayfinder: planning work larger than one context window
chunks.text:
- Wayfinder exists because some grilling can't fit in 150k tokens (his example: "build me a Stripe clone").
- Its central object is a map: the shared reference for all decisions, with milestones and a "fog of war" that opens as sessions resolve questions. He describes it as a directed acyclic graph walked toward a destination.
- Each session works one ticket on the map. Tickets can be grilling, prototyping, research, or arbitrary tasks like provisioning infrastructure.
- He has had maps of 50 to 100 tickets, and uses it for non-engineering work too: course planning and building a garden office.
- He notes that agents work well in software because inputs and outputs are all text (code, docs, test results, type checks, lint). Anything non-textual, like animation feel, they handle poorly, so he tries to make his services agent-accessible and text-based.

chunks.heading: Leading words from classic books
chunks.text:
- Matt's discovery: reading The Pragmatic Programmer, he realized its ideas were probably in the agents' priors. Using its phrases in prompts changed behavior, and the agent started saying them back (e.g. "I'll turn this into a tracer bullet").
- He calls these leading words. You repeat a simple phrase in a skill or prompt to steer the agent.
- Tracer bullets: get feedback quickly by building a thin path that works end to end. This fixes agents (even in Ralph loops) that build the whole database layer, then the whole app layer, then the whole component library, and only integrate at the end. The related idea is vertical slices instead of horizontal slices across layers.
- From John Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design, he took "deep modules".
- From Eric Evans' Domain-Driven Design, he took ubiquitous language. He built a "grill with docs" skill (which he admits is badly named) that builds a domain language while you ideate, and a domain modeling skill.
- Example: in his course app, converting a ghost lesson inside a ghost section inside a ghost course into a real one triggers what he calls the "materialization cascade", a term he and the agent coined. A shared term replaces many words, and the agent can grep for it in code.
- His framing: agents are like the character in Memento, waking up fresh every session, so optimize the codebase for a new starter. Humans can work around a bad codebase by building memory; agents can't.
- His reading list: The Pragmatic Programmer, A Philosophy of Software Design, and roughly the first three chapters of DDD.

chunks.heading: Testing, tech debt and review
chunks.text:
- TDD optimizes for small working memory, which agents don't need as much as humans. What agents do need is feedback loops, and a failing test first is hard for them to cheat.
- Even without strict TDD, he asks agents to "provide proof that your change does the thing" and give TDD evidence that it would fail without the change.
- His warning: agents often write tautological tests that just assert the implementation (e.g. write a constant, then expect it to equal that value).
- He uses an implement agent followed by an automated review agent that enforces coding standards and flags tautological tests. He asks how you know the reviewer is good, and says you must stay in a constant battle against tech debt.
- On Jared Friedman's tweet that tech debt is no longer something you have to live with, Matt's reply was "now you can live with it even in a tiny code base".
- He also runs a morning loop that executes an "improve codebase architecture" skill and proposes an improvement, which he can turn into tickets with a button.

chunks.heading: Organizations, cloud agents and gardening
chunks.text:
- For orgs, he says the first step is observability over agents: their success and failure rates, with someone responsible for analyzing it and spreading lessons from the best repos. Teams need a shared set of skills and workflow, and an experimental mindset (A/B test processes).
- He suggests spending something like 20% of time on "the factory that builds your software", and says no one will be upset if you report you also did it.
- He is moving off a local dev setup toward a remote box he reaches through Discord, Slack or Linear, with schedules and a morning standup with his agent. He argues a shared space is needed for collaborative grilling. He concedes front-end work is the exception, because of the feedback loop.
- On gardening, he says "the only thing your team needs are gardeners" and "we are our agents platform team", building the environment for agents to succeed.
- His advice for juniors: use agents as much as possible, stay curious, and be introspective about your own process. He calls the key skill introspection: turning your process into something an AI can work with.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt argues AI has eaten tactical programming, so strategic skill (design, interfaces, scoping, codebase quality) is the ceiling on what agents can do. He covers procedure vs ability skills, grill-me, AFK agents in sandboxes, queues over loops, and optimizing the harness and codebase over chasing new models.

chunks.heading: Strategic vs tactical programming: why skills are the ceiling on AI
chunks.text:
- Matt uses John Ousterhout's distinction from *A Philosophy of Software Design*. Tactical programming is day-to-day work: writing code, fiddling with syntax, fixing bugs as they appear, creating commits. Strategic programming is "winning the war, not the battle": long-term thinking about how the codebase should look and which strategies raise velocity.
- His claim: "AI has basically eaten tactical programming." AI does tactical work cheaper and better than a human, so developers need to be great at strategic programming to get value from "this infinite fleet of tactical programmers".
- Strategic programming hasn't changed. Delegating to AI is the same as delegating to junior or mid-level developers:
  - Design the hard parts up front.
  - Scope tasks tightly.
  - Think about the interfaces between modules.
  - Think about test seams and good tests.
  - Build a codebase that is easy to work in, with just enough documentation to point the AI at the right places to make changes.
- "Your skills are the ceiling on what AI can do." If your skills are low, AI can't go past that.
- Skills act as a multiplier. He reports that CTOs and others at conferences tell him AI makes senior developers about 10x better, while juniors get a smaller boost, so it makes less sense to hire many juniors. (He notes he sells developer courses, so his view should be taken with a pinch of salt.)
- He still sees great juniors as valuable: enthusiasm beats experience, and juniors learn fast. Anyone with an experimental mindset who is curious about improving the harness will thrive, junior or senior.
- Seniors are useful because they know how to build good DX (developer experience), and there is a big overlap between good DX and good AX (agent experience). Juniors who are strong with AI come at the problem from a different angle.
- Product work: he says AI doesn't change the fundamentals of building a business. Talk to customers, find what they need, build prototypes. Ask AI what to remove from your app and how to simplify the UX, "instead of ending up like one of those dreadful VC funded apps" with a thousand features.

chunks.heading: Harness over model: where Matt puts his effort
chunks.text:
- His "hot take": everyone is obsessed with the model, the engine of the Formula 1 car, when the engine is only part of the system. People should care about the harness: the right prompts, the right skills, and improving the environment the model runs in, including the codebase.
- He frames model and harness as roughly 50/50 in importance, and says you have far more control over the harness than the model.
- He raised the "bitter lesson" (raw compute beats clever optimisation) himself as the counterargument, and said he doesn't know if he's falling into it. He still believes there is a lot to gain from optimising the harness and building codebases the agent can do well in, "instead of hamstringing the agent before it even gets started".
- He declines to make predictions ("I'm not a pundit"). His approach: keep the workspace and harness agent-agnostic, apply good software fundamentals, and do "stuff that's always worked", which will probably keep working.
- Token spend: when asked how to optimise it, his answer is "Have a codebase that's easier to make changes in."
  - A better architecture means better guard rails and easier exploration, so a model spends fewer tokens "banging its head against the wall".
  - That lets you use a cheaper, "stupider" model for the same work.
  - If you hamstring the model from day one, you need a smart model to compensate.
- He contrasts this with the vibe coder who switches tools every week (Replit, Lovable, and so on) and never learns fundamentals. He says focusing on the big shiny new thing is focusing on the wrong thing.
- Model adoption: he runs Claude Code with Opus 4.8 at medium effort and says he mostly doesn't worry about models. For a new model he waits about a month to see how things shake out (as he did with Opus 4.5). He hadn't adopted "Fable" yet, citing the hype noise, token cost, availability and latency, even while granting it seems a step change.
- On the claim that a stronger model finds deeper security bugs: he says the useful lesson is that your code has security issues and you need a system that checks for them. A daily cron job reviewing a different part of the repo, even with a simpler model and the right prompt, can find them. His bike analogy: "if someone keeps stealing your bike, maybe buy a lock."
- He wants self-improving systems built from long-standing practices: test suites, human review, refactoring. When a bug surfaces, ask why it got there and fix the underlying process, not only the bug.
- On an agent doing the whole task via a browser (creating API keys, moving an app in a console): he sees that as a reasonable scoped task with tools. Deciding whether it's the right thing and security-testing the result is still the human's job.

chunks.heading: AFK agents, queues and Sand Castle
chunks.text:
- Discovering AFK (away from keyboard) agents was when he "really got into AI coding" and massively increased output. Removing himself from permission prompts and questions lets him parallelise: "suddenly there are two of me, three of me, four of me, five of me."
- Human-in-the-loop work suits planning, complicated implementation and unscoped work. AFK work suits well-scoped tasks.
- On the "loops" trend (Ralph loop, Geoffrey Huntley's article dated 14 July the previous year): the Ralph loop is a while loop that feeds a prompt to Claude Code repeatedly. He realised he only needs an AFK agent to take a specific task and do it. He calls the idea that you should be running loops mostly nonsensical, since it just means AFK agents.
- He prefers queues to loops. The queue is the backlog of tasks, as development has always worked, with multiple nodes (developers or agents) picking items off.
  - His Sand Castle repo issues get triaged and explored AFK, then put back on the queue.
  - He adds an "agent implement" label and a GitHub Action running Sand Castle implements it.
  - The item leaves the queue when the pull request merges.
- A possible extended pipeline: Sentry or telemetry creates an issue from a live bug report, an agent explores it and returns structured data on whether it can be fixed immediately, then implements and reviews it, with a tag deciding whether it can auto-merge or pings a human.
- Principle: push human-in-the-loop checkpoints "further and further right". Instead of a bug report, the human gets the bug report plus the codebase exploration plus the fix, "one button click away instead of a whole debugging session away."
- Review does two jobs: it gates dangerous changes from production, and it gives insight into the system. You are reviewing the system that produces the code, not only the code. If an AI decides some PRs need no review, you still need to spot-check those decisions and improve over time. Removing checkpoints where possible is still the goal.
- He mentioned an approach where, on a front-end change, the AI records a video walking through the change and overlays text-to-speech narration on the PR. His point: build richness like this into review and use AI to make human review faster.

chunks.heading: Sand Castle: running agents in sandboxes
chunks.text:
- Sand Castle is a tool Matt built to run agents inside sandboxes. Unsandboxed agents can do things like delete your home directory or exfiltrate environment variables to bad sites.
- It plugs into Docker or Podman and runs agents such as Claude Code inside the sandbox. It can run on his own machine or on remote sandboxes such as Vercel Sandboxes, with commits pulled back into the local workspace.
- He combines it with GitHub Actions. Example from the Sand Castle repo: an agent review action that runs on a PR, checks out the branch, runs a review prompt he keeps locally, runs type checks, and replies that it looks good.
- Benefits: parallelise as much as you like, don't constrain local machine resources, and spin up an agent quickly to do a task.
- His day-to-day setup: Claude Code for planning and some local implementation, Opus 4.8 at medium effort, and most development done AFK through Sand Castle plus GitHub Actions.

chunks.heading: Skills: procedures versus abilities, and how he writes them
chunks.text:
- He splits skills into two types:
  - Procedures: skills you invoke yourself to get the model to behave a certain way.
  - Abilities: skills the model invokes on its own, for example a "React coding standards" skill it pulls in when writing React (such as not using useEffect).
- He prefers procedures because he wants to stay in control: "I don't want to delegate my thinking to the model." His workflow chains them: grill me, then write a PRD (to-PRD), then split it into issues, then work through them.
- Superpowers (from Obra, probably the most popular skills repo) takes the opposite approach, with the model in control.
- Cost of abilities: every skill's description leaks into the context window, so 100 skills means 100 descriptions in context. Setting `disable-model-invocation: true` keeps a skill user-only and stops its description entering context. He prefers to keep most knowledge in the human, not the AI.
- Grill me is one of his most popular skills. It is about four or five sentences and turns the agent into an adversarial interviewer that asks questions and offers ideas you hadn't considered until you reach a shared understanding. He uses it as a replacement for plan mode before implementing code, to flush out surprises early.
