- Skills as reusable procedures are like extracting a repeated function in code: if you've made a plan 100 times, turn that into a skill and share it so the whole team plans the same way and contributes back. He calls it "raising the floor" for what engineers can do.
- Knowledge, skills and wisdom: knowledge is understanding in your head, skills are muscle memory from repetition, and wisdom is knowing when to do it and how it fits the real world. Wisdom is nearly impossible to gain without doing the thing in its real context. Skills can bundle the first two into something reusable.

chunks.heading: The teach skill: a stateful skill built on learning science
chunks.text:
- Matt taught singing and voice for 10 years straight out of university, then became a developer, and has taught developers for four years. The teach skill encodes teaching principles: the zone of proximal development and the distinction between knowledge, skills and wisdom.
- It creates a course on the fly on any topic. He used it to teach himself to solve a Rubik's cube from memory, and to explore how to become a senior developer.
- Skills can be stateless (no local memory) or stateful. Teach is stateful because a good teacher remembers what you've done and where you need to go next. It must be run in a workspace because it saves state there.
- Demo flow, with Matt playing a vibe coder who can read some code and use basic CLI commands:
  - He wrote a mission statement by dictation (using Whisper Flow): a voice teacher wanting a scheduling and student-notes app, likely full stack with a database and authentication.
  - The skill checked the workspace, asked a few questions to align with the mission, then wrote a `mission.md` (who the person is, what they want to build, why it matters, what success looks like).
  - It searched trusted resources, then created a learning record, a reference cheat sheet and a first lesson.
  - It started with Git, since the highest-leverage gap for a vibe coder is the stuff around the code that lets you "ship without fear".
- Lessons are generated as local HTML files, richer than the terminal ("learning stuff in the terminal is just brutal"). They include exercises to run in the terminal and are personalised to the user's machine.
- It uses quizzes ("I sort of hate quizzes but quizzes are just unreasonably effective for increasing the strength that something is stored in") with questions such as `git commit`, `git status`, `git add` and `git restore`, then points to a primary source (the Pro Git book).
- He sees knowledge as a graph, a forest to explore, and the skill builds a linear path through it, tracked in a learning record (mission, starting point, current estimates).
- Install from his GitHub skills repo: `npx skills latest add mattpocock/skills`, then choose teach. It works with Claude Code, Codex and others.
- He says skills are a good example of the point that a better teacher can use AI to teach better.

chunks.heading: Advice for getting more out of AI today
chunks.text:
- Step 1: delete every skill, plugin and MCP server, plus `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`. Go back to a blank slate and watch what the agent does. In his experience people bloat their context window with too many instructions.
- Step 2: layer things back on deliberately, as procedure skills you choose. His skills repo is a good start. If you really miss something (he gave brainstorming from Superpowers as an example), bring it back, installed in a form you can customise and experiment with.
- Step 3: when you notice a problem, find a fix for it. Delegate implementation to an AFK agent as much as possible. AFK "takes a little bit of setup, but once it's set up, it just goes crazy."
- Dictation is a big speed advantage; he says communication and speaking are "ridiculously overpowered" in development.
- Where to find him: aihero.dev (newsletter) and aihero.dev/skills for updates to his skills.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock explains how he works with coding agents after the late-2025 threshold: raise the floor of the codebase, tell agents what you care about, and surface unknown unknowns with his grill-me skill. He covers why spec-driven development failed him, domain-driven design's ubiquitous language, and why teaching sessions should point to primary sources.

chunks.heading: Communication is the core skill when working with agents
chunks.text:
- Matt argues that people underestimate the communication gap between a human and an agent. However smart the model, it "doesn't know precisely what you want" and doesn't know what you care about, so you must tell it every time.
- He says the best way to get good work from agents is to tell them what you care about.
- Agents also perform better in a good environment. In a "garbage vibe-coded crappy code base", the result is "garbage in, garbage out."
- His thought experiment: if he ran a coding organization with 100 human coders, how would he raise the floor so the worst coder performs better? The answer is decades-old practice: good tests, and checks that stop classes of bugs and prevent mistakes. He says books on this "feel like they were written last week."
- He says the top developers he has seen are all incredibly good communicators. Their code changes come with detailed, easy-to-read reports, so "the clarity of their thinking ends up in the product they create."
- Weak communicators get worse results because they can't tell the agent what they want or what is wrong.
- The quality of your thinking and language matters when talking to the client and when telling the agent what the client wants.
- He expects models and harnesses to improve but never to "read your mind", so some process layer will always be needed to bridge the communication barrier.

chunks.heading: Grill Me and unknown unknowns
chunks.text:
- "Grill me" is one of his most commonly used skills. It tells the agent to interview him relentlessly about what they're building.
- It works because it pulls out more context about what he cares about and surfaces unknown unknowns.
- He defines the key skill as being "aware of unknown unknowns": knowing you could be missing things in your design and not trusting that your design is complete.
- Examples of things people forget to mention: security, how the thing is deployed.
- If the agent isn't told, it either makes things up or assumes an unmentioned thing isn't important, and you get something different from what you imagined.
- He cites The Pragmatic Programmer: "no one knows exactly what they want."
- He says turning an idea into code exposes weaknesses in the design. Some of these only become clear once you reach code, because it is a translation from a fuzzy human brain into executable statements.
- He sees no divide between a regular person and a coder here. A normal person talking to a developer faces the same barrier as a person talking to an agent.

chunks.heading: Ubiquitous language and Grill with Docs
chunks.text:
- Matt recommends domain-driven design (DDD) for building with agents. Its core idea is a ubiquitous language.
- The terms in the code should match the terms developers use, the terms the client uses to ask for the product, and the terms users see. His example is "order": it should mean the same thing in the code, the database, the UI and the conversation with the client.
- Iterating on that language, and keeping it precise, aligns you with what the client wants and what you're actually building.
- "Grill with Docs" is his modified version of Grill Me. It builds this domain language as the interview goes.
- He admits he's "shilling DDD" and that most coders haven't heard of it, but says he's found it "extraordinary for building with agents."

chunks.heading: Why spec-driven development failed for him
chunks.text:
- Matt's war story: he saw a talk at an AI engineering event arguing "specs are the new code". The idea is to write a very detailed specification and have an agent turn it into code.
- He tried spec-driven development for months on his pride-and-joy repo, a custom video editor (a bit like Descript) with AI writing and thumbnail design.
- He kept wanting to look at the code, and saw it "getting worse and worse and worse," with the agent producing worse results.
- He kept trying because the speaker was from OpenAI and he assumed they knew what they were talking about. It still didn't work.
- His conclusion was to ditch the specs and focus on the code. Code is the environment the agent operates in, and a dog sitting in a burning house won't behave well.
- He defines a good code base as one that is easy to change: a change won't break something the agent didn't think about, and everything is easy to modify.

chunks.heading: Environment beats model choice, and how he runs agents
chunks.text:
- He uses Claude Code with Opus 5.5 at medium effort, and is considering going lower. He calls this a hot take: he thinks most people run effort levels too high.
- Lower effort gives better token efficiency and faster replies. Since he has "raised the floor" on his agents, they don't need to work hard. They write code that passes the tests, and the tests catch mistakes.
- He doesn't try lots of models and harnesses, and says "I just don't care that much about the harness." He treats agents as employees in his company and wants the company's baseline to be as good as possible.
- His biggest recent gain came from fixing a complicated project (the video editor, which depends on OBS running locally) so an agent could use the browser, click through the app, take screenshots and run it properly. He says this raised output quality massively, and that he could get just as good a result with Opus 4.5 and that setup.
- Nate's point, which Matt agrees with: someone who communicates well with an old model can beat someone who doesn't with the newest one.
- His output: about four agents on long-term tasks at once. He is trying a "chief of staff" skill that manages sub-agents, and says it is like a team of eight developers.
- His GitHub shows around 200-300 commits a day, where "20 a day would have been a good day" before.
- He calls Opus 4.5 and the OpenClaw-era releases in December 2025 the threshold where he decided he would never write a line of code himself again. Before that he was a skeptic with about 10 years of coding experience, 8 of them professional.

chunks.heading: Learning with agents and the /teach skill
chunks.text:
- Matt says to be skeptical of anything anyone tells you, including agents. He was a skeptic of AI for a long time.
- His teach skill fetches high-trust primary sources and breaks them down with quotes and attribution, linking to exactly where each claim comes from.
- Hallucinations have dropped a lot but still happen.
- He mostly uses teach sessions to get introduced to a topic, then reads the primary source himself. The session gives him the language to interpret it.

chunks.heading: Opportunities and a path for newcomers
chunks.text:
- Matt sees massive opportunity in taking agents and working out processes for knowledge work, then bringing those to organizations. Every organization does things slightly differently, and he says this is a skill that's "really hard."
- Agents are good at code and math because both are easy to verify. Real-world work is harder to verify, and it took him a long time and many processes to find something he's happy with for his own day-to-day work.
- He rejects the idea that agents have no learning curve. The curve is still there, partly hidden. The things to learn: what you can trust from an agent, how to organize agents, how to control and design the information they receive, and how to turn their work into reusable processes and your processes into something agents can follow.
- He also sees teaching demand, because organizations resist adopting this.
- On pitching clients, he has no concrete advice since he hasn't bid for roles. He thinks people want someone who understands what they care about. Vibe-coding a prototype that shows you understand their business can help, since it shows real acumen quickly. He also jokes that if speed unsettles people, "charge them for 5 days."
- His starter path for beginners:
  - Download his skills and pick any harness (Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot); don't overthink the choice.
  - Start in an empty folder, use VS Code so you can look inside the code, and have a real idea you want to build.
  - Watch the agent "like a hawk" and learn to brake before you accelerate.
  - "Climb the trust ladder": only then add a second agent, write skills, and connect Slack, Gmail or Twitter.
  - He has an agent that triages a to-do list he dictates from his watch.
- He disagrees with the advice to give models your most ambitious tasks. He says to give them menial, boring work where output is easy to check and correct, such as drafting replies. He uses Opus 5.5 to write first drafts of his written content.

chunks.heading: What he is excited about next
chunks.text:
- Software factories: automating the start of work and improving code bases over time. He wants agents to become "that annoying developer who's always on the team" who says to do it the right way, not the fast way, for the benefit of those who come after.
- He thinks agents are currently bad at thinking long-term about a code base, and that this can be fixed.
- He says nobody has found the right way to organize lots of agents yet.
- He's also excited about open models, and expects one as good as Opus 5.5 would delight him.
- He describes himself as a teacher, not a pundit, based in Oxfordshire. He declines most offers to preview things and wants to "make it work now."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock explains why his "grill me" skill works, how he keeps shared language and decisions in the repo, and why specs should be disposable. He also covers keeping agent sessions in the "smart zone" and designing interfaces while delegating implementation.

chunks.heading: Interviewing the agent with "grill me" before building
chunks.text:
- Matt built "grill me" because plan mode asks a few vague clarifying questions and then rushes to produce a plan.
- He calls this an "asset rush": the agent is sycophantic and heads for a finished artifact (a plan) as fast as it can, because that scores well in benchmarks.
- The skill is about five lines. It tells the agent to interview him about what he is building until they reach a shared understanding.
- It never mentions creating a plan. Hiding the next step makes the agent do more work on the current step, and Matt decides when to stop.
- Sessions can run to roughly 40 questions. The conversation itself becomes the asset.
- He credits Tariq, who works on Claude Code, for the idea that interviewing is a powerful technique.
- Matt's analogy: ordering a chorizo salad and getting a sandwich, so you send it back. Grilling stops that.
- Using Frederick Brooks's term, the goal is a "design concept" held clearly in the user's head. Once that is clear, the implementation is trivial for the AI.
- Grilling tests the user as much as the agent. Someone told him they use "grill me" to interview job candidates, to see how they interact with AI and whether they can hold the design concept clearly.
- He has the AskUserQuestion tool disabled. He dislikes its multiple-choice UI, and it costs about 2K tokens in the system prompt, which eats smart-zone budget.
- He sees tools converging: OpenSpec explore mode, Superpowers brainstorm and grill me are all the same idea.

chunks.heading: Grill with docs: ubiquitous language and ADRs
chunks.text:
- Code can explain what it does but not the decisions that were not taken, and it explains domain language poorly.
- "Grill with docs" is grill me plus a thin documentation layer: a ubiquitous language (from DDD) and architectural decision records (ADRs) in the repo.
- The problem it targets: AI output can be verbose and use words that feel wrong, a communication gap between Matt as product manager and the AI as developer.
- Example in his own apps (a video editor and a course planner). Instead of "when you create a real lesson inside a ghost section inside a ghost course, it should make the ghost section and ghost course real and require a file path", he can say "there's a problem in the materialization cascade."
- His pet theory: once you establish the language of something, you understand it and have a working model of it. This also applies to teaching.
- The grilling session is the right moment to settle the terms, not later.

chunks.heading: Specs are temporary; make the code easier to navigate instead
chunks.text:
- Matt is not a fan of spec-driven development, partly because everyone means something different by "spec".
- His definition: a spec is a temporary artifact for scheduling work over multiple agent sessions. Write the spec, split it into tickets (one agent session each), clear context between tickets, then delete the spec once it is in the code.
- He disagrees with persisting specs as a shadow version of the code:
  - It spends tokens keeping the specs in sync with the code.
  - It locks you into a spec-first way of working.
- His alternative: spend those tokens making the code easier to navigate and read. That means fewer cross-repo dependencies and better modules, so the agent doesn't have to search everywhere.
- The host argued that persisted specs save the cost of inferring features from the whole codebase, provided they stay up to date. Matt kept his position.

chunks.heading: Wayfinder, the smart zone and the dumb zone
chunks.text:
- Wayfinder plans big changes (or new projects) across many agent sessions, because Matt wants most work to fit in a narrow context window.
- He gets the best output in roughly the first 150k tokens. Dex Hy, behind HumanLayer, calls this the "smart zone"; beyond it is the "dumb zone".
- Smart-zone work is cheaper, and the agent avoids attention degradation.
- Mechanics:
  - It creates a map issue in the tracker (GitHub issues in his case; Linear works too). It is like a parent epic aiming at one big spec.
  - Sub-issues are decision tickets, with blocking relationships between decisions.
  - Each decision ticket is its own session: a grilling session, research on external information, or a prototype.
  - There is a "fog" section for things that can't be scoped yet because earlier decisions haven't been made.
- Prototypes are underused. A prototype that looks and behaves as wanted is "catnip" for agents: they can read the code and turn it into production code.
- On 1M-token windows, the smart zone/dumb zone is a heuristic, not a hard drop-off. Context size is a limit the labs pick for infrastructure reasons. More tokens just degrade quality gradually.
- It is fine to enter the dumb zone for mindless refactors or long implementations, at slightly worse results per token.
- He uses Wayfinder for non-coding work too, such as planning a garden office. It pushed him to call a surveyor.

chunks.heading: Strategic vs tactical programming, and who owns a spec
chunks.text:
- Matt uses John Ousterhout's distinction (A Philosophy of Software Design): tactical programming is day-to-day coding; strategic programming is the long-term view of the codebase and product.
- AI has "eaten" tactical programming. What is left is planning and review, and the middle of the process is gone.
- Open question he raises: how do juniors learn strategic programming when it normally takes months of living with your own mistakes? And how do you interview for it?
- Labor is no longer the constraint, but alignment and building the right thing still are. The host noted AI makes coding vastly faster without making ticket throughput proportionally faster.
- His view on sprints and tickets: the right unit is no longer the individual ticket. One developer should own an entire spec and manage the agents that implement it.
  - A developer might handle about four specs at once.
  - This avoids a "crisis of responsibility", where code is merged and nobody owns it ("the AI did it").
- On understanding AI-written code: delegation is healthy. Developers should own the overall shape and the interfaces (modularization, how others interface with the code) but needn't understand every line of the implementation.
  - His rule: "design the interface and delegate the implementation."
- For collaboration, he made an in-progress skill, "to questionnaire". It turns the grilling questions into a Google Doc that a non-technical person can fill in offline, then feeds the answers back to the agent. He used it with his wife on the garden office.

chunks.heading: Handoff skill and running multiple agents
chunks.text:
- Work in a session has phases (grill, implement, review). At each boundary you can continue, clear context, or compact.
- When something unrelated comes up mid-session (a critical bug, a type error), the handoff skill writes a markdown document describing the work, which you open in a new agent.
- Claude Code's agent view runs many agents under a background daemon. He now has a Claude handoff skill that spawns a new agent from the command line instead of the manual copy-paste.
- He can spawn several agents on separate tasks while the main session keeps going.
- He keeps one folder where he runs all Claude Code sessions. Its `CLAUDE.md` holds navigation pointers to each repo, acting as a router, and he keeps skills there. This gives him a single directory for all work.
- Tools he mentioned: Herder (herdr), an open-source layer over tmux with integrations for Claude, Codex and others. He hasn't fully adopted it because of a dictation incompatibility.

chunks.heading: Dictation and personal software
chunks.text:
- He dictates into agents with Whisper Flow. He argues that AI is good at picking out transcription errors and understanding what you meant, so dictated text is a great input.
- He runs several grilling sessions at once: switch tabs and dictate into each.
- He has an annual Whisper Flow subscription.
- His personal wiki: an ingest bot runs every 3 hours in GitHub Actions and pulls his inputs (Twitter, Gmail, Discord, YouTube) into a wiki of markdown files in a repo.
  - He has about 300,000 followers on Twitter and about 300,000 subscribers on YouTube, too much to read by hand.
  - He queries the wiki when planning courses ("what are people confused about?").
  - Gemini text-to-speech turns the day's changes into a private daily podcast feed, about 15 minutes of two people discussing his audience.

chunks.heading: Background and where the field is converging
chunks.text:
- Matt has done full-time developer education since 2022. His background includes the XState open-source library (and the company Stately), a short stint at Vercel as a developer advocate, then the Total TypeScript course.
- He argues type safety matters even more with agents.
- His skills repo took him by surprise. The numbers given in the episode: about 185k stars and 11 million downloads. He calls it the biggest open-source thing he has done.
- Most of 2024 he focused on putting AI into apps, such as chatbots. That knowledge carried over to working with harnesses, because the underlying models are the same.
- His view on churn: despite the pace, the fundamentals aren't changing much. Everyone is converging on plan, execute, review, human review, merge.
  - There are still disagreements, such as whether to persist specs and how much to prototype.
- That stability is why he feels he can release AI coding courses now.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock demos his open-source skills repo, showing how a short "grill me" interview before work beats a generic agent run. He covers glossaries for consistent language, splitting specs into tickets, looping agents deterministically, and cutting no-op lines from skills.

chunks.heading: Skills as encoded processes, not special sauce
chunks.text:
- Matt's most popular skill is "Grill Me": a short skill that interviews the user relentlessly about a plan before the agent does any work. He says it is "not a special sauce" and "anyone could have written this skill"; its value is that it encodes a repeatable process.
- His rule of thumb: whenever he wants to run a process again and again, a skill is the right place to put it.
- Small skills are easy to audit and easy to bring into an organization.
- The skills repo had 214,000 GitHub stars at the time of recording.
- Skills can be invokable by the model, by the user, or both. Grill Me is hidden from the model by default; the grilling skill beneath it holds the substance.
- He has two grilling skills: "grill me" and "grill with docs" (in his engineering directory), which runs a grilling session using the domain modeling skill. He calls this a hacky way to share code, since the skill spec has nothing on sharing code between skills.

chunks.heading: Align before you build: the plan, implement, review loop
chunks.text:
- Matt frames agent work as plan, implement, review. Most people skip the pre-alignment phase before the agent does the work.
- Demo: he gave Claude Code (Opus 5, medium effort, Claude Max subscription) a security review of a newly deployed app, once without Grill Me and once with it.
  - Without it, he got a general security audit with decent but generic advice.
  - With it, the agent asked a round of numbered questions first ("who is the adversary?", "what is the asset?", "what is in scope?", "what is the deliverable?"), each with a recommended answer. It then asked about rate limits, unauthenticated health endpoints and more, so the audit became tailored to his real concerns.
- Users hold an internal hierarchy of values and priorities the agent cannot anticipate. Grilling closes that communication gap, "and that's always going to be there."
- Answering is quick because questions are numbered: "For Q1, yeah, I accept your recommendation. For Q2, the worst thing that can occur is probably data loss..." He dictates the answers.
- Questions come in sensible batches, in rounds.

chunks.heading: Low fidelity first
chunks.text:
- Matt draws on Shape Up (Ryan Singer): people think they need to work at higher fidelity than necessary.
- His ladder: start with text, then move to diagrams or breadboarding, then prototypes.
- The default mistake is jumping straight to high fidelity ("produce the entire feature, then review the whole thing"), which makes review expensive and surfaces unexpected bugs late.
- Five minutes of low-fidelity alignment first lets you ship much faster.
- He does not claim low fidelity is always right: sometimes you need a prototype first. His focus is complex, production-bound apps, where "before you build anything real, you have to align."

chunks.heading: Grilling skill internals: leading words and design trees
chunks.text:
- The grilling skill is about 22 lines long. It says to interview the user relentlessly until reaching shared understanding, and to map the plan as a design tree where every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.
- Work the tree in rounds; "the frontier is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled."
- He calls the bolded terms "leading words": words designed to trigger the agent's reasoning traces and lead it to think in those terms.
- Facts are the agent's job, not the user's: "finding facts is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment, dispatch a sub agent to find it. Don't block the user."

chunks.heading: The spec, tickets and implement workflow
chunks.text:
- The main flow in his repo is grill with docs, then to spec, to ticket, to implement, to code review: essentially a software development life cycle encoded as skills that span multiple sessions.
- Grill with docs adds two outputs on top of grilling:
  - A glossary of the thing being built. Agents "thrive off consistent language"; if folders, functions and concepts are named consistently, a request like "modify the materialization cascade" tells the agent exactly where to look.
  - Architectural decision records explaining the non-obvious parts of the code.
- If the work fits in the remaining context window, jump straight to the implement skill: implement the code, commit, then run an automated review.
- For a large feature that cannot fit in one context window, write a spec (a document describing the destination, reusable for review and passed into every later session) and then tickets, where each ticket is a slice of the spec that fits in one context window.
- Tickets can be split across multiple agents or tabs, then integrated at the end.
- Contrast with superpowers: Matt says that pack aims to give the model superpowers, whereas his skills take more learning but give the user superpowers. Once you learn about five skills "you can build anything of any size."

chunks.heading: Running ticket loops overnight with Sandcastle
chunks.text:
- Matt has had specs with around 30 tickets and runs them with a GitHub Actions setup that implements a ticket, clears the context, implements the next, and so on, overnight. He reviews the resulting PR in the morning.
- This needs a layer on top of the harness: model plus harness make the agent, and the layer above issues instructions and clears context. A set of tickets is just a loop, so it can be deterministic and does not need an agent.
- He built Sandcastle for this orchestration. Alternatives he names: the AI SDK (TypeScript), and Claude workflows that schedule sub-agents with a script.

chunks.heading: Writing for agents: killing no-ops
chunks.text:
- His "writing for agents" skill packs what he has learned about writing skills and prompts.
- Core problem: agent-written skills fill up with "no-ops", instructions that change neither output nor behavior and can be removed with nothing changing. Examples: "be thorough" (like "don't make mistakes").
- He says you can often delete about half of a popular skill without changing output.
- The skill's pruning rules:
  - Keep each meaning in a single source of truth; duplication costs maintenance and tokens.
  - Check every line for relevance to what the document does.
  - Hunt no-ops sentence by sentence; an instruction the model already obeys by default adds nothing.
- Routine: once a month, run the skill over all your skills and read the diff (before and after) to see if you agree. It usually culls skills into smaller sections and is opinionated.
- It is model-invoked: it triggers when the agent is creating or editing skills or modifying AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md.
- He warns that reading skills matters: he caught an awkward sentence in the skill itself that Opus had written.

chunks.heading: The teach skill
chunks.text:
- Matt hand-wrote his "teach" skill, drawing on about 10 years of teaching experience: roughly 6 years as a voice coach (speaking and singing, lots of one-to-one) and about 4 years teaching devs.
- You create a dedicated folder and run the skill there. It creates a stateful workspace that saves information about you, tracks how you are developing, and keeps learning records, so later sessions build on earlier ones.
- On the first run it interviews you about what you want to learn and why, then finds primary-source resources and teaches itself from them. He finds it strong for academic material because the sources are often public PDFs.
- Lessons are produced as HTML. Each lesson should recommend a primary source for the user to read or watch, since "you should never really trust an LLM."
- He has used it to learn about feeding his 2.5-year-old better food, solving a Rubik's Cube, and folk harmonies.
- His engineering skills repo is aimed at engineers; the writing-beats skill was still in progress and not ready.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock explains how to move toward a software factory without producing slop. Build verification and review brakes before accelerating, use a fresh reviewer agent to stop cheating, and let a well-shaped codebase steer agents. He also covers Effect's dependency injection and why skills are really process plus leading words.

chunks.heading: Brain dump and restate for planning; paper for the hardest puzzles
chunks.text:
- Matt went back to paper for planning courses. A course is a puzzle of roughly a hundred things per section (his example was a six-section course) that must be put in the right order, with dependencies between them.
- When agents helped with this, he held less in his head. They produced a lot of plausible output, and he still had to spend time understanding their planning decisions.
- He says people underestimate the communication overhead of agents: "It is another person that you're dealing with, and that can be very tiring." For some tasks, doing it alone is faster.
- Agents work well in well-defined pipelines. His course pipeline runs: shape of the course, learning goals per section, beats (the vague things to hit in each video), animatics he reviews, then videos.
- His brain-dump flow works like this:
  - Lay out cards and read them out to the agent in a long dictated brain dump.
  - Have the agent restate what he said, so he can correct it ("maybe don't do that, maybe do this").
  - This removes the worry after 15 minutes of talking about whether you are aligned, or whether the agent latched onto something he didn't mean.

chunks.heading: Animatics: agents rehearse the course before he films it
chunks.text:
- Matt finds Opus 5.5 "very, very good at vision". He wanted a high-fidelity mock-up of each video before filming, to understand it better and verify what he was about to do.
- Before filming, his agents run through the course locally. They do the work he would otherwise have done himself, work out the gnarly parts, and produce videos back to him: "I've almost seen the course before I'm filming the course."
- Fidelity can be lowered to keep it cheap: still images and a local voice model. His setup is highly parallelizable, so animatics are very quick.
- He thinks people are sleeping on agents producing high-fidelity video for little token spend. For code review, where an agent must give rich information, he expects video to appear more and more.
- He has been a Remotion fan for ages (videos in React). He notes its popular skills library and is starting to use it in his courses.

chunks.heading: Software factory: trust ladder, triggers, and brakes before accelerator
chunks.text:
- He takes the trust ladder from Lauren: as agents can verify their own work, the benefit is outsized. If you trust an agent to build the right thing 90% of the time, that might support 50 agents at once. At 95% you get even more.
- He describes the path from idea to production as full of human checkpoints, which you can progressively remove. The first one to consider removing is initiating work.
- His definition of a software factory: "when you have triggers that initiate agent sessions on their own." One example is a loop that checks the GitHub issues on an open-source repo and spawns sub-agents to work on them.
- With triggers accelerating work, you need brakes: verification, testing, and human review. Human review need not cover every PR; you can sample some.
- Removing humans entirely creates a new class of problems. An agentic process on a code base is stateful, because the code changes under it. A bad seed in the environment sends the agent down a bad trajectory that gets worse and worse.
- He says no one working on state-of-the-art solutions seems to have solved this. The factory gets into weird patterns and eventually grinds to a halt, and he can't think of an architecture that escapes this without a sensible human intervening.

chunks.heading: How organizations should start: slow, with brakes and evidence
chunks.text:
- Start with a small amount of work, such as one issue a day. "It's just all about building trust."
- The key is giving the agent the ability to prove its change works. Many companies hamstring their agents because systems depend on complicated microservices, or on Kubernetes, which makes them hard to run, so most apps are "not factory ready".
- Get your brakes in first: "if you don't push the quality high enough, you're going to turn your app into a slop cannon."
- An ideal agent PR has these properties:
  - It ran against a staging database similar to production.
  - It attached screenshots of the thing working.
  - It rated its own blast radius, meaning how dangerous it is to merge.
- When people see that, they start to believe and can push the accelerator.
- Matt points to the large amount of available labor: have agents aggressively look for issues, run the system, read performance traces and find slow database queries.
- Once you have the brakes, look for data sources to pass to agents. For example, give the agent CLI access to your bug tracker so issues are searchable and pullable.
- Build reusable cron jobs or triggers that pull work into coding-agent sessions.
- He especially prioritizes cron jobs that just improve the code base, because every later session benefits. People underestimate how much the code base steers output: "You think of agents.md as the place where you put all of your instructions, but actually your code base is kind of like a massive agents.md, but only code."

chunks.heading: One-way doors vs two-way doors for deciding what needs human review
chunks.text:
- He borrows the AWS framing: a pull request is either a two-way door (easy to walk back) or a one-way door (never coming back, or very expensive to reverse).
- A one-way door need not be a complicated change. A small subject-line change in code that sends an email to 50,000 people is a one-way door.
- Some industries have more one-way doors. In legal or medical applications many decisions are one-way, which limits the velocity you can get from agents.
- His opinion: "every one-way door must be reviewed by a human", because an agent making that call could cause an extremely expensive mistake nobody accounted for.
- Software has many more two-way doors than fields like civil engineering, where a bridge built wrong is a one-way door. Thinking this way lets you prioritize reviews sensibly.

chunks.heading: Skills: they encode process, with leading words and a few docs
chunks.text:
- Matt thinks of skills as process. When writing them he tries to find the best process for producing software and turn it into text. Books already hold these processes, so being able to call on the literal words is useful.
- With agents, domain-driven design has "a whole new life". The old problem was teaching people the process and converting a whole organization. Agents actually read what you give them.
- Instructing agents carries no social cost: "an infinite array of people who will do my bidding." He once wrote a custom lint rule to catch an annoying pattern of a colleague (his boss, who asked "Did you do that for me?"). Now he can do the same for agents.
- Most agent workflows share a common process: align with the agent before building, build, review, then a compounding step that improves the process for next time. Opinions differ mainly on documentation and structure around it.
- His own emphasis is alignment, domain language, and code review. He says Lauren's skills lean toward implementation, getting more from tests, and detailed playbooks. He believes a combination, such as grilling for alignment plus strong implementation, would work very well.
- The only docs he adds are a `glossary.md` and architectural decision records.
- What he steals from skills are "leading words": compressions that turn a large process into a few words. "Grill me relentlessly" is one that creates an emergent behavior in the agent. Discovering them is hard, but stealing them is easy.
- Agents repeat those words in their own thinking traces, which re-emphasizes them and leads the agent down a path.

chunks.heading: Effect, constraints, and stopping agents from cheating
chunks.text:
- His premise is that agents need restrictions and flexibility around boundaries. The code base needs a certain shape to work well with agents, and Effect makes that shape "not only simple, but inevitable", as long as you don't let the agent cheat.
- He thinks people pitch Effect wrongly. The reason to adopt it is dependency injection, not error handling or type safety. It lets you build small modules you can swap out and gives nice-looking tests.
- His explanation of Effect:
  - It puts programs inside values, so a program sits idle until you execute it.
  - The type system knows everything that can go wrong with the program, everything it produces and everything it needs.
  - That gives the agent many feedback loops and a lot more information about the program.
- He sees three layers against cheating:
  1. Automated checks: lint rules that run on the implementer agent. Effect ships lint rules that hook into the TypeScript type system, plus unit tests.
  2. Automated review, which he thinks most people badly underuse. Telling an implementer "don't do X" makes it think about X. Giving X to a reviewer agent turns it into a positive instruction: look for X in the diff and excise it.
  3. Human review on top, as little as possible.
- He likes statelessness on purpose. Memory systems build up state that can include bad state. The implementer is "super overloaded" (explore, build, verify, debug). The reviewer is "incredibly underloaded", receiving a diff and reporting back, so you can load it with coding standards and give it a fresh context window.

chunks.heading: Strategic programming, taste, and the teach skill
chunks.text:
- He splits programming into tactical (on the ground) and strategic (the long view). He hasn't found agents good at strategic programming and hasn't invested much in trying.
- He thinks they may be bad at it because the median human is too. The feedback loop is slow, and "you could change jobs before your strategic mistakes come back to bite you."
- If agents became good at strategic programming, the death spiral would become a virtuous circle. He doesn't know if that is possible now.
- He thinks agents can raise the floor of a product, but not reach a Linear-level of execution without taste and hard choices. He sees the application of taste as a differentiator.
- He says he wrote his teach skill in an hour and a half on the tube, getting all his ideas about teaching into one skill. People love it, and a video on it goes viral every couple of weeks. He uses it about once a week to ask questions or organize information in his brain in a new way.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt argues the codebase shapes AI output more than prompts or agents.md. A web of small shallow modules is hard for an amnesiac agent to navigate, test and hold in your head. Restructure into deep modules with simple, taste-designed interfaces, tested as gray boxes, so the AI manages the insides.

chunks.heading: Why a codebase's structure shapes AI output more than prompts do
chunks.text:
Matt's thesis is that the codebase itself is the biggest influence on AI output, bigger than the prompts or the agents.md file. If it is designed wrong, it costs in three ways:
- The AI gets slow feedback, so it can't tell whether a change did what it intended.
- The AI struggles to find files, make sense of things, and work out how to test them.
- The developer hits cognitive burnout from holding the AI and the codebase together in their head.

His position is that "software quality matters more than ever". How easy a codebase is to change determines how well AI changes it. The software best practices known for 20 years "still hold more true than ever". He frames this for "real engineers solving real problems", not vibe coders.

chunks.heading: The AI is a new starter with no memory
chunks.text:
Matt tells people to stop treating AI as a superpowered developer heading toward AGI. Its relevant limitation is that it is a new starter in your codebase every time. He compares it to the guy from Memento who steps in and asks "Okay, I'm here. What am I doing?"
- It has no memory and has not experienced the codebase before.
- You may spawn 20 or more of these new starters a day to look at the code and make changes.
- So the codebase needs to be friendly and ready for new starters. What works for onboarding humans is also great for AI.

chunks.heading: Match the file system to the map in your head
chunks.text:
Matt describes the typical codebase as many small modules, each exporting functions, variables, or components. The developer holds a mental map of natural groupings: a thumbnail editor feature, a video editor feature, authentication, CMS CRUD forms.
- That map usually isn't reflected in the file system. Modules are jumbled together, and any export can be imported anywhere with nothing stopping it, producing relationships between things that don't relate.
- The developer understands the map. The AI sees only a bunch of disparate modules, with no natural groupings or relationships.
- His first assertion: the file system and design of the codebase must match the internal map the developer has of it.
- The point is findability. If a prompt mentions something in the video editor section, the AI should be able to find it easily, without knowing every function and module up front.

chunks.heading: Deep modules from A Philosophy of Software Design
chunks.text:
Matt's best answer is deep modules, from the book A Philosophy of Software Design. A deep module has lots of implementation controlled by a simple interface.
- In graph terms, instead of many small modules you get big chunks with simple, controllable interfaces.
- Every export from a chunk has to come through that interface.
- This makes the system easier to navigate, change, and test.
- He warns against lots of little shallow modules: tiny testable units that are hard to keep in your head, grouped and interrelated only loosely. That is the "web of interconnected shallow modules" he says most codebases have.

chunks.heading: Gray box modules: delegate the inside to AI
chunks.text:
Reading about deep modules, Matt saw a seam where he could put AI in control. He doesn't much care what happens in the implementation, only the interface.
- The interface is the publicly accessible API, which he carefully controls and applies taste to.
- The inside is delegated to AI, with tests that completely lock down the module's behavior.
- These are "gray box" modules. He doesn't need to look inside, but can if he wants to influence the outcome, apply taste to the implementation, or improve performance. As long as the tests are good, he doesn't need to care.
- This is "still a million miles away from vibe coding". You must apply taste at the module boundaries: deciding what goes into which module.

chunks.heading: Three benefits: navigability, less burnout, proven practice
chunks.text:
1. **Navigability and progressive disclosure.** Call each module a service (video editor service, thumbnail service). Document each in its own folder, with the public interface obvious in a types section. The AI can see the services on the file system and read the exported types before touching the implementation, then trust what is returned without looking inside. The interface at the top explains what the module does, and you look inside only when you need to change or understand it more deeply.
2. **Less cognitive burnout.** Instead of tracking interrelationships between many modules, he can "keep kind of like seven or eight lumps of stuff in my head". The AI manages the inside, and he worries only about designing the interfaces and how they fit together.
3. **It's what good codebases were always supposed to be.** This is a 20-year-old practice, and what works for humans also works for AI.

chunks.heading: TypeScript, Effect, and planning around module boundaries
chunks.text:
- In TypeScript and JavaScript, it is "not that easy" to make modules with real service boundaries. Some languages make this easier than others.
- He gives a shout-out to Effect. He is using it "way more than I did" when he posted his video on it a few months earlier, and says it makes this modularizing of a codebase simple.
- Think about modules and interfaces in every coding session: when writing PRDs, when turning PRDs into implementation issues, think about which modules are affected, how their interfaces change, and how they will be tested.
- Tests and feedback loops are essential for AI, as for any new starter. A well-tested codebase lets them see how their changes ripple out.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt argues AI has accelerated software entropy and walks through the cure: a shared vocabulary from Ousterhout's deep-module ideas (module, interface, seam, adapter, locality, leverage), then applies his improve-codebase-architecture skill to a real repo. The skill finds deepening candidates, but the human acts as the strategic "general" making the judgment calls.

chunks.heading: Deep vs shallow modules: the vocabulary Matt uses to talk architecture with AI
chunks.text:
- Matt's thesis: AI has "simply accelerated software entropy". Codebases fall apart faster because every change that ignores the whole codebase adds small, weird things that make the code harder to change. Over time this snowballs into "a huge ball of mud".
- He sees this video as the cure. An earlier video on deep modules covered prevention.
- The tool is his improved codebase architecture skill, part of his GitHub skills repo (about 41.5k stars at the time).
- He added a glossary of terms to the skill. A shared vocabulary with the AI lets you be more precise about what you ask for. He says understanding these terms deeply makes you a better developer.

chunks.heading: Core terms: module, interface, implementation
chunks.text:
- **Module**: a unit of something in the app. It could be React components forming a page, the functions that handle authentication, or the logger.
- **Interface**: everything a caller must know to use the module correctly. For auth, that is the sign-in and sign-out methods. It also includes less obvious information such as documentation on how to call the module.
- **Implementation**: what is inside the module, i.e. what it does when you call sign-in or sign-out.
- In a good codebase, modules talk to each other via their interfaces.

chunks.heading: Deep vs shallow modules, depth, and leverage
chunks.text:
- A **deep module** hides lots of implementation behind a simple interface. A **shallow module** has a complex interface with little implementation behind it.
- The idea comes from John Ousterhout's *A Philosophy of Software Design*, which Matt recommends.
- Deep modules are better because they hide more information. The caller only learns a tiny interface to get a lot of behavior.
- **Depth** is "the amount of behavior a caller can exercise per unit of interface that they have to learn".
- Matt cites well-known open-source libraries like TanStack Query as having deep modules, hiding a lot of complexity behind a simple interface.
- **Leverage** is the benefit for users of a module: more capability per unit of interface learned. The deeper the module, the more leverage.

chunks.heading: Seams, adapters, and locality
chunks.text:
- **Seam**: the location where a module's interface lives in the app, between dependent modules. Seams are usually where you do unit or integration testing. To test a module in isolation, you put a mock at its seam.
- **Adapter** (borrowed from hexagonal architecture): the concrete thing that satisfies the interface at a seam.
- Example: an app that depends on a clock. The seam is the clock interface. A real-clock adapter is used in production. A fake-clock adapter is used in tests, so you don't wait 2 weeks for a test to finish.
- Deciding where seams live is "crucial to getting a good architecture".
- **Locality** is the benefit for maintainers. Changes, bugs and fixes concentrate in one place, the deep module. If they are scattered across modules, locality is low.
- You want high locality: co-locate things that matter and often change together.
- Matt names leverage and locality as the two attributes the skill aims at.

chunks.heading: What a bad codebase looks like
chunks.text:
- A bad codebase is usually one with many shallow modules, poor leverage, or poor locality, where logic is spread across many places.
- Matt says "legacy codebase" really means a bad codebase, one that is hard to change.

chunks.heading: Running the skill on a real codebase
chunks.text:
- Target: Matt's course video manager repo, the software he uses to record videos. It has about 1,500 commits, uses React Router and effect.ts, and he wouldn't call it a ball of mud, but wouldn't call it perfect either.
- Steps:
  1. Open a new Claude session and run the improved codebase architecture skill.
  2. Turn off auto mode, which he says behaves oddly with human-in-the-loop flows.
  3. The skill explores the codebase first, then returns candidates for deepening. It found six.
  4. Pick one candidate.
- The candidate he picked: a concept implemented twice, once in the frontend and once in the backend, with no single seam and no tests at it. The two parallel implementations could drift out of sync.
- Refactoring it into one module would gain locality, with the clip and clip-section ordering rule living in one place.
- After a pick, the skill shows concrete code on both sides and enters a "grilling session". You discuss the proposed solution and it proposes a module shape.
- In a normal workflow, Matt would answer each question thoughtfully. For the video he asked it to use its recommended answers to speed things up.
- It then proposed a module shape, asked to verify one implementation detail, and sketched the actual TypeScript interface, i.e. which functions form the module's interface. It also raised design decisions for his feedback.
- Finally you can turn the result into a GitHub issue (via the skill's PRD or issues options) for an AFK agent to pick up. He points to his Sandcastle video for that.

chunks.heading: Strategic vs tactical programming: the human stays in the loop
chunks.text:
- The skill is not AFK. It "demands" judgment from the user, who can't just run it and rely on it to keep improving the codebase.
- Matt's framing: agents are "really, really good tactical programmers" who make changes quickly on the ground. They need a strategic programmer above them.
- The skill is the sergeant that scouts for improvement opportunities. The human is the general who decides what is good for the long-term health of the codebase.
- Cadence: run it "every couple of days", especially on fast-moving codebases, because there will be many deepening opportunities.

chunks.heading: Deep modules, testing, and legacy codebases
chunks.text:
- Clear seams let you write good tests around deep modules. Better tests lead to better agent output.
- For using AI in a legacy codebase, Matt says you first need a harness so changes don't break things. That means tests around deep modules with leverage and locality.
- His recommended starting point: run the improved codebase architecture skill.
- He is building a documentation site for the skills. For now there is a newsletter with updates, tips and resources for getting the most from agents.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt explains the types of LLM hallucination (factual errors, fabricated entities, contextual inconsistency), why they happen (compression of training data and benchmarks that reward guessing), and practical workarounds. The core advice is to feed the model information in context, tell it to use its search tool, and manually verify anything critical.

chunks.heading: Why LLMs hallucinate: guessing is rewarded over admitting uncertainty
chunks.text:
- Matt says LLMs lie all the time, and the lying is common enough to have a name, "hallucination". Having worked with LLMs for roughly 6 months, he says every developer he talks to shares his paranoia about everything an LLM says.
- He is still pro-LLM and says they have massively improved his job and what he can produce. The risk is that LLMs are presented so beautifully that people don't realize how often they are wrong.
- His mental model of training: an LLM is a compression of a huge training set into something small enough to fit on a GPU. Compression loses detail, like a heavily compressed photo where you can still see the microphone cap is blue but can't tell who the person is or their age.
- Why LLMs guess anyway: he cites OpenAI's paper "Why Language Models Hallucinate". Its argument is that training and evaluation procedures "reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty".
- Benchmarks (he shows LiveBench) rank models on reasoning, coding, agentic coding, maths, data analysis and language. Topping a leaderboard is very valuable because switching models is easy. A model tuned to say "I don't know" on maths may score lower than one that guesses, so "you miss all of the shots that you don't take".
- He compares it to people: very smart people tend to be overconfident, humble people tend to be underconfident, and model builders have to pick a point on that line. He doesn't think it is an easy problem to solve.
- His summary: LLMs hallucinate because guessing is more highly rewarded than refusal.

chunks.heading: Intrinsic vs extrinsic hallucinations
chunks.text:
- He draws on a paper with a comprehensive taxonomy of hallucinations in large language models, which lists about 10 types. He covers only a few and says the point is that LLMs are unreliable, especially on extrinsic knowledge.
- Intrinsic information is what you sent the LLM in the current conversation. Extrinsic information is what it must recall from its training data.
- Example of the distinction: tell Claude "My cat is called Bandit", then ask "What is my cat's name?" Getting that wrong would be an intrinsic hallucination. In a fresh conversation, a good model says it has no information about your cat, and guessing a name would be an extrinsic hallucination.
- His experience: LLMs are much more reliable when you send them the information first. If you rely on knowledge from their training sets, "you're going to be disappointed".

chunks.heading: Three types of hallucination, with real examples
chunks.text:
- **Factual errors.** When Google announced Bard (LaMDA-powered), the ad answered "What new discoveries from the James Webb Space Telescope can I tell my 9-year-old about?" with the claim that JWST took the very first pictures of a planet outside our solar system. That was wrong, and it was in the advert. Alphabet's share price dropped about 8%. Matt notes the model apparently wasn't given any document on JWST and answered from training data, which makes it an extrinsic case.
- **Fabricated entities.** The model invents things that don't exist, such as packages, government departments and laws. This matters for developers because asking "Does a package exist for this purpose?" often gets a confident "yep". It has happened to him dozens of times, most recently the other day. It also opens developers to supply chain malware attacks, since attackers can register the fake package names LLMs recommend and spread malicious code.
- **Contextual inconsistency.** The model ignores or contradicts context you explicitly provided, which is an intrinsic hallucination. Example: Jake Moffatt asked the Air Canada chatbot about bereavement fares. It told him to submit within 90 days of ticket issue for a reduced rate, which contradicted the actual policy, and Air Canada was found liable (article from 2024). Matt calls it baffling, comparing it to the LLM forgetting your cat's name right after you gave it.

chunks.heading: Working around hallucinations: give the model the information
chunks.text:
- Matt's main reason he stays pro-AI is that when you pass LLMs intrinsic information, they are far more accurate than when they rely on training data.
- Coding example: he passes his code base or big files to the LLM and asks it to answer questions or explore the code, and gets very good insights.
- Rule: "always make sure that you're providing it the information it needs to succeed."
- The objection he raises himself: when you are searching for something you don't know, you can't supply the information up front.

chunks.heading: The four-word fix: "Use your search tool"
chunks.text:
- His answer to that objection is a four-word prompt: "Use your search tool."
- Most chatbots and agent harnesses have a web search tool the model can call. In Claude he keeps web search turned on under files and connectors.
- Example: asking which Arsenal players are injured right now makes Claude search the web and return an answer with citations to its sources. He says Sonnet did a good job here.
- Why you need to say it: many tools won't search by default. A model that is confident it knows the answer won't call search, because using the tool requires being humble enough to say "I don't know, I need to fetch this". A model tuned to be very smart may just repeat what it believes.
- Prompting it to search pulls articles into the context window, so the answer is based on intrinsic information and hallucinations become less likely.

chunks.heading: Verify critical answers yourself
chunks.text:
- Even provided context can be ignored, as the contextual inconsistency category and the Air Canada case show.
- For life-or-death topics, health, and especially legal matters, he says to ask the model to use its search tool and then read the documents yourself.
- The same happens in his coding: the LLM reads some code, misses the full context, and confidently says something wrong, and he has to reply "No, that's actually not quite right."
- His closing stance: he hopes people stop trusting LLMs implicitly and instead use them for what they are good at, such as writing code. He made the video so people can share it with someone who doesn't yet have this intuition, and says even very smart people in his life lack it.
- He plugs a Claude Code for real engineers course running over the next 2 weeks, built on the idea that real engineering principles still apply in the AI age, and are "better than ever".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt tries Cursor's "thermonuclear code quality review" skill on his Sandcastle repo and critiques the prompt. He likes its ambition, small-file and type-boundary rules, finds it duplicative and blind to tests, and concludes noisy ambitious reviews beat missed opportunities.

chunks.heading: Matt's approach to automated code review
chunks.text:
- Matt says automated code review is "one of the most impactful ways that you can improve the code quality coming out of your agent."
- He keeps a review skill in his skills repo (about 109,000 stars), currently marked "in progress". He is "sort of okay with it" but "not terribly happy with it", so he hunts other people's skills for ideas to steal.
- He tried Cursor's "thermonuclear code quality review" skill on Sandcastle, his open-source software factory.
  - He ran it in auto mode on the last five PRs that reached main.
  - The skill is a single SKILL.md.
- His main takeaway: a review that is very ambitious and pushes many options produces more false positives, but those are "pretty easy just to say no to".
  - The dangerous ones are the improvements the reviewer misses and you never see.
- Of the findings on his Sandcastle PRs, he judged roughly five out of seven good or right.
- He plans to keep experimenting with it, and welcomes requests for other skills to review because it lets him steal ideas.

chunks.heading: Why ambition is the point of the Cursor skill
chunks.text:
- The skill asks for a deep audit of the branch's changes, rethinking the structure "to meaningfully improve code quality without impacting behavior". It says to be ambitious, to restructure the code base where there is a clear path, and to "measure twice, cut once".
- Matt's observation: given a diff, an agent usually treats the diff as its bounds.
  - This skill goes beyond that. It starts from the branch's changes but looks across the whole code base for opportunities.
- He singles out the "code judo" framing as lovely. Two of its primary review questions he likes:
  - "Is there a code judo move that would make this dramatically simpler?"
  - "Can this be reframed so that fewer concepts, branches or helper layers are needed?"
- He likes that it escalates findings where a cleaner reframing could delete whole categories of complexity, and that it suggests deleting a layer of indirection rather than polishing it.
- These questions plus the rules give the agent "a nice way into talking about the code".

chunks.heading: Rules from the skill that Matt endorses
chunks.text:
- **File size.** The skill says not to let a PR push a file from under 1K lines to over 1K lines without a strong reason.
  - Matt reached the same conclusion independently. Large files are hard for agents because the agent must ingest the whole file into its context window to find the useful part.
  - His fix is to split into multiple files and let the file name act as "the context pointer" that tells the agent what is inside and whether to open it. This is more context efficient.
  - He generally splits a file once it passes about 5K tokens, which is a similar rubric to 1K lines.
- **Boring code.** He likes "prefer direct, boring, maintainable code over hacky and magical code". He thinks the idea comes from `simplify` in Claude Code.
- **Type and boundary cleanliness.** The skill says to question unnecessary optionality, `unknown`, `any` and cast-heavy code when a clearer type boundary could exist, and to make type boundaries explicit so control flow gets simpler.
  - Matt's pet peeve is unnecessary optionality. When an agent adds a prop to a React component, it always makes it optional, even when it is always required, apparently for backwards compatibility or to shrink the blast radius. "It's so stupid."
- **Reuse canonical helpers.** Prefer existing utilities over bespoke one-offs, so the reviewer looks for places where the problem is already solved in the code base.
- **Parallelism.** Independent work that is serialized for no reason should be questioned, though the skill also says not to over-index on micro-optimizations.

chunks.heading: Where Matt is unsure about the skill
chunks.text:
- **Pushing logic out of nested ifs.** The skill treats weird `if` statements added in random places as a design problem. It prefers a dedicated abstraction, helper, state machine, policy object or separate module.
  - Matt says "it's arguable whether I prefer that. Sometimes I do, sometimes I don't", and accepted it for the experiment.
- **Vague wording.** He would rewrite parts to be more direct.
  - "Treat unnecessary sequential orchestration and non-atomic updates as design smells" is "word salad to me".
  - "Does this improve or worsen the local architecture?" is not useful unless you say exactly what good and bad look like to an agent.
- **Repetition and size.** The same points (casts, `any`, `unknown`, optional params, duplication) recur through the file.
  - He calls it a "huge ball of mud" for the agent to read, where it is hard to know what to prioritize, and says it could be "cut down quite a lot".
- **Review tone section.** He doesn't know why a "be direct, serious, demanding, do not be rude" section is there, though it does punch up the language the agent uses.

chunks.heading: Output and prioritization in the skill
chunks.text:
- The skill tells the agent to order findings so structural code quality regressions sit at the top and legibility and maintainability concerns sit at the bottom.
  - Matt likes this because it floats the important findings up and keeps the agent from flooding the output with useless findings.
- It ends with an approve or reject verdict on the PR.
- His summary of the skill: be more ambitious, here are specific things to focus on, propose many structural changes, prioritize findings so you don't flood the output, then approve or reject on stated conditions.
- On his run, the verdict was that under the skill's bar a couple of the PRs "should not have landed in their current shape". The behavior was correct, but the code base was "meaningfully messier than it was a week ago".

chunks.heading: What the review found in Sandcastle
chunks.text:
- **Large file.** An init service had grown past 1,000 lines and mixed several concerns. The review proposed a split, and a small generic make-registry function that would delete about 20 lines of duplicated boilerplate. Matt: "feels good".
- **Scattered special case.** A feature-specific `if` on a custom issue tracker name was spread across three layers. The suggestion was to push the variation into a type instead. Matt knows the code well and rated both suggestions good.
- **False positive.** Template args carried both shell commands and prose markers. The review suggested a discriminated union, command or to-do marker, to strengthen the type boundary.
  - Matt said it came from an inaccurate understanding of the system and he'd answer "this is fine". This was two out of three correct so far.
- **Hardcoded dependency.** Templates each declare their dependencies, mostly Zod, but a code path hardcoded Zod. Hard to explain, but it surfaced something weird. Three out of four.
- **Swallowed errors.** `execSync` inside an effect swallowed errors and returned false on failure. Matt wants a reviewer to catch this.
- **Half-finished decomposition.** A large file had been split into smaller files only partway. Five out of six.
- **Prompt duplication.** Two changed prompts were byte-identical in one section, and the review suggested a shared issue-list preamble.
  - Matt disagreed: the prompts should be independently changeable. Five out of seven overall.
- A final list of smaller items also looked "pretty good" on a quick scan.

chunks.heading: What Matt would change in the skill
chunks.text:
- Make it less duplicative and more DRY.
- Add a stronger focus on tests. The skill never mentions testing, seams, or improving feedback loops so future agent runs go better.
  - In his view, that is "the entire point now" of a good code base: one that is easy to change, modular and easy to navigate.
  - Everything in the skill targets source code, none of it tests.
- Bring in thinking about seams in the code base, like what his improved code base architecture skill does.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt walks through building a CLI feature with Claude Code. He starts in plan mode, answers clarifying questions, splits the work into phases, stores the plan as a GitHub issue, and clears context between phases. His memory file keeps replies concise and ends each plan with unresolved questions.

chunks.heading: Planning first, with clarifying questions before any code
chunks.text:
- Matt starts big work in plan mode (Shift+Tab until plan mode shows in the bottom left). Claude Code explores the codebase with an Explore sub-agent before it writes anything.
- His first prompt is rough. He dictates it into a dictation tool and doesn't polish it: "I haven't really put too much thought into this."
- Claude comes back with clarifying questions as a multi-step form. Examples from his CLI task:
  - Where should commit diffs come from? A CLI option.
  - Positional argument or required option? A required option.
  - Match exercise numbers strictly or flexibly? Flexible.
  - What does the "01" represent? The sequence of the diff.
- He dictates answers to the follow-up questions too, then Claude produces a revised plan.
- Nothing is written until the plan is settled: "Notice how we haven't written any code yet."

chunks.heading: Rules file: be concise and end plans with unresolved questions
chunks.text:
- Matt's user memory (opened with the `/memory` command) is only about 43 lines, with "very light hints".
- The top line is his favorite rule and he says he's never taking it out: in all interactions and commit messages, be extremely concise and sacrifice grammar for the sake of concision. That rule is why his plans are short and easy to read.
- The second key rule: at the end of each plan, give a list of unresolved questions to answer, if any, also extremely concise.
  - This puts the open questions in front of him at the exact point where he approves or rejects the plan.
- Other rules in the file are workflow-specific:
  - Use the GitHub CLI as the primary way to interact with GitHub.
  - Prefix branches with "matt" to show they came from him.
  - Rules for PR comments and for changesets, which he uses in several repos.

chunks.heading: Turning a big plan into a multi-phase plan
chunks.text:
- A plan with no open questions can still be too large. Matt's "Spidey senses" told him this one would overrun the context window.
- He rejected the plan ("no, keep planning") and told Claude to "make the plan multi-phase."
- Claude then broke the work into implementation phases that can be split across several context windows.
- He checks the `/context` command often because he's paranoid about context. After exploration and the plan he had 83.7% free space, about 33k tokens used.

chunks.heading: Executing phases and reviewing between them
chunks.text:
- After planning he switches to auto-accept edits and tells Claude to execute phase one. Once the plan exists he can be "pretty aggressive" with accept-edits, because he understands the implementation.
- Small friction: Claude still thought it was in plan mode, so he told it "crack on please with phase one."
- He doesn't review while it runs. He reviews at the end of each phase:
  - Exit Claude with Ctrl+C twice, run `code .`, inspect the diff in VS Code, then run `claude continue` to resume the same conversation.
  - He commits or at least stages changes after each phase so it's clear what each phase added.
  - Claude left a TODO in the code for phase two, which acts as a hint for the next phase.
- Phase one used only about 3k tokens, so he kept going in the same window.
- He allowed `pnpm build` commands with "don't ask again."
- When he saves a file and an auto-formatter changes it, Claude doesn't know. He tells it directly: "pull the files into your context."
- He wishes Claude Code showed tokens used in the status line, as Cursor does. His own status line shows the repo path relative to his repos folder, the branch, and counts of staged, unstaged and new files.

chunks.heading: Storing the plan as a GitHub issue and clearing context
chunks.text:
- To carry a plan across context windows he asks Claude to make a GitHub issue containing the current plan, with completed items checked off. Claude runs `gh issue create` with the plan in the description.
- With the plan saved outside the window, he clears context. `/context` then shows about 16K tokens, just memory files, system tools and system prompt, and no messages.
- He then says: get GitHub issue 24 and enact phase 4 of that plan.
- He chose accept-edits over plan mode for that fresh window. Plan mode would force extra exploration, but Claude read the right file and implemented phase four from the issue alone.
- Phase five reused the already-fetched issue, so it didn't fetch it again.
- He allowed viewing issues with "don't ask again."
- Why GitHub issues rather than a local file: other people can comment on them and add to them asynchronously, even overnight.
- You can run as many phases as you like per window. Splitting across windows is optional, and you watch the context as you go.

chunks.heading: Matt's three top tips
chunks.text:
- Put a tip in your memory file to be extremely concise.
- Get Claude to produce unresolved questions at the end of each plan.
- Get Claude to use the GitHub CLI to create issues, so context is shared across multiple context windows.
- He says this plan-heavy, accept-edits flow is how he does all his coding now, for both AI Hero and Everite. He describes it as a combination of heavy upfront thinking through planning and letting the AI work on accept mode.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt walks through a full feature build in his course video manager: a "grill me" session to harden vague requirements, a PRD, issues, an AFK Ralph loop in Docker, then human QA that feeds new issues back to the agent. He treats the LLM like a delegate: invest in the idea and architecture, lean on shared language, tests and feedback loops, and review inputs and outputs rather than every line.

chunks.heading: Starting a feature with a vague idea and grilling it into shape
chunks.text:
- Matt's example: his course video manager (React Router, TypeScript, Node, Drizzle ORM, Postgres, Vitest, run locally). About 1,200 commits and 637 closed issues.
- The feature: create real lessons directly instead of ghost-then-materialize, delete real lessons directly, and add "ghost courses" with no file path.
- He starts with a loose, dictated brain dump and invokes his "Grill Me" skill, which interviews him one question at a time.
- He says always explain the why, not just the what: "if it doesn't know the why, then it can't suggest alternatives." His why: plan courses freely without committing to a file-system shape.
- Grill Me checks the code before asking, so questions answerable from the codebase get answered there. It spawns an explore sub-agent whose summary returns to the parent, which is token-efficient.
- He used the "by the way" side-question command to ask about the course write service without polluting chat history.
- He chose to put both features in one PRD, a decision he calls "arbitrary."
- His rule on interviews: if the AI can answer from code, it should look first rather than ask.

chunks.heading: Ubiquitous language as the shared vocabulary with the LLM
chunks.text:
- Matt has been reading Domain-Driven Design and adopted a ubiquitous language glossary file. He is the domain expert and the LLM is the dev, so they need precise shared terms.
- Terms in his glossary:
  - ghost lesson: exists in the database but not on the file system.
  - materialize: turning a ghost entity real by creating its on-disk representation.
  - materialization cascade: the chain reaction when materializing a lesson inside a ghost course (assign file path to course, materialize section, materialize lesson).
- The file also lists aliases to avoid, such as "create on disk" and "realize".
- Payoff: he can say "there's a bug inside the materialization cascade" and the agent knows exactly what he means, and function names become easy.
- After the grilling session he has the LLM update the glossary and commits it himself.
- He notes the glossary still lists the old, deprecated plan entities.

chunks.heading: Decisions made during the grill session
chunks.text:
- A ghost course has no file path, so its sections and lessons are ghosts.
- Adding a real lesson to a ghost course forces a modal asking for the course file path, then cascades: course, section and lesson all become real.
- The app only points at an existing directory. It does not create the repo.
- Section state is derived from its lessons. Any real lesson makes it a real section, which is just a directory.
- Schema change: the courses file path becomes nullable. That is the only schema change.
- Once a course has a file path it stays real forever, even if all its real lessons are deleted or converted.
- Ghost courses still need versions because sections and lessons hang off them. The publish and export actions are hidden for ghost courses.
- Real lessons get both "convert to ghost" and a direct "delete", which purges disk and DB in one step.
