- The final scope was eight bullet points, which took about 22 minutes of video. His point: the more you do here, the less you need to guide the LLM later.
- He weighs UI trade-offs with the model by asking for the trade-offs of each option, and says he sometimes drives the conversation himself.
- He considered prototyping UI variants but chose to build one version and give feedback afterwards.
- He praises question-and-answer format because it co-locates question and answer, which the attention mechanism handles well.

chunks.heading: Turning the conversation into a PRD and issues
chunks.text:
- Next skill: write a PRD. It explores the codebase again, then sketches the major modules and surfaces them for review.
- Matt cares about module interfaces more than internals, and wants modules that are testable. He agreed with a new method on the course write service ("materialize course and lesson") rather than overloading the existing materialize ghost method with a parameter.
- He pushed back on deprecating the plans entity inside this PRD.
- Tests go where harnesses already exist, mainly the course write service. When the model claimed no harness existed, he said "look harder" and it found a suite of e2e tests that use a test database and a temporary Git repo.
- Course write service is built with Effect, which he says makes units easy to test. He uses it for every backend thing.
- The PRD is filed as a GitHub issue. He does not review it, trusting LLMs to summarize the conversation faithfully.
- The PRD contains user stories, implementation decisions and testing decisions. The testing section nudges the agent toward TDD and feedback loops.
- Then "PRD to issues" splits it into vertical slices with blocking relationships. The first pass gave six; he merged two small ones to get four.
- His sizing rule: not too small, because each issue costs spinning up a whole agent, and not too large.
- Issues link to the parent PRD, give acceptance criteria and blockers, and cite user stories. He says the PRD is the destination and the issues are the journey. He does not review the issues either.
- By the 15-minute mark of the grilling, context was only about 40K tokens.
- He skips the ask-user-question tool because he dislikes its UI, and not calling a tool is more token-efficient than wrapping JSON.

chunks.heading: Running the AFK agent (Ralph loop) in Docker
chunks.text:
- He runs a Ralph loop with his in-progress library, provisionally named Sandcastle. It spins up a Docker container, mounts the working directory, runs Claude inside, and extracts the commits as patches applied to his local repo.
- A Dockerfile and a prompt are all that is needed. The loop takes a list of issues and the last few commits. Command: `pnpm ralph`, max 100 iterations.
- The agent picks an issue from GitHub, works it, commits and closes it. It finished after five iterations, producing roughly six commits with detailed messages.
- The prompt says to skip issues labeled human-in-the-loop.
- Tests and type checks run on every commit; this is crucial to the loop working.
- "Day shift and night shift" idea, credited to a friend: humans think, grill, and write PRDs by day; the agent implements AFK. While it runs he starts another grilling session.
- He says the approach only seems slow because you are extracting ideas from your head, and agents work on earlier sessions in parallel.
- He would like to parallelize loops with a team of agents but likes the gaps for deep focus.

chunks.heading: QA via generated plan and a feedback button
chunks.text:
- He opens a fresh Claude session and prompts: take the last five commits and create a QA plan, saved as a GitHub issue, with a step-by-step guide to test every part. He has no skill for this yet and thinks it applies to almost any user-facing change.
- He rebuilds and runs the app locally and works through the plan himself, saying watching someone do QA is boring.
- His in-app feedback button turns dictated feedback into a GitHub issue. AI generates the title, and the route it was submitted from is included. That is enough for Ralph to do a good job.
- He relabels the QA-plan issue as human-in-the-loop so Ralph ignores it, and later closes it so it does not become the agent's source of truth.
- While he QAs, Ralph fixes earlier issues in the background. About 8 minutes of QA produced 6 issues.
- Issues found:
  - The add-course modal should only create a ghost course, with ghost terminology hidden from the UI.
  - Creating a ghost course showed a minified React error, did not navigate, left the modal open and had no loading state.
  - Separate "create ghost lesson" and "create real lesson" menu items felt wrong; he replaced them with one add-lesson modal with an "also create this on the file system" checkbox.
  - Delete of real lessons needed a confirmation modal with file details.
  - If the course repo is not a Git repository and a step fails, the created directory must be rolled back so the file system and database stay in sync.
- The UI choice only became clear in the real app, which he says could have been a prototype phase but he is fine jumping to code.
- His argument against specs-to-code: QA surfaces edge cases that are "really hard to plan for before."
- Final tally: 14 commits across the build, about 8 Ralph iterations.

chunks.heading: How Matt reviews AI output
chunks.text:
- He barely reads the code. He reviews inputs and outputs, interface changes and module shapes, and pokes at the code now and then to check direction.
- Philosophy: treat Claude like a teammate you delegate to, focus on architecture and feedback loops, and do not over-plan up front.
- He keeps a flexible backlog, so he can queue bug fixes at any time and Ralph works through them while he continues QA.
- He notes explore sub-agent calls are slow and wishes they were faster.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt explains why TypeScript's enum keyword is a poor fit: it is not native JavaScript, produces surprising runtime objects, and makes TypeScript nominal. He recommends plain objects with `as const` plus a derived union type, which is more flexible and structurally typed, and says to flag enums in PRs without rejecting them.

chunks.heading: Why Matt avoids TypeScript enums
chunks.text:
- Matt says it's fashionable to bash TypeScript's `enum` keyword (the keyword, not the concept of enums). He recommends ignoring enums and forgetting they exist.
- Enums are not native JavaScript. They were added early to give TypeScript a C#, object-oriented feel.
- Matt cites an interview with Anders Hejlsberg: with a green field, TypeScript probably wouldn't include enums again.
- He doesn't teach enums in Total TypeScript, his paid course, "that's how little I think of them".
- In PRs, he says to flag enums and suggest `as const`, but not to reject them. Monitor when enums enter the codebase and check whether they're really necessary.
- He'd revisit the question if enums land natively in JavaScript (there is an ECMAScript proposal). Native enums would be better documented and more predictable.

chunks.heading: Enums behave unpredictably at runtime
chunks.text:
- With `enum LogLevel { Debug, Warning, Error }`, the values default to 0, 1, 2. You'd expect a runtime object like `{ Debug: 0, Warning: 1, Error: 2 }`.
- The transpiled JavaScript is an immediately invoked function expression (an "iffy") that assigns both directions: `LogLevel[LogLevel["Debug"] = 0] = "Debug"`.
- The result also has reverse mappings: `{ Debug: 0, 0: "Debug", Warning: 1, 1: "Warning", ... }`.
- So `Object.values(LogLevel)` returns `0, "Debug", 1, "Warning", ...`, which is "totally not what you expect" if you treat it like an object.
- String enums (`Debug = "Debug"`) produce a plain object, but you must assign every member manually. Matt says that defeats the point of an enum, since members otherwise get assigned automatically.

chunks.heading: Enums are nominally typed in a structural type system
chunks.text:
- An enum works as both a runtime value and a type, so a function can take `level: LogLevel`.
- You must call it with `LogLevel.Debug`. Passing the string `"debug"` fails even though the value is the same.
- TypeScript is a structural type system: it cares about values, not names. Enums break this rule and make it nominal.
- Given `LogLevel` and `LogLevel2` with identical values, `LogLevel2.Debug` can't be assigned to a `LogLevel` parameter.
- Matt says this "doesn't really fit with me", since he thinks of TypeScript as structural.
- The benefit people cite: easy refactors. Renaming members updates everywhere, and it works well in VS Code. Matt notes enthusiasts name this as their number one reason.

chunks.heading: Const enums are better but still not recommended
chunks.text:
- Adding `const` (`const enum LogLevel`) makes the enum disappear at runtime. Its values are inlined wherever it's used.
- Matt calls this a decent compromise: no confusing runtime structure, type safety kept, refactors as easy as with normal enums.
- The TypeScript docs have a whole section on const enum pitfalls and pretty much say you probably shouldn't use them.
- Matt says never use them in library code: they are "really dangerous if you don't control the compiler that's emitting them".
- The edge cases are enough to scare him off recommending them, given there are simpler alternatives.

chunks.heading: The alternative: a plain object with `as const`
chunks.text:
- Matt uses (and has seen across open source and application code) a plain old JavaScript object (POJO) with `as const`:

```ts
const LogLevel = {
  Debug: "debug",
  Warning: "warning",
  Error: "error",
} as const;

type LogLevel = (typeof LogLevel)[keyof typeof LogLevel];
```

- The type is extracted from the object values, so `LogLevel` is `"debug" | "warning" | "error"`.
- A function taking `level: LogLevel` accepts either `LogLevel.Debug` or the literal `"debug"`.
- You don't have to import the object every time you want to pass a value.
- It fits structural typing: the function only cares about the value, and everything works at the type level as you'd expect at runtime.
- The runtime object is exactly what you wrote, with no reverse mappings or IIFE.

chunks.heading: `as const` is more flexible: keys as the source of truth
chunks.text:
- You can extract the type from the keys instead of the values.
- Example: an object mapping levels to human-readable titles, with `LogLevel` extracted via `keyof typeof`.
- In a `log` function, you receive the level and index into the object to prefix the message with its human-readable title.
- Matt says he has done this "dozens of times" in application code: a mapping from a semantic key to the thing it represents.
- Examples he gives: component variants, screen sizes, languages.
- Doing the same with an enum takes more code: declare the enum, declare the titles map keyed by it, extract the enum type, then use the enum in the function.
- Matt's verdict: `as const` does this "a lot better, a lot cleaner", and it is the killer feature over enums.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt walks through ten tips that take generics from intimidating to usable: generic types as type functions, generic functions, inference from runtime arguments, constraints, multiple type parameters, defaults, and linking Zod schemas to inferred return types. The recurring theme is to concentrate the advanced typing in one place so function users never pass type arguments.

chunks.heading: What generics are: type-level functions
chunks.text:
- Matt describes generics as covering "a couple of different patterns". The first is the generic type: a type that takes arguments, like a function.
- Example: `type MyGeneric<TData> = { data: TData }`. Passing `{ firstName: string }` gives `data: { firstName: string }`; passing `string` or `number` gives `data: string` or `data: number`.
- Leaving out the argument errors with "requires one type argument".
- He calls these "type helpers", "type functions" you use to build other types.
- He says TypeScript without generics "would be absolutely awful", and that most developers have used thousands of them without writing one.
- Benefits he names: abstractions, more DRY code, and no excess type annotations.

chunks.heading: Generic functions: a type helper mapped onto a function
chunks.text:
- Starting problem: a `makeFetch(url)` function returns `Promise<any>`. Typing the result means putting an annotation on the caller's side, e.g. `{ firstName: string; lastName: string }`.
- Fix: declare a type parameter on the function, `makeFetch<TData>(url: string): Promise<TData>`.
- Callers then pass a type argument and a runtime argument: `makeFetch<{ firstName: string; lastName: string }>("/api")`.
- His definition: "a generic function is just a normal function with a type helper mapped on top of it".

chunks.heading: Generics you already use in the language and in React
chunks.text:
- `new Set()` is inferred as `Set<unknown>`, so adding a number and a string both pass. Writing `new Set<number>()` makes the string an error.
- He tells you to Cmd-click into the built-in declaration to see that `Set` is generic.
- Many parts of JavaScript and React need explicit type arguments even when you pass no runtime generic argument: `useState`, `useRef`, `useReducer`, `createContext`.

chunks.heading: Inference: the source of the magic
chunks.text:
- Example: `addIdToObject<TObj>(obj: TObj)` returns `TObj & { id: string }`.
- Passing `{ firstName: "...", lastName: "..." }` with no type argument works. TypeScript looks at the runtime arguments and infers `TObj` as `{ firstName: string; lastName: string }`.
- Autocomplete for `.id` on the result still works.
- He calls this "a central idea in understanding generics": type arguments can be inferred without you passing them.
- It is "the source of a lot of the magic". The original version duplicated the object's shape in both a type argument and the runtime argument; inference removes that.

chunks.heading: Constraints with `extends`
chunks.text:
- `GetPromiseReturnType<T> = Awaited<ReturnType<T>>` fails with "Type T does not satisfy the constraint".
- Reason: `ReturnType` only accepts functions. Its declaration has an `extends` clause on `T` (a constraint).
- The fix is to give `T` the same constraint, so only functions can be passed. Passing `string` then errors.
- Constraints can be anything: `T extends string`, `number`, `boolean`.
- Example 2: `getKeyWithHighestValue<TObj extends Record<string, number>>(obj: TObj)`. `Object.keys` errors on an unconstrained `TObj`, because you can't call it on a number or string. The constraint also stops callers passing booleans as values.
- Inference is kept: the result key is still typed `"a" | "b" | "c"`, while the value is `number`.
- His rule: "when you have a generic function you're usually going to want to put a constraint on this". It controls what callers can pass and means you need less logic inside the function.

chunks.heading: Linking arguments: multiple type parameters and `keyof`
chunks.text:
- Problem: `getValue(obj, key)`.
- His first question: "what do I need to capture in the type arguments in order to do everything I need to do at the type level".
- Step 1: capture the object as `TObj`.
- Step 2: type `key` as `keyof TObj`. This gives autocomplete on `"a" | "b"`, and adding `c: true` extends it.
- Step 3: the return type is then a union of all value types, e.g. `string | number | boolean`, because the key is treated as `"a" | "b" | "c"`.
- Fix: a second parameter, `<TObj, TKey extends keyof TObj>`, with `key: TKey` and return `TObj[TKey]`.
- Now `"a"` gives `number`, `"b"` gives `string`, `"c"` gives `boolean`.
- Using `TKey` directly to index without the constraint errors ("cannot be used to index type") and loses autocomplete.
- He says this "inference happening between the arguments of your functions which then maps on to the return type" lets types propagate "beautifully through your app".

chunks.heading: Casting inside generic functions with `as`
chunks.text:
- Example: a typed `objectKeys<TObj>(obj: TObj): Array<keyof TObj>`. `Object.keys` returns `string[]`, which is incompatible.
- Matt's fix is `Object.keys(obj) as Array<keyof TObj>`.
- He knows the usual advice is to avoid `as`, but says "in this case it's actually what you need to do".
- His reasoning: inside generic functions "you know better than TypeScript", which "is going to lose its way in really complicated generic signatures".
- Many libraries add `as any` to make the return type match, and he calls this "absolutely fine to do inside a highly generic function".

chunks.heading: Default type parameters
chunks.text:
- Example: `createSet<T>()` where `T` is not referenced by any argument, so it can't be inferred and falls to `unknown`.
- Needing a `Set<string>` by default, he uses a default type parameter: `createSet<T = string>()`.
- With no type argument you get `Set<string>`. Passing one overrides the default.
- This is the TypeScript equivalent of default parameters in JavaScript.

chunks.heading: Inferring from libraries like Zod
chunks.text:
- Example: `makeZodSafeFetch`, which returns `{ firstName, lastName }` but is not safe at runtime, since `TData` is only an assertion.
- He takes a Zod schema as the argument: `schema: z.Schema<TData>`. Zod's `Schema` has type arguments, and `TData` is the output type.
- At runtime: fetch the URL, call `res.json()`, then `schema.parse(result)`.
- Pass `z.object({ firstName: z.string(), lastName: z.string() })` and drop the explicit type argument. The result is still inferred correctly.
- Adding a field to the type without the schema errors. The function is safe at the type level and at runtime.
- His takeaway: "if you concentrate your types, your advanced TypeScript, in one place it means that the users of your function don't really need to worry about it at all".
- He plugs Total TypeScript, which has a module on generics that is about a five-hour workshop.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt explains why, after 18 months of skepticism, he now recommends Effect. He covers its ugly generator syntax, type-safe error tracking, compile-time dependency injection, the built-in batteries, and how it can be adopted incrementally as a backend TypeScript framework.

chunks.heading: Why Matt thinks you should learn Effect, and how he got there
chunks.text:
- He had been asked for about 18 months whether he likes, uses or recommends Effect. After actually trying it, he concludes "I think you should learn effect."
- He calls it "maybe the most TypeScript of all TypeScript libraries".
- It maximizes type safety, including type-safe errors, and makes code more composable, reusable and testable.
- He thinks of it as a backend-oriented framework for robust applications. It can technically run on the front end.
- He lists three odd properties: unreadable syntax, a batteries-included framework, and an enormous learning curve.
- He says: "Personally, I feel like I'm writing some of the best code in my career using effect."

chunks.heading: The syntax: ugly, but treat it like a separate language
chunks.text:
- Effect code uses generators. `Effect.gen` takes a generator function, and `yield*` resolves other effects (for example fetching a transaction amount and a discount rate, then yielding a calculation effect).
- Matt admits his first reaction was horror, and says viewers will feel the same.
- His analogy is Tailwind: long, ugly class names that turn out to be nice to use once you write them.
- The "disgusting syntax" enables "TypeScript magic that I have never seen from any other library".
- He suggests thinking of Effect as a separate language that still works with normal TypeScript tooling: Prettier, TypeScript, ESLint.

chunks.heading: Type-safe errors tracked across the whole call stack
chunks.text:
- His first use was in his work monorepo, in audio and video workflows.
- In his demo, `extractAudioFromVideo` is an `Effect.fn` taking a file name. If the file name doesn't end in `.mp4`, it doesn't throw. It does `yield*` on a custom error, `IncorrectFileNameError`, which has a name and custom attributes.
- Hovering the function shows an Effect type that tracks the success type (a string) and the possible errors (only `IncorrectFileNameError`).
- Errors propagate to callers. A workflow that calls `extractAudioFromVideo` and `AI.transcribeAudio` ends up typed with `IncorrectFileNameError | TranscribeAudioFailedError`.
- This works over "a potentially infinite call stack".
- Handling errors:
  - Pipe into `Effect.catchTag`, which only catches the named error. Autocomplete shows the remaining options.
  - In his demo he logs `error.message` and resolves the failure as a success. He notes you can handle it any way you want.
  - He can move the same handling up into `extractAudioFromVideo`. It acts like "a type-safe try catch", and the handled error disappears from the resulting Effect type.
- He says homebrewed Result types he has built "haven't felt as flexible as effect", and the difference is "night and day". He may make a video comparing his homebrew version with Effect's error handling.

chunks.heading: Dependency injection is what beat Neverthrow for him
chunks.text:
- Neverthrow, a library for type-safe error handling, could imitate some of Effect's error handling. For a long time he asked "can I just do this with Neverthrow?" He changed his mind after seeing Effect's dependency injection.
- Services are classes that extend `Context.Tag`-style definitions. His demo `AIService` has one method, `transcribeAudio`. It fails half the time with `TranscribeAudioFailedError` and otherwise returns a fake transcription.
- Inside a workflow, `yield* AIService` gives access to the service.
- The third type parameter of `Effect<A, E, R>` tracks requirements. Hovering the workflow shows `AIService` there, and removing the code that uses it reverts the type to `never`.
- If you pipe to `Effect.runPromise` without providing the dependency, you get a compile error: "type AI service is not assignable to type never".
- Providing implementations:
  - `Effect.provide(AIService.Default)` supplies the default implementation (you can cmd-click through to it).
  - `Effect.provideService(AIService, ...)` supplies a different one, for example a mock that always succeeds.
- Running: call `Effect.runPromise` or `Effect.runSync`.
- Benefits he describes:
  - Code is modular and easy to test.
  - In a relatively simple local app he has defined about 30 services. He can test them independently, mock them in tests, or run integration tests across several.
  - Effect generators let him focus on business logic, which makes it trivial to test.
  - His flow is to write the business logic first, creating "typed holes" in the app that he implements later.
- He says this DI story is what "takes it over the top of rivals like Neverthrow", along with being fully type-safe end to end.

chunks.heading: The batteries: what you get for the investment
chunks.text:
- He says Effect is "a big fat batteries included standard library", not a lean core.
- Features he names:
  - Resource management.
  - Observability: `Effect.fn` wraps code in an OpenTelemetry span automatically, exportable to a trace viewer. He spots a mistake in his demo, where the span name should be `extractAudioFromVideo`, because the span takes its name from that string.
  - Type-safe access to process environment variables through config.
  - A cron module for scheduling.
  - State management, batching and caching.
  - Concurrency through a fiber model. It is like working with promises (such as `Promise.all`), but errors and dependencies stay tracked.
  - Streams, which he hasn't dived into.
  - Testing with test clocks.
  - Data types such as Either, Exit, Option and Cause.
  - A full schema validation library.
  - Pre-made solutions for common application designs such as APIs.
- His point is that investing in Effect gets you pre-made solutions to hard problems.

chunks.heading: Objections: functional programming, Rust, and incremental adoption
chunks.text:
- **"Isn't this functional programming?"**
  - He says "technically yes, but hell no."
  - He thinks FP is "so burnt out as a brand" that it shouldn't describe anything.
  - He finds the FP community "pretty gatekeepy" and maths-driven in ways he can't connect with.
  - Effect is technically a monad, but "you won't find the word monad at all in effect docs". He agrees with the docs consciously moving away from FP branding and language.
- **"Why not write your program in Rust?"**
  - You could, if you accept longer compile times and a harder learning curve for a faster program.
  - He thinks TypeScript has space for a library tackling these problems.
  - The case: a team with a hardcore backend project and only TypeScript developers can train them on Effect instead of hiring Rust devs, and end up with "a pretty decent code base". He sees that as where Effect shines.
  - He says the TypeScript ecosystem is "the best in the world in my opinion", and Effect users get it for free.
- **Incremental adoption**
  - The more Effect in a system, the better, since error handling inside that blob is type-safe.
  - You can also have smaller type-safe blobs.
  - Running non-Effect code from inside Effect is easy. Legacy code and non-effectful external libraries can sit in contained areas.
  - He says the adoption story is "actually really good" and much better than it would be with Rust.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt revisits his 2022 types-vs-interfaces video and corrects it. The real performance issue is interface extends versus intersections, not type versus interface for a plain object. He now defaults to interface for extending, and says single-object choice barely matters.

chunks.heading: Phase one: the 2022 "interfaces are the bomb" view, and what Matt got wrong
chunks.text:
- In 2022 Matt believed interfaces were faster than types, citing the TypeScript performance wiki.
- He now says he misread it: the wiki contrasts interfaces with **intersections**, not interfaces with types. It carries the warning "read carefully before you jump to conclusions on this page," which he wishes 2022 Matt had read.
- The wiki's comparison: `type Foo = Bar & Baz & { someProp: string }` versus `interface Foo extends Bar, Baz { someProp: string }`. The `extends` form is significantly faster to compile.
- Declaring a basic object as an interface versus a type gives no performance difference. The difference only appears when object types are combined.
- He also ran a 2022 benchmark of a thousand types versus a thousand interfaces. It found no difference in pure type count, which contradicted his hypothesis, and he did not change his hypothesis. He calls that "the folly of youth."

chunks.heading: Why interface extends beats intersections
chunks.text:
- Interface `extends` gives a hierarchical relationship, so TypeScript can check at each level. Intersections "smoosh" types together and are harder to compile.
- Behavior difference with conflicting properties: if `Bar` has `id: string` and `Baz` has `id: number`, the intersection allows it silently and `id` becomes `never`.
- With `interface Result extends Bar, Baz`, TypeScript errors immediately: "Interface result cannot simultaneously extend types bar and baz. Named property ID of types bar and baz are not identical."
- So the interface form is both cheaper to compile and stricter, catching the conflict where the intersection hides it.

chunks.heading: Real-world evidence that intersections hurt performance
chunks.text:
- Matt says the advice is absolutely still relevant, and it took him a long time to collect real-world data because cases are rare.
- His example, from his article "This pattern will wreck your React app's TS performance": creating a button type with all properties of the original button plus one extra property.
- Doing this with an intersection, repeated across a very large codebase, can wreck TypeScript performance. Switching to `interface extends` gives a large speedup.
- The data came from Jonas, then at Sentry, who said they halved their compile times and made developer experience reflect type changes instantly.
- Takeaway: interface extends versus intersections matters. Types versus interfaces as plain object declarations does not.

chunks.heading: Phase two: it doesn't matter which one you use, as long as you're consistent
chunks.text:
- Matt's second position: pick a convention, such as interfaces for objects and types for everything else, or types for everything. Either is fine if consistent.
- Interfaces carry features he thinks most people don't need when just defining an object shape.
- **Declaration merging** is the main pain. Two `interface Animal` declarations in one scope merge, so a value needs both sets of properties.
- He has worked in 1,000-line files with an `Event` interface at the top and another at the bottom that overrode each other, and he didn't spot it for about 20 minutes.
- Mitigation: turn on the typescript-eslint rule `no-unsafe-declaration-merging`. TypeScript still merges, but ESLint gives an error.
- Declaration merging is a critical feature for things like appending to `window`, so it exists for good reason.

chunks.heading: The index signature gotcha with interfaces
chunks.text:
- Matt covers this in his Total TypeScript article on type versus interface. It surfaced when the creator of AngularJS (Miško) asked him a question on Twitter that he couldn't solve.
- Example: `interface KnownAttributes { x: number; y: number }`, then a variable of that type, then a `Record<string, number>`-style target (an index signature).
- Logically the interface should be assignable, but it isn't. The reason: an interface could later be extended by declaration merging with a property that breaks the string key / number value contract.
- Fixes: add an extra index signature to the interface, or simply declare it with `type` instead. A type alias can't be merged later, so it is assignable.
- Matt notes it comes up so rarely that it took the AngularJS creator contacting him before he noticed it.

chunks.heading: Phase three: the current recommendation
chunks.text:
- Matt's phase three: use types unless you need a specific feature of interfaces. Use an interface when a type needs to extend another type, or when a class implements/extends it.
- There is no performance difference between a plain type and a plain interface.
- He now changes the recommendation again: the declaration-merging risk is handled by the ESLint rule, and the index signature issue is rare. The biggest danger is "the slow degradation of your TypeScript performance due to more intersections."
- Old recommendation: "default to type until you need a feature of interface." New recommendation: "default to interface until you need a feature of types."
- Practical rule he emphasizes most: **default to `interface extends` over intersections**.
- For typing a single standalone object, it does not matter: "Make it a type on Tuesday and an interface on Wednesday. Who cares?"

chunks.heading: Performance still matters despite the Go port
chunks.text:
- TypeScript is about to get roughly 10 times faster with its port to Go.
- Matt reports that Anders Hejlsberg told him you should still think about performance: a bigger TypeScript budget doesn't mean your types should be any less performant. Matt says to trust Anders over himself.
- Meta lesson Matt draws: he was wrong in 2022, ignored his own benchmark result, and has now flip-flopped enough that he cares less about the plain type-versus-interface question.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt live-builds a small testing utility that lets you pass partial, deeply partial test data into strictly typed functions without using `as`. He debates naming, tries a Proxy for runtime safety, sets up CI with changesets, and publishes to npm. Useful for testing ergonomics, library naming and shipping small helper libraries.

chunks.heading: Building a `partial`-style fixture helper to replace `as` in TypeScript tests
chunks.text:
Matt's problem: tests often need to pass less than a function's full type, which forces `as` casts. In the stream he works on a small library (repo "test utils", renamed later to "mock utils") to fix this with a type-safe alternative.

Matt's example: `type User = { id: string; name: string; reports: ... }`, and a function `(user: User) => ...` that only reads `user.id`. To test it you'd normally build the whole object or cast. Cast-based test data is the thing he wants to avoid.

The API he demonstrates:
- `fromPartial(...)`: you pass a deep partial of the expected type and it is accepted where the full type is expected. Nested objects (e.g. `reports` inside `User`) can be partial too. He notes it "looks at the expected type of the parameter" and satisfies that, "reversing what TypeScript usually does in that position".
- `fromAny(...)`: accepts anything. Less safe, for cases where you really need to pass off-type data.
- `fromExact(...)`: acts like an identity function and forces the exact type, so you must pass every required property (e.g. `reports`).
- `createMock` (earlier `createBase`): defines a reusable base fixture for a type, with `fromPartial`-style overrides. Example he builds is a `Request` from node where only `body` is set.
- Nothing generates fake data. The helpers only make the data you pass type-acceptable. "This is exactly the same as `as User`" at runtime, but more palatable and ergonomic.

chunks.heading: Why `as` feels bad, and why a helper is justified
chunks.text:
Matt works through why `as` is the wrong tool here:
- It "doesn't indicate intent" and "feels like a hack"; developers are trained not to use it.
- You must manually write out the target type. With `fromPartial` the type is inferred from the slot you pass into.
- He explicitly asks whether a library should exist just because you dislike a syntax. His answer: people ask him "all the time" how to solve this problem, and he'd have found it useful himself.
- A commenter noted `fromPartial` feels closer to `satisfies` than `as`, which Matt agrees with. He also says that if you're going to trick the compiler, it's good to be explicit about that.
- He notes the pain-point survey result: when he asked people what hurt about testing in TypeScript, they said this should be fixed.
- He mentions Zod-based mock generators (zod-mock) as a good tool when you do want generated data from a schema.

chunks.heading: Naming discussion
chunks.text:
Naming takes a large part of the stream, and Matt treats it as a core design problem.
- Candidates for the creator function: `createBase`, `createMock`, `createFixture`, `createScaffold`, `createPartial`, `stub`, `fake`, `core entity mock`.
- Why not "mock"/"stub": they imply behavior (mocking a class or endpoint), and he is not mocking behavior, only supplying dummy data. "Fixture" fits dummy data better, which pushes him toward it; he ends up changing the README and code to `createFixture`.
- He liked the names `fromAny`, `fromPartial`, `fromExact`, and kept them.
- A commenter pointed out that Cypress already has a fixture function.
- He dislikes generic names, wants a "boring" package name, and rejected naming it after himself. The package ends up as "mock utils" (he jokes about "mocky tills") and he says he is not calling it `faux` or `poMock`.
- A viewer's remark that he'd drop the underscored `_base` private concept led Matt to remove it, since he didn't need it.
- Reference point: Zod's naming (`z.object`, `z.string`) works well because the concepts are already familiar, and he compares it to tRPC's "procedures". He recalls that naming dominated his work on XState: "90% of it was picking the names of stuff".

chunks.heading: Experiment: Proxy-based runtime safety (and why he shelved it)
chunks.text:
A viewer suggests the fixture could be a `Proxy` that throws if a test accesses a property it didn't define. Matt calls this "a genius idea" because it adds runtime safety on top of type safety, and he'd never used `Proxy` before.

What he tried:
- Test: `fromPartial({})` passed to a function that reads `input.id` should throw.
- `new Proxy(target, { get(target, prop, receiver) {...} })`, throwing when `prop` isn't in the mock.
- Problems hit when used with Vitest's `toEqual`: it probes properties such as the symbol iterator and `$$typeof`-style checks (a viewer found `nodeType`/`asymmetricMatch`), causing "not found" throws. He tried ignoring symbols and adding `ownKeys`/`has` traps (suggested by chat) with limited success.
- A viewer later identified the culprits as property names Vitest's equality code accesses. After the first hour Matt returned and added a `protectedKeys` list (including `asymmetricMatch`-style keys) that the proxy lets through. That made the test pass.
- Recursion: he then wrote a failing test for nested access (`input.foo.id` should also throw) as the next step.

At the first stop he commented the proxy code out so he could ship, and said the proxy idea "feels funky" because it risks making tests fail for strange reasons. Later he re-enabled it with the protected-keys fix and opened a PR titled roughly "add proxy behavior to fromPartial".

chunks.heading: Shipping a small TypeScript library: the checklist
chunks.text:
Matt walks through his setup (this is the third time he's done it on stream):
- Turborepo monorepo, so `pnpm turbo dev|build|lint|test` runs everything.
- CI (GitHub Actions): checkout, set up pnpm, set up Node with pnpm cache, install, run `lint build test` through Turbo. The whole CI run took about 15 seconds.
- Release workflow using Changesets: a `publish` workflow runs a `release` script (Turbo build, lint, test, then `changeset publish`). `changeset init`, set `access: public` in `config.json` (he forgot this last time), and add a first patch changeset.
- Repo settings: allow GitHub Actions to create pull requests, and add an npm token as a repo secret (a granular access token with read/write rights).
- Merging the generated "version packages" PR publishes to npm.
- First publish failed because the workflow wasn't passing `NPM_TOKEN`; after fixing that it published. He then fixed `.npmignore` so the package didn't ship `.github` or the changelog.
- He prefers Vitest ("what the industry is moving to"), and likes small helper libraries rather than maintaining large ones.
- He uses Changesets over semantic-release because a former colleague used it; he hasn't tried semantic-release.
- A GitHub Actions VS Code extension gives autocomplete for workflow files.

chunks.heading: Opinions on tooling mentioned in passing
chunks.text:
- Monorepos: "they're great"; he used to be developer advocate for Turborepo, which solves scheduling and caching.
- Turbopack: he was on the team that shipped it and wrote its initial docs. It is a webpack-level bundler where the Turbo engine caches the result of every function (read file, bundle, concatenate) and parallelizes across cores, so a change to one file only recomputes that part. He predicts Vite will eventually use Turbopack, but says he has no inside information.
- Wallaby/Quokka-style live test runners: he's not sure about them since the Vitest and Jest versions "never quite work as well as I want".
- Mutation testing (Stryker): mentioned but he gave no verdict.
- He thinks TypeScript will always compile to JavaScript and won't become the base language of the web.
- On library authoring in TypeScript: "not pretty from the library side"; conditional types in particular show TypeScript is "still early on" in what it wants to be.
- His own video workflow: roughly 25 minutes of footage cut to 5 using a script that drops OBS output into DaVinci Resolve with silence-cutting, about 1.5 hours end to end. He also mentions a CLI he wrote ("Matt CLI") that wraps the GitHub CLI with custom prompts, open source in his repo.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt explains TypeScript as a shorter feedback loop in your IDE, why its open object types surprise people, and why a targeted as any beats TS ignore or TS expect error. He also argues complex types usually come from complex JavaScript and favors JSDoc plus handwritten docs.

chunks.heading: Typescript as an IDE-powered feedback loop
chunks.text:
- Matt defines TypeScript as a way of making your IDE more powerful: autocomplete, red squiggly errors, and warnings when code isn't doing what you think.
- JavaScript has no types, so TypeScript adds syntax on top so it can understand your code at a deeper level.
- Its origins: people compiled C# to JavaScript (ScriptSharp) to make big apps workable. Steve Luco and team saw that people wouldn't learn C# just for that, so TypeScript's innovation was also making types familiar to JavaScript developers.
- A type is a contract or constraint. For an add function, `a: number, b: number` is the contract for calling it correctly.
- TypeScript compiles to JavaScript and strips all types, so types don't exist at runtime. Confidence comes from TypeScript checking calls ahead of time.
- Two feedback loops: the JavaScript loop (write, switch to browser or node, run, which can be slow for a third step of a multi-step form) and a much shorter loop inside the IDE.
- Does TypeScript make you slower? Matt says no. Once you're comfortable with types, the shorter loop lets you code much longer before checking in the browser.
- He estimates an experienced JavaScript developer can get productive with TypeScript in about a week to 10 days of focused work.

chunks.heading: The three parts of TypeScript
chunks.text:
- Matt describes TypeScript as three things bundled under one name: the language, the CLI (compiler), and the language server in your IDE.
- In an open-source world these would likely be separate packages. They share a name because one Microsoft team of "seven or eight people" builds them together.
- The CLI doesn't have to emit JavaScript. It can just check the whole project.
- His metaphor: TypeScript is like the English language. The language server is a teacher looking over your shoulder with red squiggles, and the CLI is turning in the whole essay to be marked.
- ESLint vs TypeScript: ESLint is single-file and runs rules per file, so it parallelizes. TypeScript checks the whole project because global things (such as which ECMAScript version, e.g. `replaceAll` being ES2023) affect every file.
- TypeScript knows "the type of everything", so it can make much smarter judgments. Some ESLint rules use TypeScript's knowledge.

chunks.heading: Open object types, excess properties, and why TypeScript chose them
chunks.text:
- TypeScript has open (non-exact) object types. Flow had exact object types by default.
- Example: a fetch function taking `{ url, timeout? }`. Passing a misspelled `timeOut` as a fresh object literal errors. Put the object in a variable first and pass it, and TypeScript accepts it, even with a thousand extra properties.
- TypeScript treats an object literal passed directly as "fresh" and checks excess properties. Otherwise it only cares that the required properties are present.
- Upside of exact types (Flow): you know exactly which keys exist, so `Object.keys` can be typed precisely. In TypeScript, `Object.keys` returns `string[]` because extra keys are possible.
- Matt's reading of TypeScript's choice: it mirrors object-oriented subtyping. You should be able to pass a Chihuahua where an Animal is expected. He links it to C#'s creator being heavily involved in TypeScript.
- There's no real way to get exact object types in TypeScript. Generic tricks exist but "don't feel good", and fighting the language isn't worth it.
- Real-world gotcha: returning an object with excess properties from a function inside a `useState` updater doesn't error, which people complain about constantly.
- Practical answer: validate at runtime. Zod's `schema.parse` strips excess keys so you know what you're working with.
- His summary: excess properties "can just appear like wild Pokémon all the time".

chunks.heading: Self-documenting APIs with JSDoc
chunks.text:
- Matt recommends heavy, high-quality JSDoc comments on APIs and functions, so hovering in the IDE shows what they do, with usage examples and links to related types.
- Story: during night wakeups with his newborn (born January 2024), he made seven or eight PRs to the React types adding JSDoc comments, e.g. for `React.ReactNode`. They were merged.
- He's skeptical of auto-generated API doc sites (TSDoc-style tools). They give "cookie-cutter" output, mirror what's in the IDE, surface internal stuff that shouldn't be documented, and can become an excuse not to write real docs.
- His recommended combo: tons of good JSDoc plus a well-written handwritten docs site.
- Interactive playgrounds depend on the audience. They make sense for visual components or when users get real value; auto-spewing TSDoc onto a site isn't documentation.

chunks.heading: Complex types, DRY, and when to use any
chunks.text:
- Complex TypeScript comes from complex JavaScript, since types only describe what the JS does. If types get gnarly, simplify the code first.
- Often the urge to perfect types comes from wanting code to be DRY, creating abstractions (generic functions) so you don't repeat yourself. Matt's advice for a team stuck on types: simplify the JavaScript, write "dumber code", decompose into smaller functions.
- Derived vs decoupled types: an avatar component's props and a database user object shouldn't be linked just because they share fields. Linking them via clever generics couples the system so a change in one place echoes everywhere. He argues for being "stupid" at boundaries.
- Knowing when to use `any` is "game sense", built by experience and understanding TypeScript's mental models (which is what his book targets). "We're not in the business of writing complicated TypeScript, we're in the business of serving users."
- Story: he recently upgraded a package, slapped a few `any`s on the resulting errors, and the upgrade really had broken something.
- Legitimate assertions: telling TypeScript that `document.getElementById('root')` is never null, because you know more than it does. The risk is the reverse, where TypeScript knows more than you.

chunks.heading: The Redux Reselect type story
chunks.text:
- Matt tells how Mark Erikson spent about two weeks writing a long, complex generic type for Reselect's `createSelector`.
- TypeScript tests new compiler versions against the ecosystem. During 4.9 testing, that single type was the only thing in the ecosystem that broke.
- Anders Hejlsberg himself rewrote it, shorter, more elegant, faster, and compatible with older versions.
- Matt's takeaway: the TypeScript team are "wizards".

chunks.heading: ts-ignore vs ts-expect-error vs as any
chunks.text:
- `@ts-ignore` suppresses every error on the next line. `@ts-expect-error` does the same but errors if the next line has no error, so it cleans up after itself when, say, a dependency is fixed. Matt uses `@ts-expect-error` heavily in his courses to assert something should fail.
- But he says both are sledgehammers: they hide everything on the line, including misspellings, nonexistent variables, and faulty imports.
- His preference in application code: `as any` on the specific node, since it targets one thing, usually the thing you need to get past. There's no "expect error" equivalent for `as any`.
- Why `any` rather than `unknown`: `unknown` is the top type, the "upstanding country lawyer" of the type system that you can't do anything with without narrowing. `any` is assignable to and from everything and disables checking on itself, so it is "the hooligan, the destroyer of types".

chunks.heading: Where TypeScript is heading
chunks.text:
- TypeScript won't chase ecosystem trends such as typed file-based routing (Remix-style `$param` filenames feeding `loader` types). It would be possible and useful, but TypeScript has little incentive to bake in a fashion that might turn out to be a bad idea.
- Matt's wish: types in JavaScript itself, via the TC39 types-as-comments proposal (talked about at JSConf Budapest). Types would be ignored by the runtime, with the TypeScript CLI and language server still checking.
- That would remove the whole build step of stripping types and generating source maps. He hit this pain trying to set up the VS Code debugger for TypeScript files, and Node only recently added experimental TypeScript support.
- Advice for learning: function parameter annotations get you about 90% of the way, since most other types are inferred.

chunks.heading: Career, hunger, and teaching
chunks.text:
- Matt was a self-employed singing teacher for about 6 years (drama degree, a master's at Guildford School of Acting, later London drama schools), setting up three businesses in three cities. He started because a friend needed a teacher for a singing-lessons site.
- He taught himself to code and moved into development around age 25, going junior to lead in roughly 3 years.
- He then worked on XState, answering GitHub issues and writing articles for about 2 years, growing from roughly 400 to 3,000-4,000 followers, then joined Stately.
- His breakout: in February 2022 he posted a 2-minute, no-cuts video of advanced TypeScript from his XState work and gained 39 followers in an hour. He recorded about 12 tips in one Sunday and queued them out, growing from around 4K to 10K very quickly, then teamed up with Joel Hooks at Egghead.
- He says the growth wave has "crashed a little" since his baby was born, and he is grateful for it (including having more time with his son). He's open to broadening beyond TypeScript, and would even like to return to full-time engineering on a team.
- On hustle: his goal was never to work more but "to work at as high a leverage as possible" so he could earn enough without working much. He frames his 20s as "competence" and 30s as "compassion", and says hustle culture only covers the first.
- On impostor syndrome: fear of not being good enough drove him to consume everything (he cycled to work listening to the Syntax podcast). He advises turning that fear into hunger.
- On heroes: each step up in singing teaching showed him the people above him were "just people", which prepared him for tech, including seeing peers like Kent C. Dodds as regular people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A casual podcast interview where Matt explains why he prefers inferred types, how any is a tool not a sin, why people misread TypeScript errors, and how he got into TypeScript. Also covers the new using keyword and how to approach TypeScript adoption on a team.

chunks.heading: Inferred types vs explicit return types
chunks.text:
- Matt prefers inferred types because they are the most likely to be correct. On XState, types for state machines were so complex and threaded through so many functions that annotating them by hand was "way more trouble than it's worth", since it overrides what the system already knows.
- He sees explicit return types as useful mainly when you want to lock down a function that is used in many places.
- TypeScript is clever enough to work out the correct type from your if statements and switches.
- To pick one member out of a union (say a Square from Circle, Triangle, Square, null, undefined), he lists several routes:
  - a custom type predicate, such as `isSquare`
  - an `in` check on a property
  - a discriminated union with a `type` field, then `if (object.type === "square")`

chunks.heading: Using `any` pragmatically
chunks.text:
- Matt describes a mid-wit bell curve meme: beginners use `any`, the angry middle says "you can't use any", and experts use `any` again.
- If the outside of a function is properly typed, `any` inside it matters little, especially if the function is tested.
- He calls `any` "just another tool" to be used sparingly, not all over.
- Libraries such as Zod, tRPC and React Query have `any`s in their code because the types are so complex that TypeScript cannot keep up. He compares it to "locking TypeScript in a cupboard for that line".
- If you are going to come back and fix it, `any` is fine for now. If you won't revisit it, spend the time to type it properly.

chunks.heading: The biggest TypeScript mistake: not reading the errors
chunks.text:
- Matt says the biggest mistake is getting scared of errors and not reading them.
- A console stack trace puts the most relevant information at the top. A TypeScript error is in reverse: the least relevant information comes first, and the failed comparison sits at the very bottom.
- People read the first line, see an unfamiliar third-party type, and give up. His advice is to read the error from the bottom up, because the bottom shows what actually failed.
- The error language is also very precise and based on the AST (abstract syntax tree), using words like "identifier" and "name property", which is unfamiliar unless you have seen lots of these errors.
- His VS Code extension TS Error Translator rewrites errors into plain English.
- The Total TypeScript extension adds a second feature: a small blue hint on complex syntax such as generics, with a link to the relevant docs.

chunks.heading: How Matt got into TypeScript: API contracts and a generic table
chunks.text:
- At a job (the same one where he adopted hooks) a small front-end team was chasing a large back-end team. The API kept changing, with casing wrong, fields unexpectedly null, and contracts shared as Json pasted into a Google doc.
- He wanted GraphQL for a proper contract. When that did not work, he went for TypeScript instead.
- He described the API interfaces in TypeScript, replaced the Google doc, and built a proof of concept in which fetched data flows down through the app with those interfaces.
- His teammates reacted with "we're just never going to ship a bug again", since their bugs mostly came from faulty API responses. Velocity went up.
- His first TypeScript component was a generic table component whose render-row function changed based on the data passed in. That let them drop many type annotations.
- At a later job he converted a fully JS React Native app to TypeScript, and then XState exposed him to advanced types.
- The moment he fell for TypeScript was his first refactor: when the data shape changed, he changed the interface and a four-hour job became a five-minute job, because TypeScript showed everywhere that needed updating. It "felt like cheating".

chunks.heading: Adopting TypeScript in an existing JavaScript project
chunks.text:
- Matt's view is that TypeScript does not have to be all or nothing. Many projects keep a typed core (utilities, API methods, database access) at the center of the tree, with the leaf components still in JavaScript.
- JSDoc comments can give you the autocomplete without TypeScript itself.
- For him, coding without TypeScript feels like "coding in low power mode", "semi-skimmed coding", and like losing a friend.
- He says TypeScript is sticky: people who get into it do not go back to JavaScript when they are under deadline pressure, unlike practices such as unit testing or TDD that people drop on the next project.
- Generous abstractions are a benefit. A generic group-by function can be used across a code base, and consumers get inference without annotating.
- If a team is hesitant, he suggests asking whether you hit "can't call that because it's undefined" issues. If you do, TypeScript will help, and most projects grow complex enough to need it.
- For doubters, he recommends:
  - trying it on a toy project
  - installing his VS Code extension
  - reading the TypeScript handbook cover to cover, which he finds good as a beginner experience though it lacks coverage in places
- He says he no longer spends time arguing that TypeScript is good, because it is already in nearly every conversation in the industry.

chunks.heading: New in TypeScript 5.2: the `using` keyword
chunks.text:
- The `using` keyword reached stage 3 at TC39 and arrives in TypeScript 5.2 (the beta was due within a few weeks of this June 2023 recording).
- If the returned value has a `Symbol.dispose` method (or `Symbol.asyncDispose`), the resource is closed automatically when the variable leaves scope. So `using database = getDb()` replaces a try/catch/finally that closes the connection.
- It guards against forgetting to close connections, which can leave hundreds open and crash a database.
- He gives WebSockets and file reading as other uses, such as opening a socket for one call and closing it again.
- It is inspired by C#, where it is a very popular feature.

chunks.heading: React: hooks, effects and state machines
chunks.text:
- Matt put hooks into production the day they were announced, with no documentation, because they solved duplicated code in his project. He says he has "never looked back" and does not understand most criticisms of hooks.
- He views hooks as something like a domain-specific language for the React environment.
- He says old patterns such as `shouldComponentUpdate` bought performance but cost robustness and maintainability.
- `useEffect` gave "an amazingly simple API that was an extremely sharp knife": cut yourself easily, but good abstractions if you are skilled.
- He often reached for XState instead of `useEffect` because a state chart makes the lifecycle easy to follow, "if you've got it in a freaking PNG".
- On signals: he likes Ryan Carniato's framing that signals are effects used to update the DOM and create bindings. He has not used them, having focused on XState's React integration, and would like to see state machines combined with signals.
- Tailwind over vanilla CSS: he is "terrified of the Cascade". Tailwind fits the component model, and since adopting it three or four years ago the CSS bugs have gone away. The VS Code extension gives smart autocomplete, and Tailwind Merge combines variants.
- He has never used `git rebase`, only merges.

chunks.heading: Total TypeScript and his teaching approach
chunks.text:
- Matt has been a full-time TypeScript educator for about a year, working mostly through Twitter, YouTube and courses. Before that he did developer advocacy at Vercel and worked on XState at Stately.
- Total TypeScript has a free beginners tutorial and a free "beginners with React" tutorial, produced to the same standard as the paid material but shorter.
- His format is practical: about a minute of video, then a small task for you to do, then he shows how he would have done it.
- He dislikes "40 hours of content" video courses, saying "there's no way I'm gonna do that".
- The site's wizard illustrations come from illustrator Michelle Holick, who produced them from scratch with no notes from him. He said the artwork inspired the rest of the site.
- Before development he was a voice and singing teacher for about six years, with a master's in voice and singing, teaching accents, public speaking and Shakespeare. He says this is why he can hold his own in front of clients and why the teaching itch is now scratched.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock joins Sebastian Silbermann, maintainer of @types/react, to walk through how React's types live in DefinitelyTyped, how they're versioned, and why changes are hard. Matt's own contributions are mostly questions and framing on semver for types, breaking changes, and why more accurate types are good errors. Sebastian supplies most of the technical detail.

chunks.heading: Why the React types live in DefinitelyTyped, not in React
chunks.text:
- React is written in Flow, so the TypeScript types are bolted on from outside as `@types/react`, published from the single DefinitelyTyped repo. Rewriting React in TypeScript would need a big justification.
- Sebastian Silbermann (the main maintainer of the React types) says the repo's big pro is that a change to the React types gets tested against every other types package, so untested changes don't ship.
- Moving the types into the React repo would lose that infrastructure. Dimitri's paid work on the types wouldn't carry over, and he would have to watch the whole noisy React repo.
- Matt asked whether the types could live in the React repo, as Jest, Immutable.js and Yarn do with types maintained in parallel to non-TypeScript code. Sebastian's answer: React releases are too rare. Types changes like new HTML attributes or tighter literal unions need a faster cadence.
- Matt points out that a PR merged to the React types ships quickly, whereas waiting on a React release would take months.
- Decoupling also lets people upgrade React's runtime without a types upgrade. Sebastian says "I would encourage people to upgrade the runtime and deal with the types later", and warns this is hard to teach without ending up with `any`s and ts-expect-errors everywhere.

chunks.heading: Versioning types alongside a runtime library
chunks.text:
- Matt notes SemVer is well defined for runtime but not for types. Removing a function export is clearly major; removing an exported type is murkier.
- The React types keep major and minor matching React, while the patch number is completely decoupled. There may be around 80 type patches with zero React patches.
- Types can lag the runtime minor. React was on 18.2 while the types said 18.0, because 18.1 and 18.2 added no new features. Matt notes this makes it hard to know which minor of the types to pin when stuck on an old version. Sebastian agrees they should bump the minor anyway to avoid the confusion.
- Matt says it would feel strange to have React 18 with React types 26, so the types are tied to React's major.
- Sebastian's own SemVer rules for types:
  - Removing an exported utility type is a breaking change, but he argues you should just keep it and mark it deprecated.
  - Constraining a type further (a `string` becoming two literals) is breaking, "but it's kind of what you want from the types".
  - The TypeScript team's position is that every change is a breaking change, so it can't map to SemVer.

chunks.heading: What counts as a breaking change in types
chunks.text:
- Sebastian's example: adding an attribute to a shared HTML attributes interface broke users who had extended that interface with a same-named prop of a different type. CI went red, which is "a breaking change in the literal sense". Adding any property to an interface can do this.
- Matt's framing: when the new types are more truthful and accurate, the errors they uncover are good errors, not breakage.
- Sebastian weighs the fix cost. The fix there was wrapping the extended interface in `Omit`, a minor change.
- Changes that break types for users, like changing the generic parameters of `useReducer`, wait for the next React major. Sebastian tested one on his work codebase, found 10 to 15 breakages, and decided to hold it for React 19 even though it gave better contextual typing and removed an overload.
- Implicit children is the precedent. It was held back from 17 and removed in 18, merged on release day after about two years of waiting.
- Sebastian's balance: avoid piling up breaking changes in one major, because people get put off upgrading React when the types break. TypeScript is so ubiquitous that "if it doesn't work in TypeScript, many people don't consider it as working at all".
- Matt's takeaway: trying to break as few things as possible has a cost, but the reasoning is sound.

chunks.heading: Typing the DOM: why React can't inherit lib.dom.d.ts
chunks.text:
- Matt asks why React doesn't reuse TypeScript's `lib.dom.d.ts`. Sebastian says the two describe different things.
  - `lib.dom.d.ts` types DOM interface properties, such as `HTMLBodyElement` for `document.body`.
  - React's types describe HTML attributes. The two don't map one to one.
- Example: the HTML attribute is `class` but the interface property is `className`. React's handling is inconsistent, mostly following properties but sometimes making things up, like `defaultChecked`.
- Sebastian says there's no library for HTML attributes that React could use instead.
- Matt recalls the TypeScript team including DOM features that are supported in a few browsers.
- Sebastian's rules for adding attributes:
  - Experimental or single-browser attributes get a "no". Users can augment the types themselves, and the React TypeScript cheat sheet documents how.
  - Attributes React doesn't forward to the DOM the way you'd expect are left out. His example is `inert`, which in React takes a string rather than `true`, so typing it as the browser-style boolean would give the wrong runtime behavior.
- The React types sit between the DOM and React's runtime, communicating what actually works in React.

chunks.heading: How JSX is typed, and what's changing for async server components
chunks.text:
- Matt asked Sebastian to explain how TypeScript understands JSX. Sebastian's explanation:
  - TypeScript looks at the global/scoped `JSX` namespace and asks two questions. For classes, is it assignable to the element class? For function components, does it return `JSX.Element` or `null`?
  - That hardcoded check is why a component can't return a string, boolean, array, number or a Promise. If the lookup fails, types fall back to `any`.
- The problem: async server components can't be typed by the React types alone because these checks are hardcoded in the TypeScript compiler.
- Sebastian says TypeScript 5.1 changes how this is inferred. Instead of hardcoded checks, it will ask the JSX factory (historically `React.createElement`) what it accepts.
- Once that lands:
  - The React types control what a function component may return, so async components returning a Promise, or returning context, become possible.
  - The `createElement` typings could be simplified. They have eight overloads and an old to-do, and typing every host element like `div` and `input` is expensive.
- Performance is the risk. Deeply nested JSX means deeply nested factory calls the type checker has to instantiate. Sebastian says TypeScript tried this about three years ago and backed off over poor performance on deep trees. Server components and promises now make fixing it more pressing.
- Matt asks whether this would let children pick up generics from their parent, a typed child. Sebastian says people want it but it would need careful testing and may stay out of reach, or ship as an opt-in for people who accept the cost.

chunks.heading: Legacy mistakes: `useRef`
chunks.text:
- Sebastian won't call them mistakes, because the types are 8 or 9 years old and things evolve. His example is `useRef`, whose typings evolved from `createRef`, which was built for class components under different constraints. It carries a lot of footguns.
- The fix is ready but is waiting on the React 19 major.
- People get disappointed that they have to wait. Matt's reply: "That's the common thread with all of this. People are disappointed", and it's inherent to the job.

chunks.heading: Contributing to the React types
chunks.text:
- Mechanics of the DefinitelyTyped workflow, as Sebastian describes it:
  - The authors list in `index.d.ts` is used to ping the right people on any PR touching that package.
  - File PRs as drafts first. React's CI takes about an hour because it tests against roughly 700 packages. Marking a PR ready for review pings all the authors.
  - Once someone approves, a "ready to merge" comment makes DefinitelyTyped auto-merge and auto-publish.
- Start a conversation via GitHub Discussions, not Issues, because discussions allow threaded replies. Put the package name in brackets in the title, like `[react]`, so the right authors are pinged.
- Keep discussion in the open rather than on Discord, so PRs can link back to the context.
- Matt asked whether this process is documented. Sebastian admits it's mostly in the readme and assumed knowledge.
- Matt says contributors don't get a changelog for types packages. Sebastian agrees this is missing, since each change is just a new version and he doesn't see a way to go from a version to its PR. He'd like the publisher to generate changelogs from commits and PR descriptions.
- The hardest part of the job, in Matt's telling, is that everyone has a different idea of how strict types should be, and you "only hear about the problems you cause, not the services you provide".
- Matt gives a personal example of the cost. He burned out at his peak, and recalls a three-week thread about a `props with children` type that resolved only on a call, when it turned out the disagreement came down to how a non-native English speaker read the word "with".
- Sebastian's call for help: the remaining work is complicated, so fresh eyes asking "why do we have this?" are the most useful contribution, and he reads every notification. He is largely working alone and tunnel-visioning.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock defends TypeScript against panelists who prefer plain JavaScript with JSDoc. He covers refactor safety against changing back-end data contracts, TypeScript's inference strength, branded types, types-first design, and why generics mostly matter for library authors.

chunks.heading: Why Matt prefers TypeScript over plain JS and JSDoc
chunks.text:
- Matt says TypeScript "saved my life" on a React project that kept falling behind in plain JavaScript. After adopting it, the team "almost doubled" its velocity, mostly by removing a whole class of bugs.
- The front-end team received complex data structures from a back end whose contracts kept changing (a boolean became a string, uppercase "P" became lowercase "p"). In JS they had to check every change against the runtime by hand.
- With TypeScript, a changed contract produced red squiggles wherever it mattered. Some fixes could be refactored automatically. Tasks that took hours became type-level checks, and he no longer needed to test in the runtime.
- Against the argument for JSDoc, he says JSDoc is verbose, "way too verbose," and has weaker IDE support. TypeScript gives "a more complete experience."
- He is relaxed about the extra step: when coding in TypeScript he feels "in a bubble," like "a sensory deprivation tank." In JS, even with JSDoc, he has to "work harder."
- He prioritizes the feeling of safety: "I just can't make a mistake." Good tools let you "basically code while drunk" because they catch every mistake immediately.

chunks.heading: Is TypeScript forcing complexity on you? Matt's rebuttal
chunks.text:
- Matt rejects the claim that TypeScript was built as "a scripting language for C#" and pushes back on it repeatedly. In his view it is a different tool now: "it is becoming more JavaScript."
- Any JavaScript project can go into TypeScript without further changes. You can cast things as `any` and add annotations to functions. You "don't necessarily need to embrace classes or inheritance."
- Classes exist in JavaScript before TypeScript. TypeScript doesn't force them on you.
- His one concession is the `enum`. It is a TypeScript-specific feature that compiles to runtime JavaScript. He says the team "regret" adding it and "wouldn't do that anymore." The team has "calibrated itself" to support what JavaScript can already do rather than impose new patterns.
- He doesn't accept that TypeScript adds design patterns JS lacks. Apart from `enum`, he says, it doesn't.
- On generics: they exist only at the type level, not as runtime code.
- On the "raises the floor" objection, he agrees TypeScript raises the floor, but argues a higher floor means a better product. You can teach TypeScript on the job; a few annotations are quick to pick up, perhaps "20 minutes" with the start of the handbook.

chunks.heading: Inference is TypeScript's real strength
chunks.text:
- He calls inference "the thing that typescript is really really good at."
- Example: given an `unknown` variable, `if (typeof thing === "string")` types it as a string inside that block.
- He argues TypeScript "understands JavaScript's type system incredibly well" and does "deep, interesting inference" that gets better over time.
- It "doesn't impose any constraints on what you want to build." You can build anything in JavaScript with TypeScript.
- Mentions that JSDoc only provides syntax. The checking is done by `tsc`, so JSDoc without `tsc` gives no real benefit.
- Notes that the TypeScript team ships something new in nearly every minor version.
- Mentions the TC39 "type annotations in JavaScript" proposal (presented at JSConf), which would let annotations sit in JS and be checked with `tsc`. He was interested in it.

chunks.heading: Hard types, library authors and the app-user divide
chunks.text:
- He maintains XState's TypeScript surface ("xdate" in the transcript; the library is described as one of the most complicated TypeScript libraries out there). He has worked on it for about a year and a bit.
- To make the TypeScript experience good for users, the team has to "bend over backwards" and "go deep into the language." Colleague Andarist did much of the deep work and reported TypeScript bugs found along the way.
- Meta-programming heavy libraries (the panel's example was Objection.js, an ORM) produce type definitions that "look like an alien language." Generics, `extends`, `infer` and angle brackets in odd places can look "bamboozling and terrifying."
- Matt's framing: there is a divide between app users and library authors. Most TypeScript users won't touch complicated generics; that is "the work of library people".
- He worries that the syntax itself puts people off, even though the primitives are fairly simple once you know the syntax.
- He created a VS Code extension, the TypeScript Error Translator, to decode TSC errors, which he says can be "terrifying."

chunks.heading: Types first, then implementation
chunks.text:
- Matt's workflow: when building something new, he thinks about the data first, declares the types in TypeScript, and only then designs the flow and the API. TypeScript "makes me think data flow first, types first and implementation later."
- A panelist countered that Rob Pike criticizes exactly this (types first leads you to get types wrong before you know how the program works). Matt did not concede the point and said he found the idea fascinating.
- On testing: a panelist argued unit tests do not replace type checking, and Matt did not disagree. Matt said he was surprised the discussion hadn't gone the "just unit test your JavaScript" route that critics usually take.

chunks.heading: Branded types and wrapping up
chunks.text:
- He confirms TypeScript can do "branded" types (new types): for example, an alias on `number` so an imperial value can't be mixed up with a metric one.
- He has used the same trick with strings: entity IDs mapped to different types, so you can't pass a user ID where a post ID is expected. He calls this "very very powerful" and notes it is compile-time only, with no runtime equivalent.
- Panelist asked about a hypothetical subset of TypeScript that is one-to-one with JavaScript output. Matt did not argue for it.
- Closing view: compilation is sometimes hurtful and sometimes overkill, but "typescript gives you enough to make the compilation worth it," especially with the integrated tooling.
- His course (Advanced TypeScript) is at mattpocock.com; he is on Twitter at @mattpocockuk, and works at Stately AI on state machines and statecharts with a visual editor that compiles to code.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt argues you should ban `any` by default but shows two advanced cases where it is correct: wide type argument constraints like `(...args: any[]) => any`, and returning conditional types from generic functions where TypeScript's narrowing falls short. He advises backing the latter with unit tests and using eslint-disable.

chunks.heading: Why `any` is banned by default, but needed in type argument constraints
chunks.text:
- Matt says `any` "disables all of TypeScript's features - type checking, autocomplete, and safety." It lets you treat a value as JavaScript.
- Example: `const myFunction = (input: any) => { input.someMethod(); }; myFunction("abc");` fails at runtime.
- He says most of the community rightly considers `any` harmful, and the typescript-eslint `no-explicit-any` rule exists to stop it. That can put developers off `any` entirely.
- He still says there are advanced cases where `any` is "always the right choice".

chunks.heading: Type argument constraints: use `any[]` and `any`, not `unknown`
chunks.text:
- Matt's example is re-implementing the `ReturnType` utility, a generic type that takes a function type.
- With `T extends (...args: unknown[]) => unknown`, it works for functions with no arguments.
- It breaks once the function has a parameter such as `(input: string) => void`. The error is "Type 'unknown' is not assignable to type 'string'", because function parameters are checked contravariantly.
- The accidental result is a `ReturnType` that only accepts functions whose parameter is `unknown`.
- The fix is `type ReturnType<T extends (...args: any[]) => any> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;`
- He says this is safe because you are "deliberately declaring a wide type": "I don't care what the function accepts, as long as it's a function."

chunks.heading: Returning conditional types from generic functions
chunks.text:
- Matt notes TypeScript's narrowing is weaker than we'd like in some places.
- Example: `youSayGoodbyeISayHello(input: "hello" | "goodbye")` returns `"hello" | "goodbye"`, not the precise literal.
- The fix is a generic `TInput extends "hello" | "goodbye"` with a conditional return type: `TInput extends "hello" ? "goodbye" : "hello"`. Callers then get `"goodbye"` for `"hello"` and `"hello"` for `"goodbye"`.
- Problem: inside the function body, TypeScript can't match the conditional type to the runtime `if (input === "goodbye")` logic. Returning `"hello"` or `"goodbye"` errors with "Type '"hello"' is not assignable to type 'TInput extends "hello" ? "goodbye" : "hello"'."
- He first shows two ways to force it with `as`: casting to the full conditional type, or extracting a named generic type `YouSayGoodbyeISayHello<TInput>` and casting to that.

chunks.heading: Using `as any` inside generic functions, backed by a unit test
chunks.text:
- Matt says "in these situations, it often makes more sense to use `as any`": `return "hello" as any;` and `return "goodbye" as any;` in the function body, with the conditional return type kept on the signature.
- He admits this makes the function less type-safe, since you could accidentally return `"bonsoir"`.
- His trade-off: it's "often better to use `as any` and add a unit test for this function's behavior". Because of TypeScript's limitations here, "this is often as close as you'll get to type safety."
- He says there are several other cases where you need `any` inside generic functions to get around TypeScript's limitations, and that this is fine to him.

chunks.heading: Policy: ban `any`, with `eslint-disable` for the exceptions
chunks.text:
- Matt's answer to whether you should ban `any` from your codebase is yes, on balance.
- Turn on the ESLint rule that prevents it and avoid `any` wherever possible.
- The legitimate cases are worth using `eslint-disable` to get around.
- He suggests bookmarking the article and attaching it to PRs when you feel the need to use `any`.
- He invites readers to share other legitimate use cases.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt shows that swapping `any` for `unknown` only moves the problem: `any` causes bugs, `unknown` forces runtime validation boilerplate. Using a groupBy utility as the example, he argues generics are the only way to type such functions so consumers get exact types with no casts or checks.
