chunks.heading: Why `any` is dangerous and how it spreads
chunks.text:
- Matt says any `any` in a codebase is "a cause for concern" because it disables type checking on whatever it's assigned to.
- Passing an `any` to a function parameter means nothing can be guaranteed about that parameter. In his `groupBy(arr: any[], key: any)` example, there is no way to know that `item` is an object or that it has a property matching `key`.
- An `any` also "leaks" across an application. A function that returns `any` disables type checking in every place its result is used.
- In his example, `result` comes back as `any`, so `result[20].foreach(...)` (misspelled `forEach`) and `item.name` both go unchecked. A call like `groupBy(array)` with a missing argument also slips through.

chunks.heading: Why `any` gets added in the first place
chunks.text:
- One reason is trying to fix a bug the developer doesn't understand. Matt notes TypeScript has "plenty of hard edges that can feel unintuitive for beginners."
- His example: looping over `const keys = ["a", "b"]` and assigning `obj[key] = key` on `const obj = {}` errors with "Element implicitly has an 'any' type because expression of type 'string' can't be used to index type '{}'." Annotating `const obj: any = {}` makes the error vanish, but it is the wrong fix.
- Better fixes depend on how specific the type should be:
  - `const obj: Record<string, string> = {}` types the properties as any string.
  - `const keys = ["a", "b"] as const;` with `const obj = {} as Record<typeof keys[number], string>` types `obj` with exactly the keys `'a'` and `'b'`.

chunks.heading: Not enough generics is another source of `any`
chunks.text:
- Matt's second cause: not using enough generics. He asks the reader to imagine TypeScript had no generics and to try typing `groupBy` as an untyped function: "How on earth do you type this function?"
- Without generics, the only way to avoid `any` is to fall back to `unknown`, which creates a different set of problems.
- Core claim: if you are concerned about `any`s in a codebase, you need to know generics.

chunks.heading: Replacing `any` with `unknown` just moves the problem
chunks.text:
Matt walks through trying to type `groupBy` without `any` or generics:

1. Start with `arr: Record<string, unknown>[]` and `key: string`. This errors with "Type 'unknown' cannot be used as an index type" at `result[resultKey]`.
2. Cast with `item[key] as string`. This errors with "No index signature with a parameter of type 'string' was found on type '{}'."
3. Annotate `const result: Record<string, unknown[]> = {}`. The errors go away.

The outcome is that `groupBy(array, "age")` always returns `Record<string, unknown[]>`.

- **The upside ("HELL YES"):** this beats `any` because it gives proper type safety on the result's values. A misspelling like `result[20].foreach` now errors with "Did you mean 'forEach'?"
- **The downside:** "we've just changed the problem." Instead of `any`s spreading, `unknown`s spread.

chunks.heading: Why `unknown` is "yelly" and validation is runtime bloat
chunks.text:
- Matt calls `unknown` "extremely 'yelly'." It errors whenever you access a property on it (`item.name`) or assign it to a more specific type like `{ name: string; age: number }`.
- You can narrow it with validation: check `typeof item === "object"`, that `item` is truthy, `"age" in item`, `"name" in item`, then `typeof item.age === "number"` and `typeof item.name === "string"`.
- But when you already know for sure that `item` has a `name` and an `age`, this validation is "pointless runtime bloat."
- His recap:
  - Unnecessary `any`s are bad because they cause bugs.
  - Unnecessary `unknown`s are bad because they bloat runtime code with boilerplate.
  - Typing a utility function to return the `unknown`s in the right place is "NOT easy."

chunks.heading: Generics are the way out of the any/unknown Catch-22
Summary
chunks.text: A short essay sharing a .cursor/rules snippet: declare explicit return types on top-level module functions so future AI assistants understand each function's purpose. The one exception is JSX components, whose return type is always JSX.

chunks.heading: Return type annotations on top-level functions
chunks.text:
Matt recommends a `.cursor/rules` addition that tells an AI assistant to declare return types on functions declared at the top level of a module.

- The rule text he shares: "When declaring functions on the top-level of a module, declare their return types. This will help future AI assistants understand the function's purpose."
- Example from the rule: `const myFunc = (): string => { return "hello"; };`
- The stated motivation is helping future AI assistants understand the function's purpose.
- The rule as written applies to functions declared at the top level of a module.

chunks.heading: Exception: components that return JSX
chunks.text:
Matt's rule carves out one exception to the return-type convention. - React components that return JSX do not need a declared return type. - His reasoning: "as it is always JSX", so an annotation adds no information. - Example from the rule: `const MyComponent = () => { return
Hello
; };` with no return type.

chunks.heading: Writing rules for AI coding assistants
chunks.text:
The essay is a short, copyable example of how Matt encodes TypeScript conventions as instructions for an AI coding agent.

- Rules live in `.cursor/rules` and are written as plain-language guidance plus a short code sample showing the preferred form.
- This rule states the convention, gives a reason, and includes an explicit exception.
- Matt links this to his larger set of Cursor rules, which focus on TypeScript language features, documentation, structure (like Result types), teaching the AI nuances such as `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, and practical habits, rather than specific frameworks.
- He distinguishes shareable, project-specific Workspace Rules (versioned in Git) from personalized Global Rules (living in your IDE) that tailor the AI to an individual's style and workflow.
- His stated goal in sharing the ruleset is to kickstart a discussion on what makes effective AI coding guidance for TypeScript, since he found existing community rules lacking.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock argues that most frontend complexity comes from handling states, and that handling starts with how states are typed. He contrasts a 'bag of optionals' type, which permits impossible shapes, with a discriminated union that makes each state carry exactly its own data. He also extends the idea to component props.

chunks.heading: Matches data to UI with discriminated unions, not bags of optionals
chunks.text:
Matt warns against modelling frontend state as a "bag of optionals": one object with a `status` field plus optional `error?` and `data?` properties.

- Example type: `{ status: "loading" | "error" | "success"; error?: Error; data?: { id: string } }`.
- It permits impossible shapes: `status: "success"` with no `data`, or `status: "loading"` with an `error` attached.
- Optional properties suit values that may or may not be present. Here presence is fully determined by status:
  - `loading`: never `data` or `error`.
  - `success`: `data` always present.
  - `error`: `error` always present.
- His framing: most frontend complexity is handling the many states an app can be in, and "handling states starts with how they're represented in types".

chunks.heading: Building the discriminated union step by step
chunks.text:
Matt's method is to scaffold first, then fill in each branch.

- Start with a union of objects that each carry only a `status` literal: `"loading"`, `"success"`, `"error"`.
- Add each branch's own data:
  - `{ status: "loading" }`
  - `{ status: "success"; data: { id: string } }`
  - `{ status: "error"; error: Error }`
- Impossible states now fail to compile:
  - `{ status: "success" }` errors with "Property 'data' is missing".
  - `{ status: "loading", error: new Error("Eek!") }` errors because `error` does not exist on that branch.
- He says the type "now properly represents all the possible states of the feature".

chunks.heading: Why destructuring fails until you discriminate
chunks.text:
A common stumbling block is destructuring the union before narrowing it.

- Code: `const { status, data, error } = state;` where `state: State`.
- TypeScript reports "Property 'data' does not exist on type 'State'" (and the same for `error`).
- Reason: until the union is discriminated, only properties shared by every member are available, which here is just `status`.
- Fix: check the discriminant first, then destructure.
  - `if (state.status === "success") { const { data } = state; }`
- Matt calls this strictness "a feature, not a bug". It pushes developers to think in terms of states and to access data only in the states where it exists.
- He uses React in the example but says the idea applies to any frontend framework.

chunks.heading: Discriminated unions for component props
Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock gives a decision rule for runtime validation with Zod based on how much you trust and control an input. Validate anything untrusted, validate trusted-but-uncontrolled third-party data to fail early, and usually skip validation for inputs you both trust and control, with version drift as the debatable edge case.

chunks.heading: Where Matt says to use Zod: validate by how much you trust the input
chunks.text:
Matt frames the decision around the inputs to an app: points where data is injected and is unknown at runtime. His rule is a three-way split by trust and control:
- Inputs you don't trust: use Zod.
- Inputs you trust but don't control: validate them with Zod.
- Inputs you trust and control: he usually doesn't validate them with Zod.

If he were building an app with any unknown inputs, he'd "add Zod right away".

chunks.heading: Untrusted inputs: CLIs, public APIs, forms, sockets, localStorage
chunks.text:
Examples of inputs he treats as untrustworthy:
- A CLI argument, e.g. `matt run <something>`, which is unknown at runtime and might not exist.
- A public-facing API's path `:id`, REST method, headers, search params and request body (all of which anyone can ping, so unvalidated ones can be attack vectors).
- Forms (login forms, CRUD forms), websocket connections, and `localStorage` (users can manipulate it, or it may be out of date).

For a simple script he parses `process.argv` with a tuple schema:
- `z.tuple([z.any(), z.any(), z.string()])` is parsed against `process.argv`, which usually has two useless leading arguments before the dynamic one.
- `name` is then inferred as `string` with no other work.
- For more complex CLIs he points to `commander`.

chunks.heading: Validating a public API request with safeParse
chunks.text:
For an Express handler, Matt builds a schema covering the whole request:
- `body`: `z.object({ email: z.string().email() })` ensures the email exists and is an email.
- `headers`: `z.object({ authorization: z.string() })` ensures the authorization header is present.

He calls `CreateUserSchema.safeParse(req)` rather than `.parse`, so nothing is thrown:
- If `!result.success`, return `res.status(400).send(result.error)`.
- Otherwise read `result.data.body.email` safely.
- He notes Zod's errors are "really nice, readable", so the caller knows what went wrong.

chunks.heading: Trusted but uncontrolled inputs: third-party APIs
chunks.text:
For services you rely on but don't control (GitHub, YouTube, other teams' APIs), Matt still validates:
- If the API changes shape, it can cause subtle bugs. He's lost hours assuming his own code was wrong before realizing the API returned something unexpected.
- Zod still errors in your app, but the error is thrown early, right when data enters, which makes it much easier to debug.
- APIs controlled by other teams in the same organization are debatable; depending on culture he'd consider Zod an option.

Costs he acknowledges:
- Bundle size: Zod is 12kb gzipped (per his cited Bundlephobia link for zod 3.20.2), too large for some apps.
- Validation is inevitably slightly slower than not validating, so skip it if critical-path performance matters.

His weighting: in most apps he's built, robustness is the key concern. "Impossible data", meaning data you don't expect, has probably been the most frequent cause of bugs in his dev life, so he validates any input that's remotely untrustworthy.

chunks.heading: Controlled inputs: frontend calling your own fullstack API
chunks.text:
The hard case is a fullstack app (Remix, Next.js, SvelteKit, Nuxt) whose frontend fetches from its own API endpoint, which is likely already Zod-validated.
- Version drift: a user keeps a tab open (e.g. a finance app with charts refreshing every 10 seconds), you redeploy with breaking backend changes, and the stale frontend starts breaking.
- Zod on the frontend would error as soon as drift happens and could prompt the user to refresh.
- Matt usually opts not to use Zod here. The app is typically just a browser refresh from a better experience, and nothing security-sensitive is exposed to frontend code, so the blast radius is small.
- He calls it up for debate: you may want to check all incoming data so you error on any version drift.

chunks.heading: Learning resource
chunks.text: Matt points to his free 10-exercise Zod tutorial on Total TypeScript for learning Zod.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A short essay arguing that TypeScript expertise, especially turning `any` into safe types and designing type-safe abstractions, saves teams bugs and speeds them up. For security-critical apps specifically, Matt says he'd lean heavily on branded types.

chunks.heading: Branded types as the security tool for TypeScript apps
chunks.text:
- When Matt is asked how to approach a security-critical TypeScript app, his advice is to "use the crap out of branded types".
- He points to a Twitter thread he wrote on branded types (posted February 2023) as the longer explanation.
- Branded types are the tool he reaches for when the cost of mixing up values is high.

chunks.heading: Why TypeScript wizardry matters to teams
chunks.text:
- TypeScript is now the most popular language on GitHub. It overtook JavaScript in PRs per week.
- Matt says TypeScript can feel very different from JavaScript: strange syntax, arcane inference rules, generics.
- Because of that, it is "extremely tempting to just ignore the errors and slap on an 'any'".
- He notes that most TypeScript application code is written under severe time constraints. In his words, apps get built on "blood, sweat and 'as any'".

chunks.heading: Turning any into safe types
chunks.text:
- As TypeScript takes more market share, he expects TypeScript "wizards" to be in higher demand.
- His core claim: "Having the knowledge to transform any's into safe types will save your team bugs."
- This is a way to make your skills more valuable. It is not only about cleaning up legacy code.

chunks.heading: Type wizardry as a DX multiplier
chunks.text:
- Beyond cleanup, advanced TypeScript knowledge lets you build DX improvements that accelerate a team.
- Examples he gives of abstractions that need this knowledge:
  - A custom form abstraction.
  - A type-safe REST API endpoint creator.
  - A flexible Table component.
- His career argument: "The more you can enable your teammates to develop faster, the faster you'll rise up the ladder."
- He describes this as satisfying, engrossing work: designing and implementing APIs that help other developers code faster.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock explains when to derive one type from another (Pick, Omit, indexed access) and when to write a plain, decoupled type. The test is future workload: derive when types share a concern and must change together, decouple when coupling would create busywork or tie unrelated concerns.

chunks.heading: When Matt derives a type versus decouples it
chunks.text:
- Derived types (`interface extends`, union types, `Pick`, `Omit`) create a one-way relationship. The derived type inherits from the source, so changes to the source ripple down, but the derived type can't modify the source.
- Deriving couples the derived type to the source. Deriving from another derived type can create long coupling chains that are hard to manage.
- Matt frames the decision as being "all about reducing your future workload":
  - Will updates to one type need to ripple to the other? Derive.
  - Are they so unrelated that coupling could create more work later? Decouple.

chunks.heading: Decoupling props from a data type: the `AvatarImage` example
chunks.text:
- Setup: a `User` type in `db.ts` with `id`, `name`, `imageUrl` and `email`. An `AvatarImage` component only uses `imageUrl` and `name`.
- Matt's principle: make functions and components require only the data they need, which stops unnecessary data being passed around.
- The derived option is `type AvatarImageProps = Pick<User, "imageUrl" | "name">`. The problem is that `AvatarImageProps` now depends on the shape of `User` and on its existence in `db.ts`. Moving `User` or splitting it into separate interfaces means revisiting `AvatarImageProps`.
- The decoupled option is `type AvatarImageProps = { imageUrl: string; name: string }`. `User` can then be moved, split or deleted without affecting `AvatarImageProps`.
- Matt prefers decoupling here because `User` (a data type) and `AvatarImage` (a UI component) are separate concerns with different responsibilities and different reasons to change. Decoupling makes `AvatarImage` more portable and easier to maintain.

chunks.heading: Resisting the urge to feel clever with `Pick`
chunks.text:
- Matt says deriving can make you feel "clever". `Pick` tempts because it uses a more advanced TypeScript feature, which feels good to apply.
- His advice: "often, it's smarter to do the simple thing, and keep your types decoupled."
- The title's point is that being a TypeScript wizard isn't always the right move. Advanced type manipulation isn't a goal in itself.

chunks.heading: When deriving is the right call: shared concern
chunks.text:
- Matt says deriving makes the most sense when the coupled code shares a common concern.
- Example: an `as const` object and its union type.
  - `const albumTypes = { CD: "cd", VINYL: "vinyl", DIGITAL: "digital" } as const;`
  - `type AlbumType = (typeof albumTypes)[keyof typeof albumTypes];`
  - Decoupling would mean writing `type AlbumType = "cd" | "vinyl" | "digital"` and maintaining two closely related sources of truth. Because the two are closely related, deriving is better.

chunks.heading: When deriving is the right call: directly related types
chunks.text:
- Example: `type UserWithoutId = Omit<User, "id">`, used in `updateUser = (id: string, user: UserWithoutId)`.
- The concerns are closely related. Matt says decoupling them "would make our code harder to maintain and introduce more busywork into our codebase."
- Contrast with `AvatarImageProps`: `UserWithoutId` is still a variant of the same data model, so a change to `User` should ripple through. `AvatarImageProps` belongs to a different layer (UI), so it shouldn't.

chunks.heading: What counts as a derived type
chunks.text:
- `interface AlbumDetails extends Album` inherits all of `Album`'s properties, so changes to `Album` trickle down.
- `type Shape = Triangle | Rectangle` is derived from its members. `Shape` can't modify `Triangle` or `Rectangle`, but changes to them ripple into `Shape`.
- Matt's framing: DRY ("Don't Repeat Yourself") applies to types as well as variables and functions, but the coupling it introduces has a cost.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock gives three opinionated rules for organizing types in an application: colocate or inline single-use types, move shared types to the smallest shared location, and put cross-package types in a shared monorepo package. He treats types like functions, so they follow the same sharing logic.

chunks.heading: Rule 1: colocate or inline single-use types
chunks.text:
- A type used in only one place goes in the same file where it's used.
- Matt's classic example is component props: for `MyComponent` taking `foo` and `bar`, he declares `interface Props { foo: string; bar: number }` in `MyComponent.tsx`, right above the component.
- He finds a separate `MyComponent.types.ts` "pretty unintuitive to work with". When working on a component he is usually editing its implementation and its types together, and two files makes that harder.
- When a type is truly single-use, he says don't be afraid to inline it, e.g. `(props: {foo: string; bar: number}) => {...}`.
- Teams often resist inlining because it feels "messy". Matt's view: you don't always need to extract a separate `type` or `interface`, inlining is absolutely fine, and it's very low-cost to pull it out into a named type later if you need to.

chunks.heading: Rule 2: move shared types to the smallest shared location
chunks.text:
- A type used in more than one place should move to a shared location.
- His mental model: think of types in an application as functions. A function used by multiple modules gets moved to a shared location, and the same goes for types.
- In practice he creates a `*.types.ts` file in an appropriate spot in the app.
  - Types shared across the whole app: `src/shared.types.ts`.
  - Types only used inside the components folder: `src/components/components.types.ts`.
- The principle: "I share the type across the smallest number of modules that need it." The types file sits as close as possible to the code that uses it, not in a global dumping ground.

chunks.heading: Rule 3: put types shared across a monorepo in a shared package
chunks.text:
- A type used in more than one package of a monorepo should move to a shared package.
- Example layout: `apps/app`, `apps/website`, `apps/docs`, plus `packages/types/src/shared.types.ts` holding the types all three apps share.
- How the shared package is implemented depends on how the monorepo is structured.
- Matt points to a guide on internal packages he wrote for the Turborepo docs while at Vercel as a starting point for setting this up.

chunks.heading: Summary of the approach
chunks.text:
Matt's three rules, in order of escalating scope:

1. Colocate (or inline) single-use types.
2. Move shared types to a shared location, as narrowly scoped as possible.
3. Move types shared across a monorepo to a shared package.

He presents this as an opinionated take that, for most developers, will confirm existing intuitions, and which makes for "a well-structured codebase". The underlying idea is the same one used for implementation code: a type lives with its code until a second consumer appears, then it moves up exactly as far as needed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock argues you should default to `type` aliases and reach for `interface` only when you need object inheritance via `extends`. He covers the performance benefit of `extends`, the surprise of declaration merging, and the implicit index signature difference, and why these push him to the opposite default from the TypeScript team.

chunks.heading: Defaults: `type` over `interface`
chunks.text:
- Matt's default is `type`. He recommends reaching for `interface` only when a specific interface feature is needed, mainly `extends`.
- Type aliases (`type` keyword) can express any type: unions, mapped types, conditional types. Interfaces can't.
- Example: `type StringOrNumber = string | number;` can't be written as an interface.
- He argues the `type` vs `interface` difference is small enough that either works "without many problems", and the TypeScript docs agree it's personal preference.
- He disagrees with the TS team's default, which is `interface` first and `type` only when needed. His advice is the opposite: "I'd recommend you use `type` by default. It's a little more flexible and a little less surprising."
- His reason: declaration merging and implicit index signatures are "surprising enough that they should scare you off using interfaces by default."

chunks.heading: Use interfaces for object inheritance
chunks.text:
- When objects inherit from each other, Matt uses interfaces.
- Example: `interface User extends WithId { name: string }`.
- The same thing works with type aliases via an intersection (`type User = WithId & { name: string }`). Both flag excess properties like `wrongProperty: 123`. The intersection version is "perfectly fine code" but "slightly less optimal".
- The reason is type-checking speed. With `extends`, TypeScript can cache the interface by name in an internal registry, so later checks are faster. With `&`, it can't cache by name and has to compute the type nearly every time.
- It's a small optimization, but it adds up if the interface is used many times.
- The TypeScript performance wiki recommends preferring interfaces over intersections, and Matt agrees.
- This is the one case where he recommends `interface`, but he still doesn't recommend it as the default.

chunks.heading: Declaration merging
chunks.text:
- When two interfaces with the same name are declared in the same scope, TypeScript merges them.
- Example: one `interface User { name: string }` plus another `interface User { id: string }` produces a single `User` requiring both. A `const user: User = { id: "123" }` then errors with "Property 'name' is missing".
- Two `type User = {...}` declarations in the same scope error with "Duplicate identifier 'User'". This is safer.
- Matt notes merging is intended behavior and a necessary language feature. It's used to model JavaScript libraries that modify global objects, such as adding methods to `string` prototypes.
- If you aren't prepared for it, it "can lead to really confusing bugs".
- His mitigation: add ESLint and turn on the `no-redeclare` rule from typescript-eslint.

chunks.heading: Implicit index signatures
chunks.text:
- Type aliases have an implicit index signature (Matt describes it as `Record<PropertyKey, unknown>`). Interfaces don't. So object types declared with `type` are assignable to types with an index signature, but interfaces aren't.
- The error looks like: "Index signature for type 'string' is missing in type 'x'".
- Example:
  - `interface KnownAttributes { x: number; y: number }`
  - `type RecordType = Record<string, number>`
  - Assigning a `KnownAttributes` value to `RecordType` fails with "Index signature for type 'string' is missing in type 'KnownAttributes'".
- Why it errors: an interface could later be extended, for example with a property that doesn't match the `string` key or `number` value.
- Two fixes:
  - Add an explicit index signature to the interface: `[index: string]: unknown;`
  - Change it to `type KnownAttributes = { x: number; y: number }`, which then assigns to `Record<string, number>` fine.
- Matt's reaction: "Isn't that strange!"

chunks.heading: Quick rules summary
chunks.text:
- Use types by default until you need a specific interface feature like `extends`.
- Interfaces can't express unions, mapped types, or conditional types. Types can express any type.
- Interfaces can use `extends`. Types can't, though intersections with `&` give a similar result.
- For objects that inherit from each other, use interfaces. `extends` makes the type checker run slightly faster than `&`.
- Same-named interfaces in the same scope merge, which can cause unexpected bugs.
- Type aliases have an implicit index signature that interfaces lack, which comes up occasionally.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt explains why he likes the idea of enums but won't recommend TypeScript's implementation: numeric enums generate reverse mappings and accept raw numbers, mixed enums are allowed, and enums are nominally typed, breaking the "JavaScript with types" ideal. If you must use them, use string enums only.

chunks.heading: TypeScript enums: the three kinds and how they differ
chunks.text:
- TypeScript lets you declare three kinds of enum values: numeric (`Draft = 0`), string (`Draft = "Draft"`), and inferred (`Draft` alone, which becomes 0, 1, 2...).
- Matt likes enums as a concept and "would really like JavaScript to have them", but TypeScript's implementation is "weird enough" that he does not recommend them.
- Inferred enums are numeric enums with the values left implicit, so they inherit every numeric-enum quirk.

chunks.heading: Numeric enums generate a two-way mapping; string enums do not
chunks.text:
- For `enum PackStatus { Draft = 0, Approved = 1, Shipped = 2 }`, `Object.keys(PackStatus)` returns 6 entries: `[0, "Draft", 1, "Approved", 2, "Shipped"]`.
- The cause: TypeScript emits both a value-to-key and a key-to-value mapping for numeric enums.
- String enums skip the reverse mapping, so `Object.keys` gives the expected 3 keys: `["Draft", "Approved", "Shipped"]`.
- Matt's takeaway: the two kinds produce different runtime objects, so iterating over an enum behaves differently depending on its type.

chunks.heading: Numeric enums accept raw numbers; string enums do not
chunks.text:
- With a string enum, a function taking `status: PackStatus` rejects the raw string. `logStatus("Draft")` errors with "Argument of type '"Draft"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'PackStatus'". Matt calls this "correctly!"
- With a numeric enum, the same function accepts a raw number: `logStatus(0)` raises no error. Matt's reaction in the post: "WHAT?"
- Net effect: numeric enums leak their underlying number type, so the type check does not enforce use of the enum values.

chunks.heading: Mixing string and numeric members in one enum
chunks.text:
- TypeScript allows a single enum to mix string and numeric members, for example `Draft = "Draft"`, `Approved = 2`, and `Shipped` inferred as 3.
- Matt calls this "hilarious" and says plainly: "Don't do this."

chunks.heading: Enums are nominally typed, which breaks "JavaScript with types"
chunks.text:
- Matt's most subjective complaint: "I like my TypeScript to be just JavaScript with types. Enums feel like they break that rule."
- Enums are nominal rather than structural. One enum cannot stand in for another, even when the values are identical. `PackStatus2.Draft = "Draft"` is rejected where `PackStatus` is expected, with "Argument of type 'PackStatus2' is not assignable to parameter of type 'PackStatus'".
- This holds even when the second enum references the first: `enum PackStatus2 { Draft = PackStatus.Draft }` still errors.
- This is out of step with how the rest of TypeScript works, where compatibility is based on shape.

chunks.heading: Open bugs and the cost of the implementation
chunks.text:
- At the time of writing, there were 71 open issues labelled as bugs related to enums in the TypeScript repo.
- Matt has "heard hints from the TS team" that many of these are uncloseable because of the way enums are implemented.

chunks.heading: What Matt does about enums in practice
chunks.text:
- In an existing codebase, if he sees an enum he is unlikely to rip it out. If it uses inferred values, he will probably make the values explicit.
- He would not add an enum to a fresh codebase.
- If you are desperate to use enums, he strongly recommends string enums only: "They're explicit, behave more like enums, and look more like their transpiled code."
- His preferred alternative is `as const` objects used as JavaScript-style enums, covered in the "Deriving Types" chapter of his book *Total TypeScript Essentials*, in the section on using `as const` for JavaScript-style enums.
- Related post on the site: TypeScript 5.8 ships the `--erasableSyntaxOnly` flag, which disables enums, namespaces and parameter properties to enforce pure type annotations.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock argues that 'generic' is not a noun in TypeScript. There are generic types, functions and classes, which declare type parameters and receive type arguments. Using precise vocabulary makes generics easier to learn and teach.

chunks.heading: Generic is an adjective: the vocabulary of type arguments and type parameters
chunks.text:
Matt argues that "there is no such thing as a 'generic'". Generics trip people up because "generic" is treated as a noun when it is an adjective.

- Valid phrases: generic types, generic functions, generic classes.
- You cannot "pass", "declare" or "infer" a generic.
- The angle-bracket syntax looks like "a generic", but it appears on functions, function calls, types and type declarations, so the word is too overloaded to point at one thing. That overload is why the concept is hard to grasp.
- His fix: remove the noun from your vocabulary and use "type argument" and "type parameter" instead.
- One concession: the plural "generics" is too ingrained to remove. He treats it as shorthand for "generic types, generic functions and generic classes".

His definition: "**generic** - _adj_: a type, function, or class that declares one or more type parameters."

chunks.heading: Type arguments: what you pass in
chunks.text:
A type argument works like a function argument. You can pass it to a function, class or type.

- `useState<string>()` does not pass "a generic". It passes the type argument `string`.
- `Record<string, number>` receives two type arguments: `string` is the first, `number` is the second.
- Not everything accepts type arguments:
  - `PropertyKey<string>` errors with "Type 'PropertyKey' is not generic."
  - `encodeURIComponent<string>()` errors with "Expected 0 type arguments, but got 1."
  - `new Event<string>()` gives the same "Expected 0 type arguments, but got 1" error.
- What decides whether something can receive type arguments is whether it declares type parameters.

chunks.heading: Type parameters: what you declare
chunks.text:
A type parameter works like a function parameter. It declares that a type, function or class can receive a type argument.

- In `type Maybe<T> = T | null | undefined;`, `Maybe` declares one type parameter, `T`.
- Because `T` is declared, `Maybe` must be given a type argument. Writing `type Example = Maybe;` errors with "Generic type 'Maybe' requires 1 type argument(s)."
- `Maybe` is therefore a generic type.
- `PropertyKey` is not generic. The compiler's own error says "Type 'PropertyKey' is not generic."
- Matt's summary: generic types are simply types that declare type parameters.

chunks.heading: Generic functions and generic classes
Inferring type arguments from runtime arguments
chunks.text:
Generic functions and generic classes behave differently from generic types. `myFunc()` and `new MyClass()` raise no error without a type argument, but a bare `Maybe` does.

- Matt's explanation: if you don't pass a type argument to a generic function or class, TypeScript tries to "infer it from the runtime arguments".
- A simplified declaration of `useState`:

```ts
declare function useState<T>(
  initial?: T
): [T, (newValue: T) => void];
```

- It takes `T` as a type parameter and returns a tuple of `T` and an updater function.
- `useState("Hello!")` infers `T` as `string`, so `message` is `string`.
- `useState(1)` infers `T` as `number`, so `id` is `number`.
- Inference needs a runtime argument to work from. With none, the type argument has to be passed explicitly.
- Generic types have no runtime arguments to infer from, which is why they always require explicit type arguments.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock argues that "generics" is really three separate concepts: passing types to types, passing types to functions, and inferring types from function arguments. Splitting them apart makes generics easier to learn. Type functions like DataShape<T> remove repetition, and inference removes the need to pass types by hand.

chunks.heading: Three separate things people call "generics"
chunks.text:
Matt argues that what developers lump together as "generics" in TypeScript is really three separate concepts:

- Passing types to types, e.g. `Partial<{ id: string; name: string }>`
- Passing types to functions, e.g. `new Set<string>()`
- Inferring types from arguments passed to functions, e.g. `objKeys({ a: 1, b: 2 })` giving `("a" | "b")[]`

He sums it up with one example of each: `DataShape<T>`, `createSet<string>()` and `useState(0)`. Separating them is what makes generics easier to learn.

chunks.heading: Passing types to types: the "type function"
Passing types to functions
Inferring types from arguments
Constraining and typing a generic with `objKeys`
Where Matt points learners next
chunks.text:
- If the post "went over your head", he sends beginners to the free TypeScript Beginners tutorial on Total TypeScript.
- To go deeper into patterns, he points to the Total TypeScript Pro Workshops.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock explains why library authors should test their types and lays out three approaches: vitest's type-testing APIs, a hand-rolled Expect/Equal helper plus ts-expect-error run through tsc, and the tsd library. He notes that type testing is rarely worth it in application code but critical for widely consumed libraries.

chunks.heading: Three ways Matt tests TypeScript types
chunks.text:
- Matt argues that if you work on library code, you should test your types. Types are a crucial part of the API you expose to users, so you want to be sure the type-level logic works.
- He says testing types is rarely worth it in application development.
- His closing rule: for any library consumed by many people, learning to test types, and getting good at it, is "critical".
- He lists three approaches: vitest, a hand-rolled setup, and `tsd`.

chunks.heading: Testing types with vitest
Rolling your own with Expect and Equal
Asserting that something errors with @ts-expect-error
The tsd library
chunks.text:
- Matt points to `tsd` (github.com/SamVerschueren/tsd) as "a really nice library" for testing types.
- He describes it as pretty similar to the vitest runner, but it bundles everything in and is nice to work with.
- He says he has less experience with it, but it is "definitely worth a look".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock argues that test code shouldn't be held to the same type strictness as application code. Tests must often pass wrong or partial values, forcing noisy `as any` or `as unknown as X` casts. He introduces shoehorn, a library that makes passing partial or wrong types first-class in tests.

chunks.heading: Why TypeScript tests need looser typing than application code
chunks.text:
Matt argues that test code does not need the same strictness as application code. A broken type in an app often means a user finds a bug in production. A broken type in a passing test is different:

- It might signal the test is wrong, so it is worth a check.
- Once verified as fine, fixing it feels like "meaningless busywork".
- In many codebases a huge share of the code is tests, so strict typing there adds a lot of friction for little safety.

chunks.heading: Testing wrong inputs forces unsafe assertions
chunks.text:
Some tests must check that a function behaves correctly when it receives the wrong thing. Matt's example is a function typed `(a: string): void` that throws `"Oh dear!"` when `typeof a !== "string"`. The test needs to pass a number.

- The usual approach is `func(123 as any)` inside `expect(() => ...).toThrow()`.
- If ESLint bans `any` in tests, the workaround is `123 as unknown as string`.
- Matt calls this double assertion "extremely un-ergonomic", for something "extremely common" in heavily tested codebases.

chunks.heading: Mocking large types where only a few properties matter
chunks.text:
Another frequent pain: testing a function that takes a type with many properties when the test only cares about a few.

- Typical case: external-library types such as `express` `Request` and `Response` in a handler `(req: Request, res: Response): void`.
- A test may only need `req.body`, but TypeScript demands the whole `Request`.
- The result is repeated `as unknown as Request` casts.
- Each test file also has to import the type just to cast to it, which Matt describes as "a thousand tiny cuts".

chunks.heading: `shoehorn`: a first-class way to pass the wrong type
Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock explains that TypeScript's method shorthand syntax is bivariant, letting a narrower parameter type slip through and cause runtime errors the compiler never flags. Declaring members as function properties makes the check strict, and the typescript-eslint method-signature-style rule enforces it.

chunks.heading: Method shorthand is bivariant, so it can cause runtime errors TypeScript misses
chunks.text:
- Matt says TypeScript has two ways to annotate a function on an object: method shorthand (`version1(param: string): void;`) and object property syntax (`version2: (param: string) => void;`).
- They look equivalent, but he argues method shorthand "should be avoided in almost all cases", crediting his friend Andarist's tweet for the insight.
- The core problem: method shorthand can produce runtime errors that TypeScript fails to catch.
- The cause is that method shorthand is bivariant: the method accepts a parameter type that is either narrower or wider than the declared one.
- Object property syntax only accepts a type that is wider or equal (the strict, contravariant check), which is what people expect.

chunks.heading: Worked example: the Dog / SmallDog runtime error
chunks.text:
- Matt declares `interface Dog { barkAt(dog: Dog): void; }` and `interface SmallDog extends Dog { whimper: () => void; }` ("Only small dogs whimper in this universe").
- With method shorthand, this compiles with no error:
  - `const brian: Dog = { barkAt(smallDog: SmallDog) { smallDog.whimper(); } };`
  - `brian` now narrows the parameter to `SmallDog` even though `Dog` says it accepts any `Dog`.
- A normal dog is then created: `const normalDog: Dog = { barkAt() {} };`
- Calling `brian.barkAt(normalDog)` fails at runtime, because `.whimper()` does not exist on `normalDog`.
- Matt's framing: "this is TypeScript failing to prevent a runtime error", and it is all because of method shorthand.
- The same bug occurs with `type` aliases, not just `interface`. His `type` version uses `type SmallDog = { whimper: () => void } & Dog;` and still compiles and still throws at runtime.

chunks.heading: The fix: use object property syntax
chunks.text:
- Change the declaration to `barkAt: (dog: Dog) => void;`.
- Now assigning `barkAt(dog: SmallDog) {}` to a `Dog` errors with: "Type '(dog: SmallDog) => void' is not assignable to type '(dog: Dog) => void'... Property 'whimper' is missing in type 'Dog' but required in type 'SmallDog'."
- Matt calls this "more in line with what we expect".
- The implementation can still be written with method shorthand or an arrow function. Only the type declaration's syntax matters for the check.

chunks.heading: Common misconception: this is not arrow functions vs function declarations
chunks.text:
- Matt says people often assume the two syntaxes are about arrow functions versus function declarations. They are not.
- Both type syntaxes accept either kind of implementation:
  - A `methodShorthand(param: string): void` member can be assigned an arrow function.
  - An `objectProperty: (param: string) => void` member can be assigned a function declaration.
- His example uses `function functionDeclaration(param: string) {}` and `const arrowFunction = (param: string) => {};` assigned across both member styles in an `Obj[]`.
- The difference is only in how the type is declared, which controls variance, not in what function form you pass in.

chunks.heading: Enforce it with the ESLint rule
chunks.text:
- Matt recommends `@typescript-eslint/method-signature-style`, configured as `"@typescript-eslint/method-signature-style": ["error", "property"]`.
- The rule enforces object property syntax for method signatures across a codebase.
- If you see "Shorthand method signature is forbidden. Use a function property instead.", this rule is why. In his words, "some clever person has set up this rule to prevent you from doing so."

chunks.heading: Legitimate use cases are rare
chunks.text:
- TypeScript keeps method shorthand because occasionally you want bivariance on a function declaration.
- Matt admits he is "not quite sure" what those reasons are.
- He points to Michael Arnaldi, one of the authors of EffectTS, who had a good read on the situation in a Twitter thread.
- Net position: default to object property syntax, and treat method shorthand as something to avoid unless you have a specific reason for bivariance.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock argues that knowing TypeScript means combining its pieces into patterns. He walks through branded types for validation boundaries, declare global for typing globals, type predicates and assertion functions for narrowing, and classes for builder-style library design.

chunks.heading: Branded types as validation boundaries
chunks.text:
Matt presents branded types as one of four essential TypeScript patterns, a pattern that separates "using TypeScript" from "knowing TypeScript". Branded types assign different "labels" to values.

- Example: `type Password = Brand<string, 'Password'>`.
- A function like `takesInPassword(password: Password)` errors when passed a plain string such as `'4123123'`.
- It does not error when the value is branded: `'4123123' as Password`.
- The `Password` type can only be satisfied by a value that has been branded as `Password`.
- This creates validation boundaries in the app's code: validate that something is a valid password once, then safely pass it around the application.

chunks.heading: Typing globals with `declare global`
Type predicates for narrowing
Assertion functions
Classes and the builder pattern
Why classes still matter in library code
chunks.text:
Matt says classes are often misaligned and misunderstood, and anticipates the objection: "I thought we used hooks now??"

- His position: "when you're writing TS in library-land, classes are a force of pragmatic utility that you can't sleep on."
- The distinction is between application code (where hooks dominate) and library code (where classes enable patterns like builders and self-narrowing assertion methods).

chunks.heading: Shared patterns as a team advantage
chunks.text:
Matt argues that having a shared set of core patterns is "an absolute super power for any team". The docs teach the pieces (generic functions, conditional types, type helpers), but developers in the wild combine those pieces into patterns.

- The four patterns covered: branded types, globals, assertion functions and type predicates, and classes.
- He promotes his Advanced Patterns workshop, available as part of the Total TypeScript Core Volume, as the way to get a team onto these shared patterns.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt Pocock corrects a common misconception: TypeScript types are erased at compile time and have no runtime effect. He walks through types, type assertions and function parameters as examples, then covers the exceptions (enums, namespaces, parameter properties) and why TypeScript's modern philosophy is to only add types to JavaScript.

chunks.heading: TypeScript types are erased at compile time and leave no runtime trace
chunks.text:
- Matt addresses a common misconception from people new to TypeScript: that its types exist at runtime. He says they don't.
- The belief feels natural to developers coming from other strongly-typed languages, where types are a fundamental part of the language and influence runtime behavior.
- TypeScript is designed to compile down to JavaScript, which has no type system. Types exist only to help catch errors at compile time.
- Matt notes you will have "thousands of lines of type declarations" in a program, yet none appear in the emitted JavaScript.
- Types and interfaces such as `Person` and `Animal` vanish from the transpiled output, leaving only the object literals.

chunks.heading: Type assertions do not check anything at runtime
chunks.text:
- Type assertions tell TypeScript you know more about a value than it does, but they leave no runtime code.
- Asserting that a value is a `number` doesn't make it one. TypeScript trusts the assertion, and if the value is actually a string, you get a runtime error.
- Matt gives this as the reason assertions are discouraged in TypeScript: they can cause runtime errors if you're not careful.

chunks.heading: Function parameter types give no runtime guarantee
chunks.text:
- Types on a function's parameters describe the expected shape, but don't ensure the function is called with the right arguments.
- In his `add` example, the emitted JavaScript contains no extra code to validate arguments.
- The practical takeaway: data crossing a boundary (user input, network responses, `JSON.parse`) isn't checked by type annotations alone, since the annotations are erased.

chunks.heading: The exceptions: enums, namespaces and parameter properties
chunks.text:
- Matt names three features that do have a runtime representation: enums, namespaces, and parameter properties. The emitted JavaScript contains real code for them.
- Most other TypeScript features disappear at runtime, but these three can be used in the running program.
- These features are old, added when JavaScript was seen as relatively stagnant and TypeScript was attractive for supplying missing features like enums, classes and namespaces.

chunks.heading: Why TypeScript no longer adds runtime features
chunks.text:
- JavaScript is now in a much healthier place: classes are built in, and modules are an improved version of namespaces.
- Matt notes that enums might arrive in JavaScript someday, citing a proposal by rbuckton (`github.com/rbuckton/proposal-enum`).
- TypeScript now sees its job as adding types to JavaScript, not adding new language features.
- Matt states that if enums, namespaces or parameter properties were proposed today, "they wouldn't be added to TypeScript."
- His rule of thumb: think of TypeScript as just adding types to JavaScript, with the exception of enums, namespaces and parameter properties.

chunks.heading: Related follow-ups Matt links to
chunks.text:
- `--erasableSyntaxOnly` (TypeScript 5.8): a flag that enforces pure type annotations by disabling enums, namespaces and parameter properties. This is the tooling expression of the "types only" rule of thumb.
- Node.js type stripping (Node 23): Node can run TypeScript by default, which fits with TypeScript being erasable type annotations over JavaScript.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Matt shows a generic Result<TResult, TError> discriminated union, modeled on Rust, as an alternative to try/catch. Checking result.success narrows to typed data or typed error, which makes error flow explicit in complicated imperative code.

chunks.heading: Generic Result type as a discriminated union
chunks.text:
Matt describes a `Result<TResult, TError>` type as "one really nice application of generic types". It has two type parameters and returns a discriminated union:

- Success branch: `success: true` with `data: TResult`
- Failure branch: `success: false` with `error: TError`

The `success` boolean is the discriminant, so checking it narrows the type to the right branch.

chunks.heading: Worked example: createRandomNumber
chunks.text:
His example function generates `Math.random()`, a number between 0 and 1.

- If the number is greater than 0.5, it returns `success: true` and `data: 123`.
- Otherwise it returns `success: false` and `error: new Error("Something went wrong")`.
- The return type passes `number` as the data type and `Error` as the error type.

At the call site, checking `result.success` narrows `result.data` to `number`. Inside each branch of the function, TypeScript enforces the correct shape. If he changes the data type to `string`, the compiler errors with "type number is not assignable to type string" unless the returned data matches.

chunks.heading: Why this beats try/catch by default
chunks.text:
Matt notes this is how Rust handles errors, and says it means "you don't have to do any try-catching". He concedes you might still need some try/catch, but as the default way to check for errors it is annoying for two reasons:

- The error you get back in a catch block is not type safe, as covered in earlier exercises in the workshop.
- It leads to complicated logic where errors are caught at certain boundaries and "you're not quite sure where they're coming from".

chunks.heading: Explicit control flow
chunks.text: With a Result type, the flow is explicit: ask "is my result a success?" If so, proceed; if not, handle the error. Matt calls this "really, really nice for certain situations when you have really complicated imperative code flow". He frames it as a fit for particular situations rather than a universal replacement for exceptions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Describes Matt Pocock's code-review agent skill, which reviews a diff along two independent axes (Standards and Spec), each in its own sub-agent. Covers prerequisites, the Fowler smell baseline, and known pitfalls: name clash, runaway sub-agents, self-review bias, and non-convergence.

chunks.heading: Why Matt splits code review into Standards and Spec axes
chunks.text:
- Matt's `code-review` skill reviews the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point you name (a commit, branch, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`) along two axes.
- **Standards** asks "Is it built right?" It checks whether the code follows how this repo writes code.
- **Spec** asks "Is it the right thing?" It checks whether the code does what the originating issue or spec asked for.
- Each axis runs in its own sub-agent, so neither sees the other's reasoning.
- The skill never merges or re-ranks the two axes. The report ends with a worst issue per axis and declines to name a single winner.
- The reasoning: a change can pass one axis and fail the other.
  - Code that follows every convention but implements the wrong thing passes Standards and fails Spec.
  - Code that does exactly what the ticket asked but breaks the repo's conventions does the reverse.
  - A blended verdict lets the passing axis hide the failing one.

chunks.heading: How the Standards axis works: the repo overrides, smells are the fallback
chunks.text:
- The design avoids a generic review skill that does not know your standards. Such a skill flags what is deliberate in your codebase and misses the invariants it depends on.
- The repo's own documentation (`CODING_STANDARDS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and the like) is the primary source, and "the repo always overrides".
- The smell baseline sits underneath and applies when the repo documents nothing. It is twelve smells from chapter 3 of Fowler's *Refactoring*:
  - Mysterious Name, Duplicated Code, Feature Envy, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession, Repeated Switches
  - Shotgun Surgery, Divergent Change, Speculative Generality, Message Chains, Middle Man, Refused Bequest
- Smells are labelled heuristics ("possible Feature Envy"), never hard violations. Each states what the smell is and how to fix it, so a finding comes with a fix attached.
- Documented breaches can be hard violations. Smells are always judgement calls.
- Every Standards finding cites either the standards file and rule, or the named smell plus the hunk.
- Both axes skip anything the linter already enforces.

chunks.heading: How the Spec axis finds the spec
chunks.text:
- The Spec axis needs a spec that exists and is findable. It looks in this order:
  1. Issue references in commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, a GitLab `!67`), fetched through the tracker doc.
  2. A path passed in as an argument.
  3. A spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch or feature name.
  4. Asking you.
- Step 1 depends on the tracker doc written by `setup-matt-pocock-skills`. Without it the axis still works if you hand it a path.
- With no spec at all, the skill skips the Spec sub-agent and the report says "no spec available" rather than inventing requirements.
- The Spec axis reports missing or partial requirements, scope creep, and requirements implemented wrongly. Every finding quotes a line of the spec.
- A vague spec makes this axis vague, because `to-spec` and `to-tickets` produce the document it checks against.

chunks.heading: Guardrails on starting a review
chunks.text:
- You must supply the fixed point. If you do not, the skill asks rather than guessing.
- Before spawning anything, it checks that the ref resolves and the diff is not empty. A mistyped branch name fails in front of you instead of inside two sub-agents.
- It diffs `<fixed-point>...HEAD`. The three-dot form measures from the merge-base and excludes staged and working-tree changes.
- It does not review uncommitted work. Commit first, then review, then amend or add a fixup.
- Signs it is working:
  - It refuses to start on a bad ref or empty diff.
  - The report arrives as separate `## Standards` and `## Spec` blocks, not one merged list.
  - The closing summary gives a worst issue per axis and no overall winner.

chunks.heading: Known problems: the name clash and runaway sub-agents
chunks.text:
- **Name clash.** Claude Code ships its own `/code-review`, which hunts bugs in the diff (null paths, races, off-by-one). Matt's checks spec compliance and repo standards. This is the most reported problem and is not fixed.
  - With the plugin marketplace, every skill gets a `mattpocock-skills:` prefix and the built-in becomes hard to reach at the unqualified name.
  - With a plain skills install, the local file wins and shadows the built-in.
  - One answer: remove Claude Code's built-in skills entirely, which also saves context.
  - Matt calls the shadowing arguably a harness bug, since "a skill author should be free to name a skill anything".
  - Another answer: fork the skill to a new name and drop `code-review` from the managed set. `npx skills update` undoes edits to the frontmatter or a renamed directory. Note the commit you forked from so you can re-sync by hand.
- **Recursive sub-agents.** The Standards and Spec prompts do not forbid delegation, so a sub-agent can re-invoke `/code-review` and fan out again. One report reached more than 50 agents.
  - The fork fix is one line appended to both sub-agent briefs: "Do not invoke `/code-review` or spawn additional agents: perform this review directly."
  - Some prefer a harness-level guard so every skill inherits it. Neither is in the shipped skill yet.
  - If you run it unattended, watch the agent count.

chunks.heading: When and how to run it, and how far to trust it
chunks.text:
- **Use a fresh session.** An agent reviewing in the authoring session has every assumption that shaped the code in its context. A reader's line that Matt cites: "Same context reviewing itself isn't review, it's confirmation bias with a slash command."
  - That is why people want `implement` without its built-in review step, which runs inside the session that wrote the diff.
  - The independent version is to invoke `/code-review` yourself from a clean session.
- **Per ticket or at the end.** The skill does not decide for you.
  - Per ticket keeps each diff small enough for the Spec axis to have one clear spec. This is the mode `implement` uses.
  - Batching to the end of a branch catches interactions between tickets.
  - If unsure, review per ticket and run one final pass against the branch point.
- **Findings are hypotheses, not evidence.** The skill combines the two reports as they are, or lightly cleaned, and does not re-verify each claim against the files. A finding can cite the wrong location or overstate impact. Read the citation on each finding before acting. Mandatory citations (a standards rule, a smell plus its hunk, or a spec line) are what make findings checkable.
- **It never converges.** Each fix adds new code to review, and the judgement-call half of Standards varies run to run. Treat a pass as a list of leads, act on the ones with a cited rule behind them, then stop. "Do not run it in a loop until it comes back clean, because it never will."

chunks.heading: Where code-review sits in the skills chain
chunks.text:
- Install with `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills --skill=code-review`, then type `/code-review` in your coding agent.
- Matt places it near the tail of the build chain: `grill-with-docs → to-spec → to-tickets → implement → code-review → retro`. It also stands alone on any branch or PR.
- `implement` is the closest neighbour. It drives the build and calls `code-review` as its closing review before committing. `implement-spec` does the same once over the whole integration branch.
- `retro` comes after and tunes it. When a session shows the review missing a class of mistake, `retro` proposes the check or the `CODING_STANDARDS.md` rule the Standards axis then reads.
- `pr` writes the pull request body once reviewed work goes up.
- Where to reach for something else:
  - Bug hunting in a diff: Claude Code's built-in review.
  - Nothing written yet, test-first: `tdd`.
  - Whole codebase drift: `improve-codebase-architecture`.
  - Something broken, cause unknown: `diagnosing-bugs`.
- `ask-matt` routes across the whole set when you are unsure which skill fits.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Describes Matt Pocock's codebase-design skill, a reference glossary (module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality) plus four principles for designing deep modules. Covers its limits as a reference rather than a process, and how it relates to neighbouring skills and agent workflows.

chunks.heading: Skill vs. process: what `/codebase-design` is
chunks.text:
Matt's `codebase-design` skill is a reference glossary, not a process. It fixes the vocabulary for designing modules: module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality. It runs no loop, produces no artifact and never stops to ask a question.

Matt says to know this before invoking it. If you point a session at a skill with no process and no stopping rule and say "go", the agent invents a process.

- He recommends invoking a driver skill (`/grill-with-docs`, `/improve-codebase-architecture` or `/tdd`) and using `codebase-design` as its vocabulary.
- The skill is model-invoked and describes itself as vocabulary, but nothing in it hard-stops an agent from treating it as a runnable process.
- A reported failure (issue #449): told to "resume in /codebase-design and drive the open decisions", an agent picked the closest thing to a process, the parallel sub-agents in `DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md`. It re-explored code a previous session had already mapped and burned about 100k tokens before asking anything.
- The skill has none of a driver skill's guardrails: checkpoints, one question at a time, no auto-advance.
- It's working if invoking it does not start a session. If the agent begins reading files and proposing refactors from `/codebase-design` alone, it has mistaken the reference for a driver.

chunks.heading: The vocabulary and the words it bans
chunks.text:
The glossary is the skill. Each term is defined against the others, and each has a loose substitute that Matt bans.

| Term | Meaning | Don't say |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Module | Anything with an interface and an implementation. Deliberately scale-agnostic: a function, a class, a package, a slice spanning tiers | unit, component, service |
| Interface | Everything a caller must know to use it correctly: the type signature plus invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required config, performance characteristics | API, signature |
| Depth | Leverage at the interface: how much behaviour a caller or a test can exercise per unit of interface they have to learn | none |
| Seam | Michael Feathers' term: a place you can alter behaviour without editing in that place. It is the location of an interface, and where to put it is a separate decision from what goes behind it | boundary |
| Adapter | A concrete thing satisfying an interface at a seam. It names a role, not a kind of thing: an in-memory fake and a Postgres repo are both adapters | none |
| Leverage | What callers get from depth: more capability per unit of interface learned | none |
| Locality | What maintainers get from depth: changes, bugs and verification stay in one place, so one fix covers every caller | none |

- **Deep** means a lot of behaviour behind a small interface. **Shallow** means the interface is nearly as complex as the implementation.
- Matt deliberately does not define depth as the ratio of implementation lines to interface lines (Ousterhout's own definition). That metric rewards padding the implementation, so the skill uses depth-as-leverage instead.
- Discussing an interface should cover invariants, ordering and error modes, not only the type signature.
- The design conversation should stop producing "component", "service" and "boundary" and start producing "module", "interface" and "seam".

chunks.heading: The four principles
chunks.text:
- **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be built internally from small swappable parts that callers never see. A module can have internal seams its own tests use, and one external seam at its interface.
- **The deletion test.** Imagine deleting the module. If complexity disappears, the module was a pass-through. If it reappears across N callers, the module was hiding real complexity.
- **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test past the interface, the module is the wrong shape.
- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't cut a seam until something varies across it. A single-adapter seam is just indirection.
- A proposed seam should come with a second adapter named, not just the first one.

chunks.heading: When to use it, and which skill fits instead
chunks.text:
Matt's rule is to reach for `codebase-design` when you already know which code you're redesigning and need to think about its shape: where the seam goes, how small the interface can get, whether an extraction removes complexity from its callers. It also settles arguments about what a design word means.

| The problem | The skill |
| --- | --- |
| The shape of one module: its interface, seam, depth | `codebase-design` |
| The words of the domain ("account" means three things; two people mean different things by "cancellation") | `domain-modeling` |
| You don't yet know which module to redesign | `improve-codebase-architecture` (the survey that finds candidates) |
| You want the design argued with, not just named | `grilling` |
| A concrete behaviour to build, with tests that survive a refactor | `tdd` |

- `codebase-design` is a reach-for-it-anytime standalone and the vocabulary layer under the engineering skills, not a step in a chain.
- `domain-modeling` is its closest neighbour, covering the problem domain's words rather than the module's shape. Naming a deep module well needs both.
- `improve-codebase-architecture` writes every deepening candidate in this glossary, so it finds the module and you design it in this skill's words.
- `tdd` now points at this skill when the open question is the shape of the interface. `tdd` still owns "seam" as the boundary you test at; this skill owns the module shape behind it. For a long time `tdd` had no such pointer, because v1.0 removed its inline deep-module notes without adding one.

chunks.heading: Enforcing deep modules in TypeScript
chunks.text:
The skill defines what a deep module is. It says nothing about stopping a stray import from reaching past the interface.

- Issue #458 states the problem: "without linting or clear guardrails, humans and LLMs alike will start making it messy over time."
- The answer in that thread gave three options:
  - Wrap it in a class or IIFE, and accept that the class gets enormous.
  - Make it a package in a monorepo, and accept the monorepo tooling.
  - Use a linter like dependency-cruiser to forbid imports that bypass the interface.
- Matt's ranking of the mechanisms: Effect is the best, dependency-cruiser the second-best.
- A `setup-ts-deep-modules` skill sits in the repo's `in-progress/` bucket. It lays down a `src/packages/<name>/index.ts` convention but is a beta-channel skill with no docs page and ships no lint rule.

chunks.heading: It is not a file-structure convention
chunks.text:
People repeatedly push for folders, barrel files or feature slices as the implementation of deep modules. Matt's position has not changed.

- Issue #95 proposed a formalised fractal-tree file structure. His reply: "deep modules are about the design of the interface and accessing through a strict interface, no matter what the file system looks like. It seems perfectly possible that you could have shallow modules with this approach."
- On #458: "I think you might be tying the concept of modules too closely to the file system. The file system can certainly be a useful hint to the shape of modules, but there's no need to use the file system in the construction of deep modules."
- That is why **module** is defined as scale-agnostic.

chunks.heading: Supporting files, history and glossary scope
chunks.text:
Two supporting files are read on demand rather than up front.

- **`DEEPENING.md`** classifies a candidate's dependencies into four categories: in-process, local-substitutable, remote-but-owned, true-external. The category decides how you test the deepened module across its seam.
- **`DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md`** starts parallel sub-agents to produce three or more radically different interfaces for the same module, then compares them on depth, locality and seam placement. The technique comes from Ousterhout.
  - It says "spawn 3+ sub-agents in parallel using the Agent tool", and "Agent" is a Claude Code tool name.
  - Other harnesses, including Codex, may have no tool with that name, so the parallel-design phase is less portable than the skill's metadata suggests (issue #564, open).

History and scope:

- This skill replaced `design-an-interface` and took over its content, so nothing is missing.
- A separate `/interface-design` skill has been requested, but this skill already covers that deep-module/thin-interface philosophy and no separate skill is planned.
- Proposed glossary additions, both open and unmerged:
  - Issue #180: Parnas's module secrets and Page-Jones's connascence, as a naming layer for what is leaking across a seam.
  - Issue #303: progressive disclosure inside the implementation, so a module that is deep at its public interface also has structure inside it.
- The shipped glossary is small on purpose. Consistent language is the whole point, and a term nobody uses consistently is worse than no term.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Explains Matt's /tdd agent skill: build one failing test at a time at pre-agreed seams, write just enough code, and avoid three anti-patterns (implementation-coupled, tautological, horizontal slicing). Also covers why refactoring was dropped, mocking rules, and honest limits of agents following the loop.

chunks.heading: Skill identity and purpose
chunks.text:
- `/tdd` is Matt's skill for building a feature or fixing a bug test-first. It runs one failing test, then just enough code to pass it, then the next behaviour.
- It carries the standards that make that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, what mocks are for, and three anti-patterns that make a suite worthless.
- It is a reference, not a driver. It holds the rules of the loop, and something else (the user, or the `implement` skill) runs the session that applies them.
- Install: `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills --skill=tdd`, then type `/tdd` in the coding agent. The agent can also reach for it automatically when a task fits, or when the user says "red-green-refactor".
- It requires `codebase-design` to be installed. v1.0 deleted `tdd`'s own deep-module and interface-design notes in favour of that shared skill. The skill is stateless and writes no files.

chunks.heading: When Matt reaches for /tdd, and when not
chunks.text:
- Use it when there is a concrete behaviour to build, with an input and an observable output, and the tests need to survive a refactor. Examples: business logic, a request/response contract, a transformation, validation.
- If the behaviour isn't pinned down yet, go to `to-spec`, which also agrees the test seams before any code is written.
- If the question is really the shape of the interface, go to `codebase-design`.
- If there is a spec or tickets and the whole build should be run, use `implement`, which drives `tdd` per ticket.
- Config, wiring, glue, type annotations and straight CRUD delegation fit poorly. This is a known open gap (issue #746): the skill decides where seams go, but not whether a change is worth the loop at all.
- Running it on a change with no independent source of truth to assert against yields a test that restates the implementation, which is the tautological anti-pattern. Until the issue closes, the user makes that call or writes the rule into `CLAUDE.md`.

chunks.heading: The loop: red-green, vertical slices, tracer bullet
chunks.text:
- Red-green means write the failing test, then only enough code to pass it. Do not write code for the test after next.
- There is no refactor phase. The skill dropped it in June 2026 because agents almost never performed it, and because review and implementation work better as separate sessions. Refactoring now belongs to `code-review`, which carries the Fowler smell baseline. `refactoring.md` left `tdd` at the same time.
- Vertical slice: one test at one seam, then the minimal implementation, then repeat. The first cycle is a "tracer bullet" that proves a single path end to end.
- The opposite is horizontal slicing: all tests first, then all code. Bulk-written tests verify "imagined" behaviour. They check the shape of things rather than what a user does, and they commit to a test structure before the implementation is understood.
- The description still says "red-green-refactor" although the body no longer refactors (issue #589, open). The phrase still fires the skill. What you get is red-green.

chunks.heading: Pre-agreed seams
chunks.text:
- A seam is the public boundary where behaviour is observed without reaching inside.
- The rule has no exceptions: no test goes at an unconfirmed seam. Before any test exists, the skill names the public boundaries it intends to test at and stops for confirmation.
- The reason is that testing effort is finite. This step spends it on the critical paths instead of every edge case.
- In the full chain, seams are agreed earlier during `to-spec`. Matt's wording: "`/tdd` is told to only work at pre-agreed test seams, `/code-review` checks that only agreed-upon test seams were used." Invoked on its own, `tdd` asks the user directly.
- Known friction (issue #607, the most reported): the prompt lists candidate seams by name only, with nothing about what each catches or misses. No fix has shipped. The workaround is to ask the agent for trade-offs first, for example what a component-level seam misses that an integration seam catches, and how much slower it is. This is also why the chain agrees seams up front in `to-spec`, where the whole feature is in view.

chunks.heading: Three anti-patterns and the rule on mocks
chunks.text:
- Implementation-coupled: the test breaks when an internal function is renamed though behaviour didn't change. Tells: mocked internal collaborators, asserted call counts, database queries used to verify instead of the interface.
- Tautological: the expected value is computed the way the code computes it, so the test passes by construction. Expected values must come from elsewhere: a known-good literal, a worked example, or the spec.
- Horizontal slicing: a batch of tests lands before any implementation.
- Mocks are for system boundaries only: external APIs, time, randomness, and sometimes the filesystem or database. Never mock your own modules.

chunks.heading: How to tell it's working
chunks.text:
- It stops and names the seams it intends to test at, and waits, before any test file exists.
- One test appears, goes red, gets just enough code to pass, and only then does the next test appear, not a batch of tests then a batch of code.
- Test names read as capabilities ("user can checkout with valid cart"), not internals ("checkout calls paymentService.process").
- Assertion expected values are literals traceable to the spec.
- Renaming an internal function breaks nothing in the suite.
- Mocks appear only at external boundaries (the payment API, the clock), never around your own modules.

chunks.heading: Agent compliance, browser tests, and ticket scope
chunks.text:
- Agents sometimes write the implementation before the test. One user pushed the model and got: "I knew the skill said 'one test at a time, watch it fail for the right reason'. I read it. I just defaulted to my normal habit."
- Matt's stance is that no instruction makes an agent comply 100% of the time, and stricter wording restricts the agent's creativity for little gain. The loop is worth running even when followed loosely, because results are still better overall. If strict adherence matters for a slice, watch the run rather than trusting the skill to enforce it.
- Browser or end-to-end tests first is usually a bad idea. One user saw the agent write a Playwright test first, then spend a long loop re-running it and conclude the test was broken for a feature that didn't exist yet. Browser tests are slow enough that the red-green feedback loop stops paying for itself. The fix is to state in the repo's `CLAUDE.md` that browser tests come after the behaviour works.
- Run against one ticket, `tdd` has no view of the issue graph and can propose work belonging to a sibling ticket (issue #129). Passing the spec alongside the ticket helps, and right-sizing the tickets helps more.

chunks.heading: Where /tdd fits in the skill chain
chunks.text:
- Chain: `grill-with-docs → to-spec → to-tickets → implement → code-review → retro`. `tdd` runs inside the build step and is not a step of its own.
- `to-spec` agrees test seams up front, `implement` drives `tdd` per ticket, and `code-review` checks afterwards that only agreed seams were used and owns the refactoring `tdd` no longer does.
- `/tdd` does not replace `/implement` or the course's `/do-work`. `/tdd` documents the methodology, while `/implement` is a simple work→feedback→commit loop and the direct stand-in for `/do-work`. The old single `/do-work` step is now split across `/implement`, `/tdd` and `/code-review`. Asked which to run against a ticket, the answer is almost always `/implement`.
- `codebase-design` is the shared source of the seam and deep-module vocabulary `tdd` uses. `ask-matt` routes the user when unsure which skill fits.
- `tdd` can also be used on its own whenever there is a concrete behaviour to build and no full spec is in play.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Describes a skill that surveys a codebase for deepening opportunities (shallow modules that could become deep), writes a visual HTML report, and then grills you on the candidate you pick. It never changes code; it queues up refactors for a later spec-and-build flow.

chunks.heading: What the skill does and what it never touches
chunks.text:
- `/improve-codebase-architecture` surveys a codebase for "deepening opportunities": places where a shallow module (an interface nearly as complex as the thing it hides) could become a deep one.
- It writes the findings as one self-contained HTML report in the OS temp directory (`<tmpdir>/architecture-review-<timestamp>.html`), then grills Matt's reader through the one candidate they pick.
